articles.title: 'Palong-palo': Jeepney driver in trouble over 'trip to heaven' mode, LTFRB summons PUV operator
articles.summary: A passenger jeepney driver is now in deep trouble for the alleged “trip to heaven” mode in a viral video wherein the uploader and the netizens pointed out the possibility of illegal substance use.…

blocks.text: A passenger jeepney driver is now in deep trouble for the alleged “trip to heaven” mode in a viral video wherein the uploader and the netizens pointed out the possibility of illegal substance use.
“Palong-palo”, a netizen commented, referring to the alleged visible effects of illegal drugs use while the driver was plying a route on a busy road as seen in the viral video.

On Saturday, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) issued a show cause order (SCO) to the operator of the passenger jeepney to demand an explanation over what it described as disturbing content involving a public utility vehicle (PUV).

Acting LTFRB Chairman Atty. Greg G. Pua, Jr. said the investigation is intended to identify the driver and set the record straight on insinuations of the netizens of the possible illegal substance use as seen in the behavior in the viral video.

“This is really dangerous if the allegation is true, something that we in the LTFRB will not let pass. We assure the public that we will look into this case and part of our initial action is to ensure the driver involved will not be allowed to temporarily operate pending the result of the investigation,” said Pua.
In the viral video, the driver was seen unsafe driving practices and appeared to have been unmindful of the safety and comfort of the passengers.

Pua said the hearing was set on Sept. 10 to clear things up on the possibility of illegal drugs use as he noted that if the observation is true, the incident was a clear violation of the conditions set on the Certificate of Public Convenience (CPC).

As operators, he said they have the obligation to ensure that the drivers they would hire are not reckless drivers and are always in good mental and physical condition since what is at stake is not only the safety of the passengers but also other road users.
The viral video was monitored by the LTFRB Social Media Monitoring Team and was immediately acted upon by sending SCO to the registered operator of the passenger jeepney.

Pua stressed the importance of reporting any cases or incidents of abuses and violations of public utility drivers and operators, saying the LTFRB and the public are partners in ensuring a safe and comfortable public transportation.
In this case, he said the posting of the video led to the LTFRB acting on the matter.
He then urged the public to report similar cases and other road safety violation involving PUVs through the LTFRB Hotline 1342, and even via social media accounts.

articles.title: When school violence happens, the whole community needs to listen
articles.summary: Psychologists say young Filipinos need safe spaces to be vulnerable without judgement — and that starts with listening to children and their families, and giving the support within their communities

blocks.text: This is Part 2 of a two-part story. Read Part 1: Psychologists want us to rethink what we ask about school violence
When it comes to school violence, psychologist Jannah Trixie Cuevas said it’s the whole community that must be held responsible for what could’ve been done differently.

“When we talk about the whole community, it’s the schools for not having interventions about it. It could be the parents for not seeing the warning signs right away. It could be a lot of pressures that we don’t see, that are being put on the children.”

Hannah Pellejo Jara, CEO and founder of Sapphire Clinics East Inc.’s Aura Health Rehab, a Filipino-owned rehabilitation and psychological services network where Cuevas works, also points out that the issue isn’t always about negligence.

Jara, who has heard many different stories of troubled kids and distressed families, said socioeconomic factors affect not only the mental health of the child, but of entire families and communities, especially caregivers and breadwinners.

“I think a lot of the fatigue of the families is because [of financial issues, like they think], ‘I have to earn, I can’t take care of my child’…. So, their economic state is still a factor, them being stressed about money, and then affecting the child as well.”

The conflicts parents go through because of money, work, or relationship difficulties affect how much they’re able to be attentive to their kids. The questions then expand from asking how supported the children are within the family, to how supported the family is within their community.
“I think the more complex route that may take a longer time to address are the family dynamics, even the community dynamics,” Jara said. “How supported are the families?”

“When I say this, for example, here in the Philippines, if I can’t take care of my child, my neighbor is there, or my mother is there, my brother is there who can help me carry this emotional burden. But for example, for single parents, everything is a burden on you, right? So, we have cases of single parents here that we’ve seen that they cry after. They’re like, ‘No one is supporting me. I’m all alone. I can’t take care of my child.’ They already have guilt because they have to work.”
Aside from factors preventing parents from being there for their children physically, generation gaps tend to create emotional gaps within families as well.

“Based on the patterns that I’m seeing, parents have been comparing what’s happening to the kids nowadays to the time that they were kids,” Cuevas said. “There was a disconnection emotionally. Physically, most of the time they’re present, but emotionally, they’re absent.”

Fellow psychologist Arnel Sarte Jr. observed that this distance isn’t exactly because of a lack of trying on the parents’ part. The good intentions are there, but their expression of support and concern to their children can sometimes get lost in translation.

“Sometimes the support system thinks that they’re being helpful, with most parents telling their kids, ‘You can do it, just keep going.’ On the surface, when the child is doing okay, it’s a good validation. But for those kids that don’t even have the energy to keep moving forward, not knowing how they can do it, for them, it feels more like a responsibility when they hear, ‘keep going.’”

Dealing with kids struggling with depression and mental health issues also challenges parents to change how they make their kids feel loved. “It really depends on the state of the kids. They can take those words properly if they aren’t severely depressed, if they don’t feel like they’re completely alone, they can take that,” Sarte said.

“But what if they’re so severely depressed that just thinking already takes a toll on them? So if they’re told, ‘Don’t give up,’ they’re going to think, ‘How can I not give up? I don’t have the energy.’ So instead, make them feel that, ‘I’m here. You can lean on me.’ Ask them, ‘What do you want to eat? Is there anything you’re craving? Let’s eat.’ Simple ways like that can make them feel like they aren’t alone.”
That is ultimately what psychologists say young Filipinos need: safe spaces to be vulnerable without judgement, as well as support through loneliness.

“If the safe space is not available, if they don’t have a home, if they cannot communicate at their school, at least they should have someone inside the school or maybe someone that they can talk to, another person that they won’t feel judged,” Cuevas said.
“Now, everyone’s going through a lot of things already. Maybe just providing a safe space for a person, just listening to them without judging what they feel.”
Hand in hand with safe spaces, both children and family members would benefit from receiving psychoeducation on how to manage and regulate emotions and recognize difficult feelings.

Both Sarte and Jara also acknowledge how much damage bullying can inflict on a child and call on schools to intervene. Jara adds that social media usage significantly magnifies the impact of bullying on victims, and suggests that the Philippines follows the example of other countries like Australia to restrict the access of children below 16.

“It’s true what they say that social media contributes to mental health problems. For example, bullying. Before, when you were bullied in school, it was just in school. At home, it’s like, no matter what, you’re peaceful. Now, you’re being bullied in group chats or you’re being bullied on social media,” Jara said.

“So, all the time, it’s like the bullying is non-stop, and your outlet is also social media. It’s like this vicious cycle. At least for the parents, I think a low-hanging fruit will also be to really control the social media exposure of the children.”

But with all the questions that psychologists ask to look after the mental well-being of young Filipinos, their most pressing question is: what really happened during those school violence incidents? Why, after so long, do we know so little about the perpetrators and what drove them to commit fatal acts?

“And especially for the Tacloban case, it has been months, but there are no clear answers about what really caused those behaviors,” Cuevas said. “I think there was a lot of speculation, but no psychological evaluation right away. It was more of, okay, being told that a psychological evaluation needs to be done. But what was the result of the evaluation? That’s why there was no proper intervention set in place.”

blocks.caption: Tacloban school reopens after shooting, but trauma lingers

blocks.text: With so many questions, where are the answers? Why is no one answering them?

“It happened once already, but the only resolution was to hire more school counselors. But what really happened there? The next step would have been to prevent incidents like this, because if there really is a group of people really targeting teenagers in the Philippines about having that sense of violence, how can we prevent it if we haven’t pinpointed who or what organization that is?” added Cuevas.

To protect and save Filipino children from future fatal incidents, it is not enough for conversations around the recent school violence incidents to be centered around what should have been done in hindsight. It requires serious follow through of psychological evaluations, the effort to understand more deeply our country’s youth, and the urgency to be truly attentive to the needs of the children and their families within the communities.

It requires the entire community to acknowledge the shared responsibility we have towards the children, and to be willing to change our ways and ask better questions for the sake of their futures. – Rappler.com
Elise Suarez is a Rappler intern from Puerto Princesa City and a Humanities student of the University of Asia & the Pacific.

articles.title: La Mesa Dam nears overflow level amid heavy rains—PAGASA
articles.summary: The water level of La Mesa Dam in Quezon City rose to 79.81 meters on Saturday morning, Aug. 29, just 0.34 meters below its overflow elevation of 80.15 meters, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical…

blocks.text: (MB FILE PHOTO)

The water level of La Mesa Dam in Quezon City rose to 79.81 meters on Saturday morning, Aug. 29, just 0.34 meters below its overflow elevation of 80.15 meters, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said.
In its hydrological dam situationer issued at 10 a.m., PAGASA said a further increase in the dam’s water level was expected due to continued rainfall.
“The water level of La Mesa Dam as of 10:00 AM is 79.81 m, which is still below its overflow elevation of 80.15 m,” PAGASA said.
“However, due to the observed 24-hour rainfall of 137.5 mm and a forecast 24-hour rainfall of above 60 mm, a further increase in the water level is expected.”
The weather bureau warned that excess floodwater would flow directly into the Tullahan River should the dam reach its overflow level.

The agency said low-lying areas that may be affected include Fairview, Forest Hills Subdivision, Quirino Highway, Sta. Quiteria, and San Bartolome in Quezon City; Caloocan City; North Expressway and La Huerta Subdivision in Valenzuela City; and Malabon and Navotas.
“It should also be noted that aside from the outflow from the reservoir, continuous rainfall over the watershed may further increase the river water level,” PAGASA said.
Residents of the identified areas, particularly those living near riverbanks, were advised to take the necessary precautionary measures.
Earlier, PAGASA said the southwest monsoon, locally known as “habagat,” continued to affect Luzon and the Visayas.

articles.title: In Quake-Hit Kumamoto, Kids Back to School after Summer Break
articles.summary: Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Pref., Aug. 28 (Jiji Press)--Children returned to school after the summer break in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture on Friday, a month after a major earthquake struck the…

blocks.text: Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Pref., Aug. 28 (Jiji Press)--Children returned to school after the summer break in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture on Friday, a month after a major earthquake struck the southwestern Japan prefecture.
The second term started at 40 elementary, junior high schools and special- needs schools in the city.
Following the July 28 quake, which measured up to 7, the highest level on the Japanese seismic intensity scale, shelters were set up for evacuees at almost all of the schools.

blocks.caption:
Schoolchildren raise their hands in class on Friday as the new term begins in
Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture.

blocks.text: Schoolchildren raise their hands in class on Friday as the new term begins in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture.

Shelters have been consolidated to make space for students to study aheadof the second term, according to the city’s education board. Currently, 16 schools in severely affected areas are hosting shelters.
At Otago Elementary School, children arrived with smiles, rejoicing at reunion with friends.
Shortly after 7 a.m., a girl was seen playing on an exercise bar in the schoolyard. Schoolchildren came down to the playground one after another, and some played soccer before school started.
“I couldn’t play with friends because of the clearing work after the quake,” an 11-year-old girl in sixth grade said. “I’m happy that I can come to school.”

In Yatsushiro, all six school lunch centers were damaged by the quake, and the kitchens in most schools are not usable. Until the lunch centers become operational, schools will serve vacuum-packed food for lunch, except for those with functioning kitchens.
Students need to bring empty lunch boxes and chopsticks from home to use when they eat school lunch, because used dishes cannot be washed.
In Kumamoto, 359 schools sustained damage from the quake, such as broken windows and cracks on buildings, the prefectural education board said.
The second term will start on Tuesday at five elementary and junior high schools in the town of Hikawa.

articles.title: Monica Lorenzo builds for lasting value, with sustainability at the foundation
articles.summary: In real estate, what lasts isn’t just concrete and steel. For Monica Lorenzo, director for leisure and business development at Torre Lorenzo Development Corporation (TLDC), lasting value looks like…

blocks.text: In real estate, what lasts isn’t just concrete and steel. For Monica Lorenzo, director for leisure and business development at Torre Lorenzo Development Corporation (TLDC), lasting value looks like something else entirely. It means developments that strengthen the communities around them, treat the environment as a partner rather than an obstacle, and still make sense to the people living there decades from now. It’s a simple enough principle on paper. Developments shouldn’t come at the expense of the people and places it’s supposed to serve. Living up to it is the harder part.

PROTECTING THE ISLAND’S NATURAL BEAUTY. The waters surrounding Dusit Thani Lubi Plantation Resort in Davao De Oro have been designated a protected coral sanctuary, in partnership with the Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources.
A house built on lies falls with the first storm.

The simple, almost proverbial line reflects a philosophy that would be profound in an industry where foundations, structures and promises carry heavy weight. Honesty, then, becomes both a simple and complicated word. And it is the exact word Monica Lorenzo, this year’s PropertyGuru Rising Star Awardee, gave when asked to describe the work virtue she lives by.
“It is my personality. It is who I am,” she said.

blocks.caption: Monica D. Lorenzo received the Rising Star Award at the 14th PropertyGuru Philippines Property Awards.

blocks.text: Monica D. Lorenzo received the Rising Star Award at the 14th PropertyGuru Philippines Property Awards.

Monica works and lives by that same virtue. For her, success is not measured only by what is built. It is gauged by what endures; what continues to inspire, uplift and strengthen communities while caring for the planet.

TLDC is the pioneer builder of premium university residences in the Philippines. What began as a desire to improve the cramped, unconducive living conditions of students in Metro Manila has grown into a full-scale residential and hospitality developer with projects across Manila, Lipa and Davao, partnering with Dusit International and The Ascott Limited of Singapore on its hospitality developments.
For Monica, part of the appeal of real estate and hospitality has always been how tangible it is.
“You really see what you created and what you’ve worked on. You see how your ideas are coming to reality.”
But admittedly, that tangibility comes with a constant stream of challenges.

Monica describes the company’s position as often introducing concepts to the Philippines that already existed elsewhere but had never quite landed here. Demanding discipline as much as ambition, the company is selective about where it puts its resources.

blocks.caption:
Monica D. Lorenzo, director for leisure and busi-
ness development at Torre Lorenzo Development
Corporation (TLDC).

blocks.text: Monica D. Lorenzo, director for leisure and busi- ness development at Torre Lorenzo Development Corporation (TLDC).
“We are very choosy and picky as to where we decide to put our resources, investment and energy,” she said. “We operate on the fact that each building is a better version of the last.”

She sees the Philippines’ young, increasingly upward mobile population as an opportunity to build things people never thought possible for themselves. It is a philosophy she traces directly back to her father, who once told her: “You have to show them it can get better. This is what we can give you.”

When asked what motivates her, she said, “It is the sense of responsibility to help the company be the best it can be. I am not just an employee, and ties run deeper. This is something that my father built for the next generation, and I want to do the same. To pass it on and get it through to the next generation.”
Being named PropertyGuru’s Rising Star, she says, is a welcome vote of confidence to that mission.
“It helps build confidence that we are pulling things in the right direction. We are always evolving and changing and we’re not slowing down. There is so much we can do.”
Learnings from the shoreline
Monica’s understanding of environmental stewardship did not come from a classroom. It came from watching a place she loved slowly change.

Her family’s island resort, now known as Dusit Thani Lubi Plantation, was somewhere she visited throughout her childhood. She vividly remembers the lush greenery and the vast shoreline. Over the years, she watched as the shoreline visibly retreated.

She remembers how different the environment on that island was 20 years ago. Watching the changes firsthand raised an unavoidable question: What can be done to prevent further damage, so that the next generation can enjoy these same places?
For her family, the answer was to act.

The waters surrounding the island were designated a protected coral sanctuary, with strict bans on fishing and coral harvesting. Roughly 15 years later, the results speak for themselves. Fish populations have returned and the reefs that were once damaged by overfishing and bleaching are healthy again.

That same resort now runs on the kind of sustainability infrastructure that sounded aspirational. On the island is a solar farm of 1,836 panels that supplies up to sixty percent of the resort’s energy needs.. This cuts roughly 985 metric tons of CO2 emissions a year.

blocks.caption: POWERING THE ISLAND WITH THE SUN. The on-island solar farm powers up to 60 percent of the resort’s energy needs.

blocks.text: POWERING THE ISLAND WITH THE SUN. The on-island solar farm powers up to 60 percent of the resort’s energy needs.

Heat recovery systems repurpose warmth from air-conditioning units to heat water for every room and villa. Through reverse osmosis and desalination systems, seawater is turned into the island’s drinking supply. Pools, pathways and roads are designed with sustainability in mind.
This is the balance Monica tries to strike across every project: comfort and luxury that does not come at the planet’s expense.

blocks.caption:
TURNING SEAWATER INTO LIFE-SUSTAINING FRESHWATER. Lubi's Reverse Osmosis and desalination systems convert seawater into clean, drinkable water for the entire island. This reduces reliance on imported water, lowers our carbon footprint, and
supports sustainable water independence.

blocks.text: TURNING SEAWATER INTO LIFE-SUSTAINING FRESHWATER. Lubi's Reverse Osmosis and desalination systems convert seawater into clean, drinkable water for the entire island. This reduces reliance on imported water, lowers our carbon footprint, and supports sustainable water independence.
Listening before building
Ask Monica what role culture and local context play in her projects, and she describes a process that starts long before the ground is broken.

By talking to the people who already bought from them and to residents living in their buildings, and by asking what is working and what is not, the company stays in tune with where they are at. With that, they are able to adapt their plans and designs.
“Flexibility matters,” she says, considering that a single building can take five or six years to complete.
That same philosophy shapes how she thinks about the difference between a development and a destination. For Monica, real estate was never meant to be one-and-done.
“It’s really a whole community; a whole masterplanned development,” she says, “because that is how you’re actually able to build a community.”
In hospitality terms, she frames the challenge simply: getting someone to book that first stay.
“We know, and we are confident enough in our brand, with our developments, and with our projects. Once they stay, they will want to come back.”
Growth and environmental responsibility, in her view, were never meant to be separated.
“It has to go hand in hand,” she says.

She acknowledges that they play a direct role in the community and that it is their responsibility to take care of it. Every project, she says, comes with the same underlying question: How do we integrate ourselves and work together with the people already there to genuinely uplift the towns and barangays we invest in?
Bridging old habits and new standards
Real estate, by nature, is a slow-moving, brick-and-mortar industry, and Monica is candid about the limits that come with that.
Sustainability, she points out, doesn’t only live in construction; it also lives in operations, planning and design.

“Technology hasn’t caught up, “ she admits. “We can’t do things a hundred percent greener and sustainable given there are certain regulations that need to be met, and the environment we are constructing in, the weather, and all other factors.”
Where the technology and the regulatory room exist, though, her team integrates it, steadily pushing each new building to be greener than the one before it.
Building for the generations to come
When Monica talks about legacy, she thinks of generations instead of years as the timeline.
“We at TLDC are building things to last. We are building for the next generation,“ she says.
The goal, as she puts it, is making sure a building still stands for the grandchildren of the people who first bought it.
“If we build, we better do it right. It is a matter of being flexible and open to changes, so that whatever headwinds come, we will be able to adapt.”
Her hope and optimism carry into how she talks about the future, for what these projects leave behind extends beyond the buildings themselves and to the land they are built on.

“There is so much that can be done for the planet,” she says. “It is leaving the planet the same shape and condition it was given to us. We regenerate or replenish what is taken. It should not be a leaky bucket.”

In the end, Monica’s one-word answer, honesty, brings the story back to its foundation. Honest about what a building can deliver. Honest about what a piece of land can and can’t withstand. And honest about what developers leave behind long after the ribbon has been cut.

Because for Monica, building for the future is not only about making something that lasts. It is about making sure that what lasts is worth keeping. That means communities that are stronger, environments that are cared for, and places that future generations can still enjoy.
That, perhaps, is the real foundation of lasting value.

articles.title: Facial Care Centre sets the standard for facial contouring treatment with Ultraformer MPT
articles.summary: At Facial Care Centre, one treatment consistently stands out for lifting sagging skin, tightening it back into place, and reducing stubborn fat with more precision than most non-surgical options on…

blocks.text: At Facial Care Centre, one treatment consistently stands out for lifting sagging skin, tightening it back into place, and reducing stubborn fat with more precision than most non-surgical options on the market: Ultraformer MPT.
Chesca Kramer for Ultraformer MPT
One treatment, tailored results

Most ultrasound facial treatments are built to do one job. Ultraformer MPT does three: reaching deep to lift, staying shallow to refine, and targeting fat separately – all within a single session. Macro energy reaches the same structural layer targeted in a surgical facelift. It lifts jowls and cheeks from underneath, rather than smoothening them from the surface. Micro energy, meanwhile, works closer to the skin. It softens fine lines, tightens pores, and addresses the sagging that develops around the eyes and mouth. For clients with a stubborn double chin or fuller cheeks, the machine’s MP mode breaks down fat cells while tightening the skin at the same time. Intensity is adjusted session to session based on the client’s face and not applied at a fixed setting.

blocks.caption: Bambi Young for Ultraformer MPT at Facial Care Centre

blocks.text: Bambi Young for Ultraformer MPT at Facial Care Centre
Why the expertise matter more than the machine

Ultraformer MPT is a powerful treatment, but the device is only as good as the hands guiding it. Practitioners get real flexibility from its range of energy levels. That flexibility is where skill separates one’s clinic’s results from another’s.

At Facial Care Centre, treatment begins with an assessment and not a preset. Doctors evaluate skin thickness, fat distribution, and structural support before determining the appropriate settings for each client. This is the philosophy behind Facial Care Centre’s reputation: technology provides the tools, but clinical judgement delivers the results. Clients who have undergone Ultraformer MPT elsewhere often recognize the distinction immediately.

blocks.caption: Facial Care Centre’s Ultraformer MPT

blocks.text: Facial Care Centre’s Ultraformer MPT
Results that build and last

Results with Ultraformer MPT build steadily over time. The treatment works with the body’s own collagen production, rather than following a fixed pattern. Lifting and tightening continue to develop over the weeks after the treatment as new collagen forms. Fat reduction tends to become visible sooner, and results continue to improve thereafter.

blocks.caption: Ultraformer MPT at Facial Care Centre

blocks.text: Ultraformer MPT at Facial Care Centre
Start with a consultation

Every treatment with Facial Care Centre begins with a consultation. It is in this initial conversation that the treatment plan is built. Skin, age, and goals differ significantly from client to client, which is why that first conversation is where the plan truly takes shape.

articles.title: Trump hails 'historic' deal for US to control 65bn barrels of Venezuela's oil
articles.summary: Venezuelan interim president says the unusual agreement will help revive her country's economy.

blocks.text: The US has reached a deal with Venezuela to control more than 65 billion barrels of its proven oil reserves, President Donald Trump announced.
"This Historic Transaction MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves, greatly increases our Oil Supply, and will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans," Trump posted on social media.
Venezuela's interim President, Delcy Rodriguez, hailed the agreement as one that would help her nation's economic revival.

Trump vowed to tap Venezuela's reserves, the world's largest, after the US captured its then-President Nicolás Maduro this year. More recently, Trump has been under pressure to tame domestic petrol prices, which spiked amid the Iran conflict.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the oil deal "a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people". Few details were released.

"For the Venezuelan people, this deal will bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs, and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela's economy," Rubio said on social media.
In his own post, Trump said Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had reached the agreement with Venezuela's leadership "through a partnership with private business".
He did not elaborate on the partnership or describe possible commitments and terms for the US in the deal, but he claimed the agreement was reached "at no cost to the American Taxpayer".
Venezuela's interim president said in a statement that the agreement would have "a significant impact on our nation's revival".

The deal calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, as well as "an investment of more than $100 billion, and more than $209 billion in taxes for the State", Rodriguez said.

"These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country's economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere, and greater balance in international markets," she said.
Under the deal the US government will retain 55% control of a joint venture with an "experienced private operator in Venezuela", a US official told the BBC's media partner CBS News.
Rodriguez gave the venture a 100-year concession to operate in the oil fields, according to the official.
Trump gave few specifics of the highly unusual agreement, which apparently grants the US direct governance over a foreign country's sovereign national resources.
The deal would also appear to be wider in scope than the US-led Coalition Provisional Authority's control over Iraq's oil revenues after Saddam Hussein was ousted in an American-led invasion in 2003.

But it is unclear whether the Venezuela agreement could face legal and constitutional challenges in the South American nation. The official text of the agreement between Washington and Caracas has not been released.
President Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were seized in a US special forces operation authorised by Trump on 3 January.

In the hours after the raid, Trump said his administration would run Venezuela until a "safe, proper and judicious transition" could take place, adding that the US would indefinitely control the sale of the country's oil.
Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world - an estimated 303 billion barrels. However, production has plummeted since its peak in the late 1990s.
Trump has asked US oil firms to invest at least $100bn (£75bn) to restore the country's oil industry.

He has also claimed the rights to Venezuela's oil after saying that the country had in the past "unilaterally seized and sold American oil, American assets and American platforms, costing us billions and billions of dollars".

articles.title: Japan to Set Up Multifunctional Defense Hub in Hiroshima
articles.summary: Tokyo, Aug. 28 (Jiji Press)--Japan’s Defense Ministry on Friday concluded a contract with Nippon Steel Corp. to acquire a former plant site in Kure in Hiroshima Prefecture, western Japan, to develop…

blocks.text: Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi speaks at a press conference in Tokyo on Friday.

Tokyo, Aug. 28 (Jiji Press)--Japan’s Defense Ministry on Friday concluded a contract with Nippon Steel Corp. to acquire a former plant site in Kure in Hiroshima Prefecture, western Japan, to develop a multifunctional defense complex there.

The approximately 140-hectare land plot, Nippon Steel's former Setouchi Works Kure Area site, is expected to host Self-Defense Forces buildings, barracks, a defense equipment manufacturing facility, a supply depot and a heliport.
The ministry will soon start accepting bids from companies for contracts to manufacture, maintain and repair defense equipment at the planned complex and engage in research and development there.
The Kure area is an extremely important region for national security as it is home to major Maritime SDF facilities, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said at a press conference.
We aim to use (the planned complex) to fundamentally strengthen the country’s defense,” he added.

articles.title: 1st-Half Births in Japan Rise for 1st Time in 11 Years
articles.summary: Tokyo, Aug. 28 (Jiji Press)--The number of births in Japan rose in the first half of the year for the first time in 11 years, health ministry data showed Friday in a sign that the figure’s rapid…

blocks.text: Tokyo, Aug. 28 (Jiji Press)--The number of births in Japan rose in the first half of the year for the first time in 11 years, health ministry data showed Friday in a sign that the figure’s rapid decline is ending.

The preliminary data showed that the number of births in the January-June period edged up by 2,788, or 0.8 pct, from a year before to 342,068, still below 400,000 for the fifth consecutive year. The rise may have reflected increases in marriages in 2024-2025.

The number of births by Japanese nationals in Japan stood at 671,236 in 2025, marking a record low for the 10th straight year, according to data released in June. The size of decrease shrank to 2.2 pct from around 5 pct since 2022, however.
The number of marriages grew by 418 to 238,979 in the first six months of the year, while that of divorces fell by 3,578 to 90,177.
Deaths totaled 778,982. The natural decrease in the population, or the number of deaths minus that of births, was 436,914.

The preliminary data includes births by foreigners in Japan and those by Japanese nationals who live overseas. Revised data, which will be disclosed later, only counts births by Japanese nationals who live in the country.
The annual number of births in Japan has been on a declining trend since 1975. It went below one million in 2016 and fell below 700,000 in 2024.

articles.title: Former Ecuadorian President Lenín Moreno sentenced to 5 years for corruption
articles.summary: QUITO, Ecuador (AP) — Former Ecuadorian President Lenín Moreno was sentenced Friday to 5 years in prison after a court found him guilty of accepting bribes from a Chinese company in exchange for…

blocks.text: QUITO, Ecuador (AP) — Former Ecuadorian President Lenín Moreno was sentenced Friday to 5 years in prison after a court found him guilty of accepting bribes from a Chinese company in exchange for helping it secure a contract to build a hydroelectric plant.
Moreno, who was present for the reading of the verdict, is 73 years old and has a physical disability that prevents him from walking. He will serve the sentence under house arrest.

Moreno was convicted as a direct participant in the bribery scheme during his tenure as vice president under Rafael Correa. His wife and daughter, two brothers and a brother-in-law were convicted as accomplices. The wife and daughter each received 30-month sentences. All were ordered to repay triple what they received illicitly within a period of 90 days.
Moreno is the third former Ecuadorian president to be sentenced for corruption, though he was tried for crimes before reaching the presidency.

Correa was sentenced in 2020 to eight years in prison in a bribery case involving Brazilian construction giant Odebrecht but remains in Belgium, where he has lived for years. Former President Jamil Mahuad was also sentenced in 2014 to eight years for misuse of public funds. Another former president, Abdalá Bucaram, is awaiting sentencing after being convicted of organized crime.

Prosecutors said a corruption network operated from 2008 to 2018, collecting bribes equal to 4% of the value of the project carried out by Sinohydro. They said the money was distributed through domestic and international transactions to public officials and other beneficiaries, including Moreno.
Sinohydro began building the roughly $2 billion Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant in 2010 and handed it over to Ecuador in 2016. The project has since faced criticism over structural defects.

Moreno, a tourism entrepreneur, rose to national prominence in 2007 when he became vice president under Correa, who governed Ecuador for a decade. Moreno served until 2013, when Jorge Glas succeeded him.

In 2017, Moreno won the presidency as a candidate of the Correísta movement founded around Correa, with Glas as his running mate. Glas later left office and is now serving a prison sentence for corruption.

articles.title: New QCPD chief assumes command
articles.summary: Police Brig. Gen. Christopher F. Olazo assumed his post as Quezon City Police District (QCPD) director on Friday, Aug. 28, succeeding Police Brig. Gen. Randy Glenn Silvio. A Philippine National…

blocks.text: Police Brig. Gen. Christopher F. Olazo assumes command of the Quezon City Police District (QCPD) on Aug. 28, succeeding Police Brig. Gen. Randy Glenn Silvio during a turnover ceremony at the QCPD Hinirang Social Hall, Camp Karingal, Quezon City. (Photo courtesy of QCPD)
Police Brig. Gen. Christopher F. Olazo assumed his post as Quezon City Police District (QCPD) director on Friday, Aug. 28, succeeding Police Brig. Gen. Randy Glenn Silvio.

blocks.caption: Police Brig. Gen. Christopher F. Olazo assumes command of the Quezon City Police District (QCPD) on Aug. 28, succeeding Police Brig. Gen. Randy Glenn Silvio during a turnover ceremony at the QCPD Hinirang Social Hall, Camp Karingal, Quezon City. (Photo courtesy of QCPD)

blocks.text: A Philippine National Police Academy (PNPA) Kabalikat Class of 1998 alumnus, Olazo formally took over the district during a turnover ceremony at the QCPD Hinirang Social Hall in Camp Karingal, Quezon City.

The event was attended by Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte and presided over by National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) officer-in-charge Police Brig. Gen. Christopher N. Abrahano. Also present were National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) Vice Chairperson and Executive Officer Rafael Calinisan, Congressman Ralph “Raffy” Tulfo, and other officials and guests.
In his inaugural message, Olazo vowed to lead by example, uphold accountability, and maintain professionalism in keeping Quezon City safe.

“I understand the demands of this District and the importance of maintaining the standards that the QCPD has established through the years. To the QCitizen, I assure you that the QCPD will remain committed to maintaining peace and order, preventing and responding to crime, protecting our communities, and providing professional and accessible police service,” Olazo said.

Before assuming the QCPD directorship, Olazo held various key positions in the Philippine National Police (PNP), including chief of police of Bacoor City and Taguig City, QCPD battalion commander, provincial director of the Cavite Police Provincial Office, and senior police assistant to the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) secretary.

Belmonte welcomed Olazo to his new post and assured him of the continued support of the Quezon City government as he leads the district in upholding the city’s standards of public safety and public service.
Silvio, in his final message as QCPD director, expressed pride in what he and his personnel accomplished during his tenure and thanked them for their trust, support, and commitment.

Abrahano also directed the regionwide adoption of the Investigation Solution Automatic Verification (ISAV), an initiative implemented under Silvio’s leadership, to further strengthen police operations.
He said the directive supports the initiatives of PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. aimed at achieving three key outcomes: less crime, faster response, and better-behaved policemen.
Under Olazo’s leadership, the QCPD is expected to build on its gains, pursue innovations, and further strengthen its delivery of responsive police services to QCitizens.

articles.title: Eight PH films shortlisted for Oscars 2027 consideration
articles.summary: The Film Academy of the Philippines (FDCP) has narrowed down submissions for consideration to the 99th Academy Award's Best International Feature Film category, Eight films have been named with the…

blocks.text: The Film Academy of the Philippines (FDCP) has narrowed down submissions for consideration to the 99th Academy Award's Best International Feature Film category,
Eight films have been named with the country’s official entry set to be announced on Sept. 4.
The contenders include films tackling Philippine history, identity, relationships, social issues, and contemporary life.
Among them is “58th,” Carl Joseph Papa’s animated docu-drama centered on the 2009 Maguindanao Massacre, told through the perspective of one of the missing victim's daughter.
“58th” has screened at several international festivals including Rotterdam and Annecy, as well as the Oscar-qualifying Doc Edge.
Jade Castro’s “All the Things I Leave You (Patawid),” an Ilocano-language BL film, is also in contention.

“Filipiñana,” directed by Rafael Manuel, recently opened in Philippine cinemas after making its way through the international festival circuit. The film premiered at the Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Dramatic Special Jury Award for Creative Vision. It follows a young woman working at a posh golf course.
“I’mPerfect,” directed by Sigrid Andrea Bernardo, is another contender. The film was a Metro Manila Film Festival winner. It centers on a couple with Down syndrome.
“Manila’s Finest,” directed by Raymond Red, is also on the shortlist. The film is set shortly before the First Quarter Storm.
Jerrold Tarog’s “Quezon,” meanwhile, is the third installment in the director's so-called “Bayaniverse” franchise and stars Jericho Rosales as Manuel L. Quezon, the Philippines’ second president.

Hilda Koronel marks her return to film with “Sisa,” directed by Jun Robles Lana. The veteran actress plays a woman believed to be mentally unstable who secretly works as a spy for Filipino revolutionaries during the Philippine-American War.
Rounding out the contenders is Lawrence Fajardo’s “Silenced Nights,” inspired by the 2017 killing of Kian delos Santos during the Duterte government’s war on drugs.
Film Academy Director-General Paolo Villaluna said the eight films present different perspectives on the Filipino experience.
“They look at our history, the issues we continue to face and the ways Filipinos deal with questions of power, identity, love, freedom and survival,” Villaluna said.
He added that each film has “its own voice and approach,” with the potential to connect with audiences outside the Philippines.

The eight films will undergo evaluation by a selection committee organized by the Film Academy and composed of local film industry experts as approved by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.
The committee will consider each submission based on artistic merit, cultural relevance and its potential for an international campaign.
Despite decades of submissions, no Philippine film has been nominated for or made the shortlist for the Academy Awards’ International Feature Film category.
Past Philippine entries include “Dekada ’70,” “Heneral Luna,” “Ang Babae sa Septic Tank,” and “Magellan,” which was considered one of the country’s strongest chances of making the first cut.
Shortlist for the Philippines’ Oscars 2027 entry:
“58th” — directed by Carl Joseph Papa
“All the Things I Leave You (Patawid)” — directed by Jade Castro
“Filipiñana” — directed by Rafael Manuel
“I’mPerfect” — directed by Sigrid Andrea Bernardo
“Manila’s Finest” — directed by Raymond Red
“Quezon” — directed by Jerrold Tarog
“Silenced Nights” — directed by Lawrence Fajardo
“Sisa” — directed by Jun Robles Lana

articles.title: ‘The only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art’: Remembering Yayoi Kusama
articles.summary: She suffered from hallucinations from childhood and by the age of 10 had created paintings in watercolors, pastels, and oils using polka dot and net motifs that she encountered in her visions

blocks.text: In the history of the National Gallery of Victoria, their most successful ticketed exhibition did not feature the work of Vincent van Gogh, Claude Monet or Pablo Picasso. It was of the veteran Japanese artist, Yayoi Kusama, who has died aged 97.
Held over the summer months in 2024–25, the Melbourne exhibition attracted 570,537 ticketed visitors.

Kusama’s exhibitions throughout the world have attracted huge crowds. Her infinity mirror rooms, sprawling seas of polka dots, dancing pumpkins, and huge expanses of reflective surfaces have become some of the most photographed art objects in human history.
Her art has had a huge impact on many art movements of the 20th and 21st centuries, including pop art, performance art, minimalism, environmental art, video art, fashion, filmmaking, and feminism.
Kusama was born on March 22, 1929 in Matsumoto, Nagano Prefecture, Japan, to parents who were merchants and operated a plant nursery and seed farm.
She suffered from hallucinations from childhood and by the age of 10 had created paintings in watercolors, pastels, and oils using polka dot and net motifs that she encountered in her visions.
She described her childhood as traumatic, with a physically abusive mother and a womanizing father, and a time when her artistic endeavors were discouraged. She found refuge in her art.

Her childhood was overshadowed by World War II. By the time she was 13, she was sewing parachutes for Japanese soldiers and was aware of American bombers flying overhead and of constant air-raid sirens. She attended Arigasaki High School and, in 1948, studied Nihonga painting at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts.

By 1950, Kusama was exhibiting in Japan, to some acclaim, her sprawling paintings, mainly on paper, of abstracted natural forms and would cover all surfaces — floors, walls, ceilings and naked assistants with polka dots that she would term “infinity nets.”
Concerning her painting, Flower (D.S.P.S), 1954, she wrote:

One day I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows, and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe. I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space and be reduced to nothingness.

In 1957, Yayoi Kusama traveled to the United States and settled in New York. She was at the heart of the American post-war art movement where she exhibited to considerable applause large paintings, soft sculptures and environmental sculptures using mirrors and electric lights.
In the 1960s, she staged many happenings, such as body painting festivals, fashion shows and anti-war demonstrations.
It has been argued that her work had a profound impact on artists, including Claes Oldenburg and Andy Warhol.
She was also involved in film productions and newspaper publication.

In 1968, the film Kusama’s Self-Obliteration, that Kusama produced and in which she played the leading role, won a prize at the Fourth International Experimental Film Competition in Belgium and the Second Maryland Film Festival and the second prize at the Ann Arbor Film Festival.

She held exhibitions and staged happenings in various countries in Europe and participated in the Venice Biennale in 1966, where she exhibited her Narcissus Garden comprising of hundreds of mirrored spheres.
(Narcissus Garden entered the collection of the National Gallery of Victoria in 2024, in its new iteration of 1,400 stainless steel balls, each 30cm in diameter.)
The artist’s physical and mental health deteriorated while she was in America and she attempted suicide.
For her, her art was the path to salvation.
Kusama returned to Japan to live there permanently in 1973.
After experiencing a further suicide attempt, in 1977 she admitted herself into the Tokyo psychiatric institute, the Seiwa Hospital for the Mentally Ill, from which she was never discharged.
She lived in the hospital and made daily excursions to her studio where she maintained a frenetic pace of work.

Yayoi Kusama was one of the most acclaimed artists of her time. A major retrospective exhibition of her work held in 1998 at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art traveled to the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Tokyo.

There were also major retrospective exhibitions at the Whitney Museum, New York, and Tate Modern, London, in 2012, and at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington, DC in 2017. In 2017, the Yayoi Kusama Museum opened in Tokyo.
Commercially, her work achieved record prices and she has received various awards for her novels, poetry, and films.
In an interview with Infinity Net in 2012, Yayoi Kusama said:

I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art. I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live.
If this article has raised issues for you, or if you’re concerned about someone you know, call the National Center for Mental Health Crisis in the Philippines at hotline number 1553.
– The Conversation/Rappler.com
Sasha Grishin is an Adjunct Professor of Art History at the Australian National University

articles.title: LPA may enter PAR this weekend, develop into tropical cyclone—PAGASA
articles.summary: A low-pressure area (LPA), which has a moderate chance of developing into a tropical cyclone, may enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) this weekend, the Philippine Atmospheric,…

blocks.text: (MB FILE PHOTO)

A low-pressure area (LPA), which has a moderate chance of developing into a tropical cyclone, may enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) this weekend, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said on Saturday, Aug. 29.
According to PAGASA weather specialist Veronica Torres, the LPA outside PAR was last spotted at 3 a.m. about 1,080 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon.

“Ito ngang low-pressure area na ito ay katamtaman ‘yung tiyansa na maging isang ganap na bagyo. And then, possible din na pumasok ito ng ating area of responsibility this weekend (This low-pressure area has a moderate chance of developing into a tropical cyclone. It may also enter our area of responsibility this weekend),” she said.
“Kaya patuloy pa rin tayong mag-antabay sa mga update ng PAGASA (That is why we should continue monitoring updates from PAGASA),” she added.
PAGASA, meanwhile, is also monitoring another LPA inside PAR, which was last located about 520 kilometers north-northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, as of 3 a.m.
Torres noted that the LPA was already near the PAR boundary and could leave the country’s monitoring area within the next few hours or days.

“Nakikita nga natin na napakalapit na nga nitong low-pressure area na ito sa boundary ng ating PAR line at posibleng lumabas na ng ating Philippine Area of Responsibility sa mga susunod na sandali o mga susunod na araw (We can see that this low-pressure area is already very close to the PAR boundary and may leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility within the next few hours or days),” she said.

blocks.caption: (DOST-PAGASA)

blocks.text: (DOST-PAGASA)
The weather specialist said the LPA has a low chance of developing into a tropical cyclone within the next 24 hours.
“At if ever man maging bagyo ito, ito na ay nasa labas ng ating area of responsibility (If it develops into a tropical cyclone, it will already be outside our area of responsibility),” said Torres.
The state weather bureau said the southwest monsoon, locally called “habagat,” continues to affect Luzon and the Visayas.

“Samantala, ‘yung southwest monsoon o habagat ay patuloy pa rin ang epekto sa Luzon pati na rin sa Visayas, kaya asahan nga natin ‘yung mga malalakas na pag-ulan dala pa rin ng southwest monsoon, mostly sa western sections ng Luzon (Meanwhile, the southwest monsoon or habagat continues to affect Luzon and the Visayas, so we can expect heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon, mostly over the western sections of Luzon),” she said.

In Heavy Rainfall Warning No. 13 issued at 5 a.m. on Saturday, PAGASA placed Bataan, Zambales, Pampanga, and a portion of Bulacan under a red rainfall warning due to rains brought by the southwest monsoon.
Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, and portions of Tarlac, Bulacan, Batangas, and Laguna were under an orange warning, while portions of Tarlac, Laguna, and Batangas were placed under a yellow warning.
Per PAGASA, a red warning means serious flooding is expected in flood-prone areas, while an orange warning indicates that flooding is threatening and a yellow warning means flooding is possible.

articles.title: Red, yellow alerts raised over Visayas grid on Aug. 29, 2026 -- NGCP
articles.summary: Power interruptions may hit electricity consumers in the Visayas on Saturday afternoon and evening due to limited power supply as multiple power plants remain unavailable.

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 9:57am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.
Power interruptions may hit electricity consumers in the Visayas on Saturday afternoon and evening due to limited power supply as multiple power plants remain unavailable.

In an 8 a.m. bulletin, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said yellow alert will be in effect from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m., followed by red alert from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m., then back to yellow alert from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.
The grid operator said the Visayas grid is currently operating at 2,300 megawatts (MW) capacity against a peak demand of 2,355 MW.
The following were cited as factors that contributed to the red and yellow alerts in the Visayas grid:

items: Unavailability of Visayas' large coal plants TVI 1, TVI 2, KSPC 1 and emergency shutdown of PEDC 3
Limited power import from Mindanao

blocks.text: The NGCP said 13 power plants are on forced outage in August 2026, one plant since July, three plants since June, seven plants since May, one plant since March, three plants since 2025, two plants since 2024, two plants since 2023, and one plant since 2021.
Meanwhile, 15 plants are running on derated capacities, "for a total of 1,094.4 MW unavailable to the grid."
A red alert status is issued when power supply is insufficient to meet consumer demand and the transmission grid's regulating requirement.
Widespread power interruptions or rotational brownouts are expected.
In this situation, electricity might be cut temporarily in certain areas on a scheduled basis to prevent the entire grid from collapsing.
On the other hand, a yellow alert is issued when the operating margin is insufficient to meet the transmission grid's contingency requirement.
While supply is still enough to meet current demand, it no longer reaches the required safety margin.
At this level, the possibility of rotational power interruptions increases.
In a separate advisory, the NGCP said the power interruption covering parts of Iloilo province and Iloilo City has been deferred.
It was scheduled for Sunday, August 30, and would have affected the following:

items: MORE — Arevalo, Molo, Diversion, IPG, Bolilao, Tabuc Suba and Megaworld substations
ILECO 1 — Pavia substations

blocks.text: The NGCP will issue another advisory upon finalizing the revised schedule. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Not your usual cup of matcha
articles.summary: Matcha is usually associated with lattes, desserts, and the popular familiar green-hued treats that have become fixtures on menus. Ebi10 and The Matcha Tokyo Philippines, however, are taking the…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Food
Ebi10 and The Matcha Tokyo bring the beloved Japanese ingredient to tempura, seafood, and dessert

Matcha is usually associated with lattes, desserts, and the popular familiar green-hued treats that have become fixtures on menus. Ebi10 and The Matcha Tokyo Philippines, however, are taking the Japanese ingredient in a different direction — bringing it into savory territory.
Until Sept. 23, the two brands are joining forces for a limited-time menu that pairs Ebi10’s Japanese comfort food with The Matcha Tokyo’s premium, 100 percent organic matcha.

Created with Chef Mikko Reyes of Ebi10, the collaboration explores matcha’s earthy flavor and gentle bitterness alongside seafood, tempura, and other familiar Japanese ingredients. The result is a menu that treats matcha as more than a beverage or dessert ingredient.

At the center of the collaboration is the Mentai Matcha Jumbo Tempura, featuring two jumbo white shrimps coated in matcha tempura batter, filled with mentaiko and served with organic matcha salt. The dish brings together the briny richness of mentaiko, the sweetness of shrimp and the subtle bitterness of matcha in a crisp bite.

The Matcha Scallop Popcorn takes the same approach with local scallops. The seafood is coated in matcha tempura batter and served with organic matcha salt, fried nori, and sesame yuzu aioli. The citrus and creamy sesame notes provide balance to the earthiness of the matcha while allowing the natural sweetness of the scallops to come through.

Matcha also makes its way into dessert. The Banana Tempura with Matcha Custard Cream pairs Ebi10’s warm, crisp banana tempura with silky matcha custard cream and organic matcha sugar, keeping the green tea flavor at the center of the dish.

blocks.caption: (Photo: The Matcha Tokyo)

blocks.text: (Photo: The Matcha Tokyo)

“Matcha is something people usually associate with drinks and desserts, so we wanted to have fun with the idea and show how well it can work with savory food too,” said Mica Viray-Aguila, managing partner of Ebi10 during the press preview last Aug. 25. “Working with The Matcha Tokyo gave us the chance to bring together what both brands do best and create something familiar, but with a completely new flavor.”
For The Matcha Tokyo Philippines CEO Charles Paw, the collaboration is also about finding new ways for people to experience matcha.

“I’m a firm believer of the quote from James Beard that says, ‘Food is our common ground, a universal experience,’” Paw said. “That’s why we’re always excited to find new ways for people to experience matcha, especially through collaborations like this one with Ebi10 that bring different ideas together.”

The Matcha Tokyo, established in 2018, brings premium organic matcha into modern everyday life. Rooted in Japanese matcha culture, the brand describes its approach as a contemporary take on how matcha is enjoyed, with its philosophy centered on “Matcha for a healthy and beautiful life.”

Ebi10, meanwhile, is a Japanese comfort food restaurant inspired by a family trip to Osaka and a love for freshly made tempura. Since opening its first location in Poblacion, Makati, the restaurant has expanded across Metro Manila and beyond, offering approachable Japanese dishes made with the Filipino palate in mind.

articles.title: What to know about the backlash against Infantino
articles.summary: MONACO (AP) — Gianni Infantino, the increasingly embattled FIFA president, was everywhere in the conversations as European soccer leaders gathered this week in Monaco for the Champions League draw.…

blocks.text: MONACO (AP) — Gianni Infantino, the increasingly embattled FIFA president, was everywhere in the conversations as European soccer leaders gathered this week in Monaco for the Champions League draw.
UEFA, the European soccer confederation, is spearheading the backlash against Infantino over his failed World Cup sell-off plan that created a deep rift in the sport one month ago.
Many of its member federations have withdrawn their support for the FIFA leader, who is up for re-election in March 2027, and some have called for his resignation.
Infantino has not given any indication he plans to step down.
Here’s what to know about the growing pushback against the FIFA president.
UEFA ramps up the pressure with legal action

On Thursday, UEFA escalated the situation by revealing that it is preparing a possible criminal complaint against the FIFA president in Switzerland – where the organization is based – for alleged mismanagement.

The European soccer confederation filed requests in U.S. courts seeking evidence about Infantino’s secretive plan to give private investors led by Joshua Kushner a stake in the profits of future World Cups and other FIFA tournaments for $4.2 billion.
FIFA withdrew the proposal on Aug. 1, just days after it was made public, after intense pushback.

UEFA’s lawyers called the plan “a vehicle for Infantino and that small circle to acquire a permanent stake in and otherwise profit from FIFA’s most valuable assets to the detriment of FIFA, its members, and other parties within the football family.”

FIFA did not comment on UEFA’s move, which increases pressure on Infantino and puts other FIFA staffers at risk of legal exposure relating to a project that its now-fired chief operating officer said was Infantino’s idea.

It also means Kushner, the younger brother of U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, faces increased scrutiny at a time when he is involved in a $12 billion takeover deal for the Los Angeles Lakers.
Some of Infantino’s critics want him to step down before the vote.
“Infantino is polarizing the world in a way we haven’t seen in history,” Norwegian soccer federation president Lise Klaveness said in Monaco.
Norway was the first FIFA member federation explicitly asking Infantino to resign in the wake of the World Cup investment plan.
Infantino’s re-election no longer a foregone conclusion
Just months ago, ahead of the World Cup in the U.S., Canada and Mexico, Infantino was cruising toward an uncontested election win next March, with a clear majority of FIFA members backing him.
Things look less certain now, with UEFA, Asian confederation AFC and CONCACAF, the governing body for soccer North and Central America and the Caribbean, accusing the FIFA president of “ deception.”

Together those groups represent a majority of FIFA member federations. However, several AFC and CONCACAF members have declared continued support for Infantino as have a series of soccer federations in Africa and South America, many of which depend on FIFA funding. He needs just over half of FIFA’s 211 member federations to vote for him to be re-elected.

Infantino spent last weekend in the Dominican Republic meeting FIFA members from the Caribbean, despite a request by FIFA’s Canadian vice president and CONCACAF leader Victor Montagliani not to visit.
The Kushner-backed $4.2 billion investment would have funded $20 million offers to each of FIFA’s 211 member federations. That would be game-changing money for the 25 members in the Caribbean.
On Wednesday, Infantino’s Instagram account showed he was in Vietnam.
So far, no challenger has emerged to run against Infantino. The candidate deadline is Nov. 18, four months before election day in Rabat, Morocco, which is a FIFA stronghold.
Key dates on the soccer calendar

Infantino would be expected in Poland soon for the FIFA-organized Under-20 Women’s World Cup played from Sept. 5-27. But one Polish soccer official in Monaco said they had no idea of Infantino’s plans to be in the country.
It is a long-standing quip that FIFA staff read Instagram to learn where he is.
UEFA has an executive committee meeting Sept. 15 in Thessaloniki, Greece.

The influential European Football Clubs group meets Sept. 29 in Copenhagen. It is close to sealing a joint venture deal with FIFA overseeing the 2029 Club World Cup that Infantino wants to be worth $2 billion.
The clubs’ leader Nasser al-Khelaifi, from Paris Saint-Germain, is a key ally of UEFA and also a member of the government of Qatar which has backed Infantino in this crisis.

articles.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
articles.summary: Two ships were seized within four days last week raising to at least 13 the number attacked since January.

blocks.text: A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.

Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.
It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.
"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."
That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.
Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.

"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.

Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.
The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.

Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.

The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.

That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.
A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.
But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.
Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.
And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.

The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.
"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.
"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."
He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.

But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.
"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.
Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.

Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.

The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.

"There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital.
He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday.
"The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more."

Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes.
Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them.
Puntland authorities have been more outspoken.

Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast.
The BBC has not independently verified his allegations.

The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operation… in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out.

Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say.

There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed.
Additional reporting by Mohamed Gabobe in Mogadishu and the BBC Somali Service
