articles.title: Sabalenka shrugs off struggles, eyes historic third straight US Open crown
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Aryna Sabalenka has appeared to be having fun everywhere but the tennis court lately. Her Instagram account is filled with photos where she is fashionably dressed in beautiful…

blocks.text: NEW YORK (AP) — Aryna Sabalenka has appeared to be having fun everywhere but the tennis court lately.
Her Instagram account is filled with photos where she is fashionably dressed in beautiful settings, or lounging in a bikini in relaxing ones. Life looks great.
On the court, it's as bad as it's been in a while.

The top-ranked women's player hasn't even gotten past the fourth round of her last few tournaments, and she hardly looks ready to become the first player to win three straight U.S. Open titles since Serena Williams from 2012-14.
Sabalenka doesn't sound concerned. She sounds defiant.
Her response to those wondering what's wrong with her game: “Maybe there’s something wrong with people,” she said.
To those who don't like the black mesh-covered outfit she's wearing on the court in New York: “Who cares about people, right? All matters for me is that I love it,” Sabalenka responded.

Sabalenka looked headed for a superb season at the start of the year. She lost in the Australian Open final to Elena Rybakina, but then won back-to-back hard-court titles at Indian Wells and Miami. Even after she was knocked out by Naomi Osaka in the fourth round at Wimbledon, it was assumed Sabalenka would quickly return to form when she came back to North America and the hard courts where her power is so tough to handle.

Then she was upset by Ekaterina Alexandrova in the fourth round in Toronto and blew leads in both sets and was ousted by Sara Bejlek in Cincinnati, appearing frustrated at times with her game the way she used to earlier in her career.
She won't specify what was wrong, but hinted that everything wasn't right.
“It wasn’t the best period. I don’t want to defend myself, but obviously I just don’t want to talk about that period. I’ve been dealing with several things,” Sabalenka said.

“But who cares, right? Yeah, I didn’t perform my best. These tough lessons are definitely going to make me way, way stronger and working even harder. I work on my mental side of the game. I was trying to reset my mind and to come back stronger, so it’s only going to make me stronger. It’s only a matter of time for me to come back.”
It wouldn't be a surprise if it was in New York, where she won the title for the first time in 2024 by beating Jessica Pegula in the final. She defended it last year by topping Amanda Anisimova.
Reaching the top has given the 28-year-old from Belarus plenty of benefits off the court. Endorsement deals and photo shoots. Vacations during the season to Greece with her fiance.
It gives critics who see Sabalenka detail all of that on social media the opportunity to question whether it's too much fun and not enough work.
“She’s still No. 1 in the world. So I think the results are there,” said Paula Badosa, Sabalenka's friend on tour who has been pictured in some of those photos with her.

“Of course, everyone is going to expect for her to win every tournament. That’s very, very difficult. And at the moment, that one player is not winning what they expected. Of course, they’re saying that it’s because of the photo shoots or the TikToks and all this stuff, and I’m not going to lie, she’s been doing that since she was maybe out of the top 100. And when she was winning, nobody says anything, you know? And when she loses a couple of matches, it’s because of that. I think it’s none of it.”
The No. 1 ranking is in jeopardy after Sabalenka's summer swoon. She may need to make a deep run in New York with the likes of Rybakina and Pegula gaining on her.
Sabalenka has done it before. She may be down now but doesn't sound like she plans to stay there.
“Well, that’s the beauty of the sport,” she said. “Throw tough challenges at me, I will come back only stronger.”

articles.title: What Filinvest City reveals about the future of business districts
articles.summary: As hybrid work reshapes employee expectations and labor markets become more competitive, companies are taking a broader view of what a business address needs to provide. Increasingly, businesses are…

blocks.text: As hybrid work reshapes employee expectations and labor markets become more competitive, companies are taking a broader view of what a business address needs to provide. Increasingly, businesses are evaluating whether their location can support workforce needs, future growth, and continuity over the long term. This shift has increased the importance of the business district itself, with companies placing greater emphasis on the strength and completeness of their surrounding ecosystem.

In Alabang, Filinvest City offers a compelling case. Spanning 244 hectares, the master-planned garden CBD of the Metro South has grown into one of the country's most established business locations by integrating workplaces, residences, healthcare facilities, educational institutions, retail destinations, hospitality offerings, and public spaces within a single urban environment.

With limited commercial lots remaining, Filinvest City continues to welcome businesses and investors seeking to build within a proven business district supported by decades of development, strong market confidence, and sustained growth.

The advantage now lies in both proximity and functionality. Daily needs that would typically require travel across multiple locations are concentrated within the district, allowing employees and businesses to operate within a more connected setting. The result is an environment designed to support both business activity and everyday life.

blocks.caption: Filinvest City's Northgate Cyberzone offers businesses a competitive advantage through its strategic connectivity, and access to a rapidly expanding talent pool across Metro Manila and the South. (Photo: Filinvest City)

blocks.text: Filinvest City's Northgate Cyberzone offers businesses a competitive advantage through its strategic connectivity, and access to a rapidly expanding talent pool across Metro Manila and the South. (Photo: Filinvest City)
Talent beyond the metro core
The growing importance of geography is perhaps most evident in the competition for talent.

As companies expand their hiring footprint beyond traditional business centers, accessibility has become a strategic consideration. The ability to draw from multiple labor markets can widen recruitment opportunities and provide greater flexibility as workforce requirements evolve.

Filinvest City's location in Alabang positions it at the intersection of Metro Manila and Southern Luzon. Through major transport links including the South Luzon Expressway, the Skyway System, the Muntinlupa-Cavite Expressway, with the future railway system set to enhance regional connectivity, businesses can access talent pools that extend across Muntinlupa, Las Piñas, Parañaque, Cavite, Laguna, and Batangas.

For employers, that reach can translate into a wider pipeline of professionals and a reduced reliance on a single labor market. In an environment where workforce availability increasingly influences business performance, connectivity becomes more than an infrastructure feature. It becomes an operational asset.
The value of a proven district
Corporate tenants are also paying closer attention to the maturity of the locations in which they operate.

Filinvest City's growth has been supported by measurable market performance over the past decade. Land values within the district have increased by 346 percent, equivalent to a 17 percent compounded annual growth rate, reflecting sustained demand driven by real business activity and long-term investor confidence. Commercial land that traded at approximately ₱50,000 per square meter in 2010 now commands prices approaching ₱500,000 per square meter.

Beyond valuation growth, the district has matured into a fully operational urban center, with approximately 19 million sqm of gross floor area already delivered, and daily foot traffic estimated at 220,000 people. Its appeal is further evidenced by the presence of major locators such as PLDT, SONAK, and Pepsi, whose investments underscore Filinvest City's role as an established business destination.

The township remains the first and only LEED- and BERDE-certified central business district in the Philippines. In the Corporate Home of the South, businesses operate alongside multinational corporations, technology firms, professional service providers, and BPO companies. Northgate Cyberzone, the township's PEZA-accredited business district, has long served as a hub for organizations seeking a stable operating environment supported by established infrastructure and business services.

The CBD’s integrated masterplan also recently received international recognition when Filinvest City earned gold at the FIABCI World Prix d'Excellence Awards, becoming the first Philippine township to receive the distinction. The recognition reflects decades of coordinated planning across accessibility, sustainability, community development, and economic growth—elements that increasingly influence corporate location decisions.

blocks.caption: The integration of offices, parks, residences, and lifestyle destinations reflects Filinvest City's thoughtfully planned approach to creating a community that supports business growth and long-term value. (Photo: Filinvest City)

blocks.text: The integration of offices, parks, residences, and lifestyle destinations reflects Filinvest City's thoughtfully planned approach to creating a community that supports business growth and long-term value. (Photo: Filinvest City)
A strategic business decision
As organizations prepare for the next phase of growth, location strategy is becoming more closely aligned with broader business priorities.

With only a limited number of commercial lots remaining, Filinvest City continues to offer prime commercial land for businesses and investors looking to establish a permanent presence in Metro South's leading central business district. Backed by decades of consistent value creation, sustained investor confidence, and continued commercial growth, these remaining lots provide a strong foundation for long-term business and investment success.

Beyond commercial value, locating within a master-planned city allows organizations to create a better everyday experience for their people. From walkable amenities and green open spaces to retail, dining, healthcare, and residential communities, Filinvest City enables businesses to offer employees an environment that supports productivity, convenience, and overall quality of life.

In Filinvest City, geography is no longer simply where business happens. It has become a strategic advantage that shapes how companies attract talent, strengthen their operations, and position themselves for the future.
To learn more about the commercial lot opportunities in Filinvest City, you may visit www.filinvestcity.com and follow the Facebook page @FilinvestCityOFFICIAL.

articles.title: Filipina American artist Thea Canlas wins 2026 Sondheim Art Prize
articles.summary: Filipina American artist Thea Canlas has been named the winner of the 2026 Janet and Walter Sondheim Art Prize, receiving the $30,000 award for her work exploring diasporic Philippine identity. Thea…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Arts and Culture
Her work explores Philippine identity and the diaspora through textiles, sculpture, and installation
Filipina American artist Thea Canlas has been named the winner of the 2026 Janet and Walter Sondheim Art Prize, receiving the $30,000 award for her work exploring diasporic Philippine identity.

Thea was announced as the winner Aug. 27 during an awards ceremony at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore. The honor is presented annually to support the career of a visual artist or visual artist collaborators living and working in the Greater Baltimore region in USA.

Thea has a conceptual, research-driven practice that examines Philippine identity through craft and material histories, sculptural objects, textiles, installations, and digital media. Her work also considers how Philippine materials and cultural forms are represented and transformed through migration and diaspora.

The artist earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Fibers from the Maryland Institute College of Art in 2006 and a Master of Fine Arts from Emily Carr University of Art and Design in Vancouver in 2023. She works as a studio artist, freelance designer, and educator.

Thea lives in Baltimore with her husband, David, and their son, Isagani. Her research has taken her to the Philippines and Spain, where, as a Jacques and Natasha Gelman Travel Fellow, she studied Spanish colonial-era archives and textile collections. She also spent a year researching Indigenous textile weaving practices in the Philippines, work that informed her investigations into colonial economies and the country’s history of labor migration.

The recognition comes two years after Thea was selected as a semifinalist for the Sondheim Art Prize in 2024. This year, she was one of five finalists, alongside Leigh Davis, Brandon Donahue-Shipp, Curran Hatleberg, and Danni O’Brien.

Works by the five finalists are currently featured in the Janet and Walter Sondheim Art Prize Finalists Exhibition at the Walters Art Museum’s Hackerman House. The exhibition, which opened June 25, runs through Sept. 13.

articles.title: What keeps Filipino political dynasties in power – a Rappler series
articles.summary: Why do political dynasties endure in the Philippines? Rappler looks at the families behind them and the forces that have allowed their influence to last for generations.

blocks.text: Why do political dynasties endure in the Philippines? Rappler looks at the families behind them and the forces that have allowed their influence to last for generations.

items: The 1987 Constitution prohibits political dynasties, but no legislation has been enacted to limit political power concentration in families.
A Rappler series investigates the enduring political power of certain families, examining their influence, political networks, and roles in government.
The series aims to map family connections among elected officials and will publish two profiles weekly leading up to the 35th anniversary of the Local Government Code of the Philippines.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The 1987 Constitution directs the state to “prohibit political dynasties.” But nearly four decades later, no enabling legislation has been enacted to set limits on the concentration of political power within families.

As a result, political families continue to wield significant influence across national and local politics in the Philippines. The same family names repeatedly appear on ballots and, after elections, on the lists of officials taking their oaths of office.
Why do Filipinos keep electing people from the same families? The answer is not always straightforward.

This Rappler series looks at the families that have held political power for generations, tracing how they built their influence, where such influence is strongest, and how it has endured over time. The profiles look at their family ties, political networks, how they rose to power, business interests, and roles in local and national government.

We chose these families based on the extent of their political presence, including the number of relatives who have held public office and cases where family members have simultaneously occupied multiple government positions. The selection was also shaped by the availability of contributors and reporting capacity in different provinces, so this series is not intended to be a definitive list or ranking of the country’s largest political dynasties.

The series draws on Rappler’s ongoing effort to map family connections among elected officials. Our team compiled and verified information from official government and public records, then used these data points to trace relationships and see how political power is passed, shared, and consolidated across generations.
Rappler will publish two profiles each week leading up to the 35th anniversary of the Local Government Code of the Philippines on October 10. Bookmark this page to catch the latest report.
The Dutertes’ 40-year reign: Forged from strongman and victim

blocks.caption: Person, Face, Head

blocks.text: It’s been 38 years since Davao City knew any other kind of governance but the Dutertes’.

What began with one man brandishing a local peace and order campaign in 1988 has expanded into a Philippine allurement to safety — a move that solidified the Dutertes’ political stronghold with three generations now being elected into city and national government positions.
Read the full story by Raizza P. Bello here.
The Pinedas of Pampanga: A dynasty by succession

More than three decades after Lilia “Nanay” Pineda first won the mayoralty of Lubao in 1992, the Pineda family remains firmly at the center of Pampanga politics, extending one of Central Luzon’s longest-running political dynasties.

Since 2010, the family has continuously occupied Pampanga’s two highest elective offices, with Lilia and her son Dennis “Delta” Pineda alternating between the governor and vice governor posts across successive elections.
Read the full story by Ahyenne Neleah Estacio here.

How the BARMM vote works
How will those in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) vote?

Because this is a parliamentary election, they will vote for a regional political party and one district representative. Voters don’t get to choose the BARMM chief minister. Rather, the elected parliament will pick the chief minister.

The BARMM parliament will have 80 members. Forty seats will go to party representatives (from the regional political parties), 32 seats go to parliamentary district representatives, and eight seats are reserved for sectoral representatives.

Delayed services an injustice to Bangsamoro — Loong

“Sang-ayon tayo sa decentralization kasi bakit natin i-centralize dito kung ang outcome ay kalahati ang nagagastos natin, kung ang outcome ay two years tayong delayed sa implementation. Because that is an injustice to the Bangsamoro people,” said engineer Don Mustapha Loong of the Progresibong Bangsamoro Party.
Loong defended decentralization as a way to make government services more efficient and responsive to communities.
He questioned the value of centralizing services when it results in lower spending outcomes and delays of up to two years in implementation.
Loong called the failure to deliver the gains of the Bangsamoro transition “the greatest injustice that could possibly happen.”
He said the “fruits of the revolution” may already be within reach, yet many Bangsamoro people remain unable to experience their benefits. – Angelle Matura
Angelle Matura is a Mover from Cotabato City.
Aug 27, 2026 6:47 PM PHT
Lim urges responsible spending, Kashim hits BARMM failures

“We have to take care of taxpayers’ money. Every family, every working-class family, every month, nakikita nila sa payroll nila, tax withheld. Can you imagine that money could’ve gone to one more sack of rice, one week’s worth of grocery?” said Nur-Ainee Tan Lim Misuari of the Mahardika Party.

Lim called for greater accountability in the use of public funds, pointing to the underutilization of the block grant, limited absorptive capacity, and inefficiency in spending within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
She said the region needs leaders who can restrain themselves, put people first, and use public funds for the Bangsamoro.
“This is a government of failure,” Abdulhussein Kashim of Indigenous, Settles, Sama and Minorities Alliance Party described the situation bluntly.
He said the government has a strong legal foundation to deliver resources to the people but has failed to do so.
Despite the criticisms, Lim said there remains an opportunity for the Bangsamoro to “rise from the ashes,” particularly for undecided voters who are weighing their choices.
She reminded the audience that “our children are watching,” and that the region’s youth continue to dream of a better future. – Angelle Matura
Aug 27, 2026 6:28 PM PHT
Sema, Basher clash over national interference in BARMM polls

A tense exchange unfolded between lawyer Omar Yasser Sema of the Bangsamoro Party and Alipikre Basher of the People’s Consultative Party, also known as the Mushawara Party, over electoral reform and possible national government interference in the regional elections.
Sema asked whether Basher would support reforms if interference occurs, clarifying that it was a serious question.
Basher affirmed his commitment to an “honest and credible election,” saying they are “101%” committed to a credible electoral process.
“Hindi ka matatakot sa national government?” Sema asked.
Basher hesitated before cackling in response, drawing attention from the audience. – Angelle Matura

articles.title: Close race as Iceland votes on whether to restart talks on joining EU
articles.summary: Turbulent international affairs have brought the vote forward, but the campaign has focused more on Iceland's vital fishing industry.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Latest opinion polls have been so close that the result is impossible to call
ByPaul Kirby
Europe digital editor
Icelanders are voting in a referendum to decide whether to resume talks on joining the European Union, 13 years after they were broken off.
In an indication of how tight the result is expected to be, the latest opinion poll put the No campaign in the lead with 51.6%. An earlier poll had put the Yes campaign ahead.
Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government had already intended to hold a referendum, but turbulent international affairs prompted her to bring it forward.
But the debate was fought less over Nato member Iceland's security concerns than over its vital fishing industry and sovereignty.
Voting is due to go on from 09:00 to 22:00 GMT on Saturday and the result is expected in the early hours of Sunday.
Iceland has a population of under 400,000. More than one in five voters had already cast their ballots in early voting before Saturday, according to Iceland's public broadcaster RUV.
What is the vote about?
The question on the ballot is, external: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"

Although Iceland is already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone as part of the European Economic Area, EU membership would bring it into the customs union and eventually the euro.

Iceland's application to join the EU was already well advanced when it put talks on hold in 2013, and European Commission officials have indicated that talks could be finalised in one or two years. Of the 35 so-called chapters of talks ranging from fisheries and economic policy to freedom of speech and free movement of goods, 27 had begun and 11 of them were provisionally complete, external.

A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU. It would mean backing a move towards an accession agreement. Any deal would then have to be approved by a second referendum, as well by parliament, and the constitution would have to be amended. The EU's 27 member states would also have to sign it off.
One Yes-campaign group, "Yes to See", says Icelanders should at least see what deal they can get, so they have all the information before a final decision.
Equally, a No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.
What are the key issues?

Sovereignty has been a crucial issue in the pre-referendum debate. Iceland fought hard to become fully independent from Denmark in 1944, and its fishing and marine industries make up almost 40% of exports.

No campaigners fear losing control over Iceland's prized fishing grounds under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy and they have vowed never to share their waters with anyone. Brussels has indicated Iceland could earn some kind of exemption, but it is considered potentially the biggest obstacle to any agreement.
Many Icelanders remember the so-called Cod Wars with the UK that Iceland won in the 1970s. And fisheries was always the issue that stopped Iceland joining the EU before.
However, in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system, Reykjavik moved to start accession talks in 2009, only to bring them to a halt in 2013.
Iceland is now one of Europe's most affluent nations and Eirikur Bergmann, professor of politics at Bifröst University, told the BBC that "many people attribute this to Iceland's independence".
One Icelandic trade union survey suggested this year that the country was more expensive than the next 10 most expensive countries in the world.
Although it has the fifth highest GDP (economic output) per capita in the world, interest rates are stubbornly high at 8% and inflation has climbed to 5.6%.
Yes campaigners argue that the economic benefits of the EU would help bring the rates down.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The "Yes to See" campaign believes Icelanders should see what EU deal can get

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The "Yes to See" campaign believes Icelanders should see what EU deal can get
What are Iceland's security concerns?
Iceland may be a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.
A bilateral US defence agreement has been in place since 1951 and the No campaign has said Iceland's security rests on both Nato and the US and EU membership is not a substitute for Nato.
Iceland has been a strong supporter of Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have viewed Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island with alarm.
However, there has also been concern at US President Donald Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland, and the fact that he has confused it with Iceland has caused alarm.
This year the EU and Iceland signed a security and defence partnership, and EU officials said the EU "offers an anchor in a community of values, prosperity and security".
What do the Yes and No campaigns say?

Ahead of the referendum, the two sides held a televised debate where the Yes campaign team was headed by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir and the No campaign was led by Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, chair of the opposition Independence Party.
Kristrún told the audience that Iceland was already well integrated in the European Union, and becoming a member would be "one of the biggest risk-reducing steps we can take".
She also made clear that a Yes vote did not necessarily mean that Iceland would join, and that if there was a No vote, the result would be respected.
Guðrún, meanwhile, stressed that the vote was not about whether Iceland should work well with Europe: "We already do, and we want that to continue."
Instead, she portrayed the referendum as a vote on whether Icelanders wanted to hand "decision-making powers" to Brussels on fisheries, agriculture and their natural resources.
Although geopolitics kick-started the government's decision to push for a return to EU talks, there has been little discussion of it during the campaign.
"It's lower on the agenda than many would think," says Hallgrimur Oddsson, director of EU-Iceland think-tank European Currents.

articles.title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE
articles.summary: The British citizen, who lives and works in the US, has supported Trump and ICE agents in the past.

blocks.text: British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is awaiting deportation.
Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and onetime political aide to rapper Kanye West, appears to be held in Louisiana, according to ICE's inmate registry.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said he "was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing", and will remain in custody pending deportation.
The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet". His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech.
Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, was arrested on 27 August after arriving at the airport in New Orleans.
He flew into the US in May 2019 and "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws", said DHS.
The DHS statement referred to him as "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom".
The BBC has asked the British embassy in Washington for comment. Yiannopoulos did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
"Being in detention is a choice," the DHS statement continued, calling on migrants who are in the US illegally to "self-deport now".
Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event that year called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention.

Yiannopoulos has become a critic of Trump, but still voices support for the Republican president's agenda. He posted in March this year on X that Trump "has lost his way, bought off by foreign interests".

Yiannopoulos has courted controversy with his comments on transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. He now calls himself an "ex-gay".

In 2020, he assisted Kanye West in the rapper's bid to become president. He also worked for Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former Republican congresswoman who fell out with Trump and became a fierce critic before resigning from office.
He has written columns titled "Birth Control Makes Women Unattractive and Crazy" and "Would You Rather Your Child Had Feminism or Cancer?"
He has also cheered on ICE raids, writing on X last year: "Total legal immunity for ICE agents when they're on duty."
He posted in 2025: "We have got to deport millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters."
Yiannopoulos also advocated on social media for "on the spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally".
Laura Loomer, a far-right commentator and Trump ally who has feuded with Yiannopoulos, took credit for his arrest by ICE.
She posted on X on Friday night that his flight back to the UK had already departed.
"This subversive foreign agent is already out of the United States and DHS tells me he's NEVER allowed to come back to the United States ever again," she said.

In 2017, he was uninvited from speaking at CPAC, a US conservative conference that also hosted Trump, after footage emerged of Yiannopoulos appearing to condone paedophilia. He also later apologised and resigned from Breitbart.
He denied the allegations, and said he had been speaking about his own experiences as a child.
Yiannopoulos was once regularly linked with the alt-right, a disparate group that is outspoken against political correctness and feminism and which includes neo-Nazis and white supremacists.
He has said he does not consider himself part of the alt-right, although he has called it "energising and exciting".

articles.title: How 'Book Queen' Dolly Parton inspired millions of children with gift of reading
articles.summary: Families across the globe share how free books from Parton's Imagination Library helped their children.
articles.byline: Sheila Flynn, Claire Keenan and Emily Holt

blocks.text: Dolly Parton first launched Imagination Library in her home county in Tennessee
BySheila FlynnReporting fromColorado, US and Claire Keenan and Emily HoltReporting fromAustralia and UK
One child in Denver called her "The Book Queen".
Another in Alabama calls her "Ms Dolly".

Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted her family with her first word - "orange" - after she and her twin sister received a free book in the post about colours. It came from Imagination Library, the literacy programme begun by late global superstar Dolly Parton.

Parton, who died this week aged 80, launched the philanthropic effort in 1995 to honour her father - whose difficult Appalachian upbringing never allowed him to finish school or learn to read and write.

"He was the smartest man I have ever known, but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," wrote Parton in an open letter on Imagination Library's website.
"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."

blocks.caption: Image caption, London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe signed her daughter up for the scheme when she was three months old

blocks.text: Image source, Harriet Anscombe
London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe signed her daughter up for the scheme when she was three months old

Imagination Library sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five. It first launched in Tennessee's Sevier County, where Parton grew up, before expanding across the US in 2000. The programme, which partners with local organisations, launched in Canada in 2006, the UK the following year, then Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.
By 2025, as Imagination Library celebrated its 30th anniversary, it had distributed more than 300m books - equating to one book mailed every 78 seconds, according to the organisation.
And for the families in receipt of the storybooks, the impact has been invaluable.

"It just blows my mind that it's readily available for every family that lives in my borough," said London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe, whose four-year-old daughter has been receiving Imagination Library books since she was three months old.
The free books helped Anscombe establish a reading-focused nighttime routine.

"I think that, if I didn't get those books, maybe I wouldn't have started doing bedtime stories till she was two - but because we were getting them so early, it embedded story time into our routine from when she was just a couple of months old," Anscombe said. "She probably doesn't remember a time when we weren't reading stories."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colorado mother Ciara Fernandez Faber's son called Parton 'the Book Queen'

blocks.text: Image source, Ciara Fernandez Faber
Colorado mother Ciara Fernandez Faber's son called Parton 'the Book Queen'

Imagination Library became part of the family routine for Ciara Fernandez Faber, too, after she signed up her son about eight years ago in Colorado. His favourite book for years was one written by Parton herself: I Am A Rainbow.
"We read it almost every night, and I never got tired of reading it to him," said Faber, 42.

"It's a book about different emotions, and so we would act out the different emotions, the different faces," she said. "At the back of the book, there's a little excerpt by Dolly talking about how everybody has a rainbow of feelings, and we would read that - and he would always point to her picture and say, 'There's the Book Queen.'"
Families like Faber's repeatedly remarked on how well curated the books were - detailing how topics helped their children not just with reading, but also with social and emotional development.
"There were themes that were addressed in a lot of the books that would have really helped us navigate issues," said Helen Cashell, of Dublin, Ireland.

She signed up both of her children, now aged seven and five, for the scheme. "Whether it was same-sex families or just different types of families, things about bravery, courage, bullying, things about different identities."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fernandez Faber's son, Aster, reads a book to his younger sister, Maya, in Colorado

blocks.text: Fernandez Faber's son, Aster, reads a book to his younger sister, Maya, in Colorado
Author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice Is Best was selected for distribution through Imagination Library, noted how the plotline features a black protagonist.
The programme also helps promote authors like herself; because of the selection, it "means 14,000 copies of my book have been sent to children in the UK".
"To choose between gas, electric, food or a book, you're going to choose a core need - but with the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, you don't have to do that," she said.
In inner-city Sydney, Australia, first-time mum Paige Stewart was astounded as she watched her children's progress with the programme.
Her twin girls, now four, "had a speech delay and some learning difficulties" - but Stewart noticed a change after just the second book.
"Not only did they learn their colours from that book… it kind of set the tone for them speaking and their joy for books."
She's become a vocal advocate for the programme, telling others: "It's so helpful, honestly."

blocks.caption: Image caption, In Dublin, Ireland, Helen Cashell's two children read books atop a pile of other titles they received in the post through Parton's Imagination Library

blocks.text: Image source, Helen Cashell
In Dublin, Ireland, Helen Cashell's two children read books atop a pile of other titles they received in the post through Parton's Imagination Library
Alabama grandmother Kristina Hadley also promotes the programme to friends and family - even incorporating Imagination Library into baby gifts.

"I'll pull up the Imagination books website, and I'll print that, and I'll put it in a picture frame, and I'll get little newborn books and stuff like that, and I'll put it with that for like a suggestion for new mothers," said Hadley, 53.

She signed up her nearly three-year-old granddaughter, Eillie Elaine, "before she was actually born". Now the child has her own bookshelf in their shared household - "and one whole shelf is for her Dolly books".
"She likes to go to go to the mailbox, and she's like, 'Ms Dolly! Ms Dolly!' and I'm like, 'Well, let's go see if Ms Dolly sent you a book!'"
A lifelong Parton fan, Hadley chokes up while detailing how she was at work when a friend texted to say the singer had died.
Imagination Library, she says, "is going to keep her memory going with the younger generation, and I hope and I pray that this is something that goes on for years and years and years."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Children's author Selina Brown saw 14,000 copies of her book sent to kids in the UK

blocks.text: Image source, Selina Brown
Children's author Selina Brown saw 14,000 copies of her book sent to kids in the UK
It's a legacy that Parton built quietly in the background as she presided over pop culture for more than six decades.
"The biggest thing that I like is the fact that she didn't do anything for recognition," said Geoff Blacklin, 67, of Manitoba, Canada.
He and his wife signed up their grandchildren for Imagination Library after a local doctor brought the programme to their region.
"She gave families more than books," Blacklin said. "She gave children a love of reading, precious moments with loved ones, and opportunities to learn and dream."
Such family stories and gratitude would undoubtedly have been music to Parton's ears; the expansion of the programme was truly a realisation of her own dream.

"In the beginning, my hope was simply to inspire the children in my home county, but here we are today with a worldwide programme that gives a book a month to well over 3 million children," she wrote on the Imagination Library site - also taking care to thank the partners "who have embraced my dream and made it their own".
At the centre of it, always, was her love for children - and her love for her father.
"Before he passed away, my Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done," Parton wrote.
"I can't tell you how much that meant to me, because I created the Imagination Library as a tribute to my Daddy."

articles.title: Landlady to 9/11 hijackers reveals their links to alleged Saudi spy
articles.summary: A woman who rented out homes to two al-Qaeda members speaks publicly for the first time - to the BBC.

blocks.text: Holly Ratchford has decided to speak out publicly for the first time
ByJane McMullen
BBC Panorama and BBC Radio 4
Holly Ratchford still cannot believe that the man who moved into the residential complex she once managed would go on to be accused of involvement in the darkest day in recent US history.
"It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that," she tells the BBC.
The man, Omar al-Bayoumi - a Saudi in his early 40s - moved to the complex in San Diego, California, with his family in September 1999.
The new resident at number 152 Parkwood Apartments quickly became a regular at Ratchford's pool parties. "He was always so bubbly and smiling," she recalls, "and just very, very friendly."
A few months later, Bayoumi would introduce Ratchford to two apparently unassuming, "polite" men, who would also become her neighbours.
The pair would become infamous for hijacking American Airlines flight 77, and crashing it into the Pentagon, in the 9/11 attacks.
Ratchford has been haunted by her connection to these three men for the past 25 years. She feels she was taken in by Bayoumi from the start.
"Whenever I had parties he would come and be a part of the activities," she recalls, adding that his family would invite her in for food.
"I enjoyed going over."

But Bayoumi, the one-time resident of 152 Parkwood, is now at the centre of the $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by several thousand families of victims and as well as survivors of 9/11.

On 11 September 2001, four passenger aircraft were hijacked by 19 members of the Islamist extremist network, al-Qaeda. In addition to the crash at the Pentagon - the US military's headquarters near Washington DC - two planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, causing both buildings to collapse. A fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, following resistance from passengers on board.
In all, almost 3,000 people were killed, including about 300 firefighters and other emergency workers at the World Trade Center.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The aftermath of the attack on the Pentagon on 9/11

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The aftermath of the attack on the Pentagon on 9/11

Bayoumi is alleged to have facilitated the 9/11 plot through the support he provided for the first two hijackers to arrive in the US - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - who lived at Parkwood for several months prior to the attacks.

The federal judge in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in New York found a year ago that the evidence created "a reasonable inference" that Bayoumi and a Saudi diplomat based in the US had been "co-ordinating with the Saudi government when providing assistance to the hijackers".
The judge's ruling has allowed the families' case to move forward. Saudi Arabia is appealing it and, together with Bayoumi, has always denied the allegations.
Ever since the attacks, Bayoumi has been the subject of reporting and speculation.
Ratchford - who saw him interacting with the hijackers and witnessed him providing a crucial act of support for them - has given a sealed declaration to the New York court.
But she has never spoken publicly about what she saw.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ratchford was property manager of Parkwood Apartments in the late 1990s

blocks.text: Image source, Holly Ratchford
Ratchford was property manager of Parkwood Apartments in the late 1990s
Finding Holly Ratchford was not easy.

After unwittingly becoming embroiled in the investigation into what the US government has described as "the most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history", she moved about as far from humanity as you can get in the United States.
I tracked her down to the high desert in the western US - rattlesnake country. She told me she avoided the news, and definitely did not speak to journalists. But, to my surprise, she agreed to talk.

Her interview with me casts doubt on the version of events Bayoumi has told police, the FBI and the New York court, and features in the BBC Radio 4 podcast, Intrigue: A 9/11 Story, and an upcoming BBC Panorama, 9/11: The Saudi Connection.
Intrigue: A 9/11 Story
Twenty-five years on from the deadliest terror attack in history, Jane McMullen asks why thousands of grieving families are still fighting for answers.

In early 1999, Ratchford landed on her feet. Life before then had been untethered - she had moved around, been married, pregnant and divorced before she was 21. But now, aged 27, she had a job she loved and a home.

As the new property manager of Parkwood Apartments, a squat complex of 175 low-rise apartments and townhouses in the San Diego suburbs, she says she excelled. Properties were never empty for long. But it was not the paperwork, nor the healthy pay check, that made the job a dream, it was the people.
Ratchford not only worked at Parkwood, she lived there too. Her clients were also her neighbours. And many were more than that - she says they became her friends.
"I always told my staff: 'You make them feel like this is their home, and they'll stay,'" she recalls.
As Ratchford made her mark at Parkwood, she was happy and secure in the world she had built - a world in which she knew everyone and everything.
Then, things fell apart in a dramatic and unexpected way.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Parkview Apartments complex, seen here today, in the San Diego suburbs

blocks.text: The Parkview Apartments complex, seen here today, in the San Diego suburbs
Omar al-Bayoumi moved into Parkwood claiming to be a mature student.
"I knew he was going to school. I'm not sure, other than that, what he did," Ratchford says.

More than two decades later, declassified FBI documents and court filings would reveal that Bayoumi's studies had, in effect, come to a halt in 1998. He was spending much more time organising religious activities in the Muslim community, which he often videotaped.
His constant filming, and his inquiring questions, aroused suspicions.

"It was a general consensus of people in the San Diego Muslim community that Bayoumi was an operative of the Saudi intelligence service," Richard Lambert, who led the city's FBI office investigation after 9/11, tells me.
But it was not Ratchford's business to pry. What mattered to her was whether he could pay the rent. And he could.
The FBI would later discover he was being paid about $90,000 (£55,600 at the time) a year.
Home videos show Bayoumi visiting Las Vegas and SeaWorld, and playing poolside with family
Bayoumi presented himself as an ordinary family man.
The Bayoumi who Ratchford saw was captured on his never-before-broadcast home movies - throwing a ball around with his family by the Parkwood pool, laughing when it drifted into the water.
Another video reveals him on an excursion to Las Vegas with his family. Wearing a floral shirt, he points out the rollercoaster by the New York, New York hotel casino.
"I bought into everything that he told me. I really thought that's how he was," Ratchford says.
But that version of Bayoumi is at odds with the man who emerges from other videos.
In summer 1999, Bayoumi filmed the United States Capitol in Washington DC from different angles, noting a "plan", and turning the camera on himself to deliver a reporter-style commentary.
The 9/11 families' lawyers allege he was surveilling the building as a potential target for the attacks. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia maintains it is a tourist video.
In his August 2025 judgement, the New York judge found that "all the Court can conclude" from the video is that Bayoumi "visited Washington DC and that he filmed the city".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bayoumi noted a "plan" while filming outside the Capitol

blocks.text: Image source, SDNY
Bayoumi noted a "plan" while filming outside the Capitol

On 3 February 2000, Bayoumi brought two young men into Ratchford's San Diego rental office. In an obvious hurry, she says, he perched on the filing cabinet as he told her that the two men were from his mosque and were staying with him while they looked for a place to rent.
"There was absolutely nothing unusual about them. They were nice, they were polite," she recalls.
The two men spoke no English, but Bayoumi took charge. Ratchford says he asked her what the two men would need to show in order to qualify for a Parkwood apartment.
"They didn't meet the income criteria at all, or the bank account. They had none of that," she tells me.
Ratchford had rules. It was a quick no.
But the two men did have several thousand dollars in cash. Bank records show that, the following day, Bayoumi took them to the nearest bank and helped them open an account.
Back at Ratchford's office on the third day, he figured a way around the problematic income criterion. He would co-sign their lease - becoming the legal guarantor for their apartment.
The rental agreement shows Bayoumi's multiple signatures. He was their guarantor, their friend, their emergency contact, and his Parkwood home was listed as their current address.
Without further delay, the two men moved into number 150, a one-bed apartment just a few doors down from Bayoumi's poolside townhouse.
The two men Bayoumi was assuming legal responsibility for - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - would become 9/11 hijackers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar

blocks.text: Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar
Holly saw the pair repeatedly in the following few months.
"I would have cookies and tea with them. It wasn't like they were just someone that came into the office and rented from us," she says.
Hazmi and Mihdhar stayed in their apartment until the end of May that year, and then moved out. Ratchford thought no more about it.

Sixteen months later, as America reeled in shock and grief in the days following the 9/11 attacks, she says a woman called asking her for a rental reference for them. Without thinking, she rattled off their details.
But the woman was not a property agent - she was a reporter.
Her next question shook Ratchford: "Did you know that they were two of the terrorists that flew their plane into the Pentagon?"
"And I went, 'What?'"

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bayoumi was arrested by the Metropolitan Police's anti-terror branch

blocks.text: Bayoumi was arrested by the Metropolitan Police's anti-terror branch
Then, the FBI came knocking.
On 14 September 2001, two special agents interviewed Ratchford in her Parkwood office.
She gave them Bayoumi's guarantor form, triggering an investigation into the man they would come to see as the main facilitator of the two hijackers' lives in San Diego.

Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI and working as a consultant to the 9/11 lawsuit families, says "as we began to identify the hijackers' associates, what became clear is that there was a network headed up by Omar al-Bayoumi".

The FBI found that Bayoumi's contacts had helped Hazmi and Mihdhar obtain California driver's licences, apply to flight schools, receive Middle Eastern wire transfers, and even arrange dental treatment.
The FBI agents wanted to interview Bayoumi. They traced him more than 5,000 miles (8,000km) to the UK, to Birmingham, where he had moved just before 9/11.
On 21 September 2001, he was arrested by the Metropolitan Police's anti-terror branch and detectives began questioning him.
Seeming unflustered, and at times indignant, Bayoumi initially denied knowing any of the hijackers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI, says Bayoumi headed up a network that involved the hijackers

blocks.text: Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI, says Bayoumi headed up a network that involved the hijackers
He said he had often helped people find accommodation but, when detectives pressed him, said he could not remember the names of anyone for whom he had guaranteed an apartment.
A day later, he said he remembered helping two individuals, "Nawaf" and "Khalid" - the first names of Hazmi and Mihdhar.
He admitted they were the only two people to whom he had given this level of support.
Bayoumi claimed he had met the pair in Los Angeles, after briefly overhearing them speaking Arabic in a restaurant. He said he had told them that if they ever went to San Diego, he could help them.

The next day, he told the British detectives, the men had shown up at his local mosque in San Diego saying they needed a place to live. He had then driven them back to Parkwood to see Ratchford about finding them an apartment.
After Hazmi and Mihdhar had moved in, Bayoumi said he had avoided them. He said he had left town, and that when he returned, he found they had moved on.
In his account, Bayoumi's association with the future hijackers was fleeting. But his story does not match Ratchford's version of events.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ratchford refutes Bayoumi's claim that his interactions with the hijackers were fleeting

blocks.text: Ratchford refutes Bayoumi's claim that his interactions with the hijackers were fleeting
"I know that's what he said, and I know that's bullshit," she says.
Before he brought the hijackers to her office, Ratchford says Bayoumi had asked her several times about finding an apartment for two people.
"I would tell him what would be available and he'd be like, 'oh no, no, I want that one'," she says. "He wanted something near him, and he was hoping for the least expensive place."

She also contradicts Bayoumi's claim that he hardly saw the hijackers after he secured their apartment, explaining that she had seen them together over the weeks that followed. On one occasion, the three of them had come to her office for tea and cookies.
"It's not like he just found them an apartment and never talked to them again," she says, adding that the three men "were definitely friendly".
Ratchford also told the FBI that when the hijackers had fallen behind with paying their rent, Bayoumi had paid it.
The Met Police held Bayoumi for seven days - the maximum at the time. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) decided not to extradite him to face charges.
On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.
Ratchford is still stunned.
"I can't believe he got away," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bayoumi has never been prosecuted but the 9/11 families have pursued him through the courts

blocks.text: Bayoumi has never been prosecuted but the 9/11 families have pursued him through the courts
The FBI continued to build a case against him, however.
San Diego agents discovered that two companies linked to the Saudi Ministry of Defence were providing Bayoumi with his $90,000 pay, but that he never went to work and accrued "outrageous" expenses.
His pay more than doubled just after the two hijackers' arrival in San Diego, agents found, and fell again after they left the US west coast.
Meanwhile, agents from the New York FBI office combed through a trove of documents received from the Met Police, following the search of Bayoumi's properties in Birmingham, the BBC has learned.

The FBI uncovered letters to a Saudi government-linked charity with direct ties to al-Qaeda, materials which they assessed could "demonstrate Omar al-Bayoumi's anti-American sentiments and beliefs", and writings by Bayoumi himself which they determined "can be interpreted as jihadist".
But none of this led to an indictment or prosecution.
The DOJ told the BBC it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there.
Bayoumi left the UK for Saudi Arabia in August 2002.

Two years later, he was, in effect, cleared when the US's 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the attacks - concluded he was "obliging and gregarious" and "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists". The FBI had not shown the Commission all the evidence it had gathered - and declined to comment when the BBC asked about this.

Meanwhile, the 9/11 families had started their attempts to pursue him through the courts, adding him as a defendant to their $1tn suit against various individuals, companies and governments for allegedly supporting al-Qaeda.

For years, the families campaigned for the FBI's investigation to be declassified. The wait was agonisingly slow, but since 2018 tens of thousands of pages of documents have been released to the New York court and via a presidential order signed by Joe Biden - including the FBI's interviews with Holly Ratchford.

In August last year, having considered the entire body of evidence, the judge in the 9/11 families' legal case said the evidence did not support the conclusion that Bayoumi had been "just an innocent participant".

Judge George B Daniels also noted later in his judgement that there was "a reasonable inference that all the apartment-related assistance he [Bayoumi] provided for the hijackers was not just acts of a good Samaritan, but rather that he was following" instructions from the Saudi government.

Saudi Arabia denies any involvement in 9/11 and has consistently argued that Omar al-Bayoumi was not a Saudi agent and did not have any involvement or foreknowledge of the attacks. It maintains that, under US law, it has sovereign immunity - official exemption of a ruler or state from certain types of civil suit and criminal prosecution - and that the case should be struck out.
The case is now with the US Court of Appeal, which will hear oral arguments in October.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ratchford now lives in an isolated area in the west of the US

blocks.text: Ratchford now lives in an isolated area in the west of the US
9/11 was a catastrophe that wrought personal trauma on tens of thousands of people - the families of the victims, the survivors, first responders and witnesses.
For Holly Ratchford, all the certainties and securities of her years at Parkwood came to an abrupt end.
Nothing was as it had seemed.

"I know a lot of peoples' lives changed immediately during 9/11. For me, within a week or two, my life, my ideals, my beliefs, everything changed so quickly. It was like a flip of a switch," she says.
"I felt so stupid. I trusted and I cared about people that did bad things. I don't ever want to be as blindsided as I was by them not being who they said they were."
Soon after 9/11, Ratchford quit Parkwood, property management, and the big city.
She moved first to the beach, then to a reservation, and later, to the middle of nowhere - all in an effort to escape the feeling she was being tricked.
Ratchford kept to herself, she tells me, interacting only with people she absolutely trusted.
"9/11 made me afraid of people," she says.

"Now I just prefer to be away from people that might be lying about who they are. You can't keep a secret when you live in a small town and that makes me feel more safe. I like being in a place where I can trust people."
But even as she has sought to escape further and further from the outside world, she is haunted by questions about what happened at Parkwood.
"Part of me wonders if there's something I could have done if I was more strict," she says.

articles.title: The Cultural Center of the Philippines in the 21st Century
articles.summary: The creation of the Governance Commission for Government-Owned or Controlled Corporations (GCG) through R.A. No. 10149 in 2011 marked an important turning point for the Cultural Center of the…

blocks.text: The creation of the Governance Commission for Government-Owned or Controlled Corporations (GCG) through R.A. No. 10149 in 2011 marked an important turning point for the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP). Among its significant effects was a stronger emphasis on board accountability and more active board involvement in policy formulation, decision-making, and institutional oversight.
The CCP main building restoration (Photo: Mark Balmores/Manila Bulletin0

The establishment of board committees, prompted by the GCG, has further strengthened governance. These committees have enabled more thorough deliberation of management proposals and board initiatives and have helped make decision-making more informed.
Performing arts network

The CCP has long worked closely with professional resident companies in music, dance, and drama, and has strengthened its continuing annual events, namely Pasinaya, Cinemalaya, and Virgin Labfest, to which Ternocon, a celebration of Filipino formal wear, was added in 2018.

With the closure of the main building, performances have been held at the Metropolitan Theater, the Samsung Performing Arts Theater at the Circuit in Makati City, and elsewhere in Metro Manila and the regions.

The outreach program has been active, sponsoring nationwide concerts of the Philippine Philharmonic Orchestra (PPO) and other groups. The PPO has continued to perform abroad, most recently in 10 cities in the United Kingdom. Ayala Land Malls has co-sponsored Metropolitan Opera HD and British National Theatre presentations of grand opera and Shakespeare plays.

This resident company network has expanded to include National Performing Arts Companies. More outstanding groups will be added as official CCP partners, creating more opportunities for collaboration.
Working with Generations X, Y, Z, and Alpha

Venturing beyond the established boundaries of the performing arts, the CCP conceived of Kanto Kultura to encourage the artistically inclined among ordinary young Filipinos. Its first project, Kanto-Kanta, sought to inspire young people to compose and perform using indigenous themes and musical instruments.

The concept was simple and accessible: participation was affordable, and the rules were straightforward. The response was enthusiastic, and many of those who took part have since gone on to pursue successful artistic careers.

With young audiences and emerging art forms in mind, the CCP also started projects in animation based on selected “Lola Basyang” stories, produced in partnership with De La Salle–College of Saint Benilde.

Continuing into new territory, the CCP launched an Animation, Comics and Game Development Grants Program. The results have been encouraging: one grantee, Ranida Games' “Sinag Fighting Game” (inspired by Philippine mythology), has achieved over 900,000 downloads on both Google Play and Apple iOS from numerous players worldwide.

To help deepen cultural roots among young Filipinos, initiatives were also taken to revive vanishing arts, notably traditional lullabies. “Himig Himbing: Mga Heleng Atin” was launched in 2022, consisting of audiovisual renditions of eight lullabies based on ethnomusicological research. Professionally arranged and produced, the selections are in Tagalog, Bicol, Kalinga, Subanon, Ilocano, Cebuano, and other Philippine languages.

Great art can hardly flourish without an appreciative audience. For creativity to flourish, people must have opportunities not only to experience the arts but also to have the knowledge and ability to understand and appreciate them.

The CCP has therefore partnered with the Philippine Normal University (PNU) on a program designed to deepen future teachers’ knowledge and appreciation of culture and the arts. The initiative has a powerful multiplier effect: PNU graduates will eventually teach in schools throughout the country, influencing not only their students but also their fellow educators. In this way, appreciation for the arts can reach far beyond the walls of the CCP and into classrooms and communities nationwide.
The visual arts

During its first five decades, the CCP devoted much of its attention to music, dance, drama, and film. For the CCP’s second half-century, the board has resolved to give greater prominence to the visual arts, covering painting, sculpture, graphics, photography, and other forms of visual expression.

The CCP has an outstanding collection of paintings, musical instruments, and ethnographic items. The painting collection includes the work that introduced modern art to the Philippines, Victorio Edades’ “The Builders,” as well as important works by Amorsolo, Zobel, Joya, and others through the 1980s. Dubbed the 21AM (21st Century Art Museum), it is being digitized and expanded to include more recent works and emerging forms such as installation and video art. More importantly, the CCP hopes to help bring greater international recognition to Philippine visual art and Filipino artists among leading museums and collectors around the world.

There are sculptures in various places within the CCP premises, including some by artists from ASEAN countries. These are now arranged on the lawn beside the Philippine Navy Headquarters along Roxas Boulevard.

Plans are underway to create a permanent ASEAN sculpture garden within Liwasang Kalikhasan, the tree-covered four-hectare area south of the main building. The Liwasan is planned to be a cultural destination in its own right, with sculpture, fountains, open-air performance areas, perhaps a grove of native flowering trees, and a pool where children can sail miniature boats. It could be a welcoming place where art, nature, recreation, and community can come together.
Renovating the CCP main building

The renovation of the CCP main building became necessary after more than five decades. Structural and mechanical deficiencies had accumulated, including leaks through the concrete roof, water seepage from below, deteriorating electrical systems, damaged drainage and sanitary facilities, and concerns about the building’s structural integrity.

When the CCP was inaugurated in 1969, it ranked among the finest in the world. More than half a century later, however, technology has advanced dramatically. Acoustics, theatrical lighting, stage engineering, audiovisual recording, and production systems have all undergone major transformations. The renovation represents not simply the repair of an aging structure but also an opportunity to equip the CCP for the next generation of artistic production.

For the medium term, the complex development plan envisions a separate building for administrative offices not directly required for main building productions. In keeping with this plan, administrative offices will continue to be housed in the CCP Annex. The space released in the main building will therefore be devoted to conference rooms, exhibitions, official reception areas, and other public-oriented functions, helping transform the main building into a destination that visitors will experience as a cultural attraction in its own right.

With global warming and a rising population, the CCP is exploring possibilities of building facilities at the Clark Economic Zone. As the CCP looks beyond its historic home, its continuing challenge—and promise—is to ensure that the arts remain a vital, accessible, and evolving part of the nation’s future.

Note: The CCP Board of Trustees consists of the following: chairperson emerita, Imelda Romualdez Marcos; chairman, Jaime C. Laya; vice chairpersons, Ma. Carissa O. Coscoluella and Ma. Margarita M. Floirendo; president Kaye C. Tinga; and trustees Isidro A. Consunji, Felix S. Duque, Gizela M. Gonzalez, Teodoro S. del Mundo, Jr., Marivic del Pilar, Jose Tomas C. Syquia, and Jonathan M. Velasco. Dennis N. Marasigan is vice president and artistic director and Jose Victor M. Gaite is vice president for Administration and Finance.
Comments are cordially invited, addressed to [email protected].

articles.title: What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans
articles.summary: Households and businesses have become used to tariffs impacting the cost of living for more than year now, so what will change now?

blocks.text: If Trump's threat to raise tariffs on Canadian vehicles from 25% to 50% from 1 January 2027 becomes a reality, then that would deal a further blow to the automotive industry.
Cars, trucks and parts are among the main goods traded between the US, Canada and Mexico, with the manufacturing sector and supply chains stretching across borders.
Despite previous tariffs increasing costs for manufacturers, car dealerships have absorbed the "lion's share" to date, according to Bernard Yaros, lead economist at Oxford Economics.
"But that cushion is wearing thin," he adds. "The recently threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, trucks, and car parts would feed through to consumer prices more readily than before."

Yaros thinks higher costs on imports to the US could accelerate a trend of manufacturers prioritising luxury cards, SUVs and pick-up trucks and push up prices in the used-car market if supplies of new but less-expensive vehicles becomes tight.
Carney has decided not to match Trump's 50% tariff threat so far, but a 25% import tax on certain American vehicles has been in place since last year.
Construction materials such as steel, aluminium as well as lumber wood have had tariffs in place before the latest escalation, though Canada has now matched US rates on the metals at 50%.
Carney has also imposed import taxes on several US wood products, such as plywood, and even screws used to fix timber together.
That means building firms that import such materials will face higher costs and may choose to pass those on through higher prices - pushing up the cost of homes, for example.

The Forest Products Association of Canada says tariffs would "raise costs on both sides of the border", while on the US side, Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) urged Trump to make building materials exempt from his tariff agenda due to an "ongoing housing affordability crisis".
"Building material tariffs heighten market uncertainty, strain supply chains and increase construction costs," he says.
In 2024 the US imported $23bn (C$32bn, £17bn) worth of wood products, with almost half from Canada, according to a US Congress report.
But the so-called "lumber wars" between the nations on soft wood used in housebuilding are not new and stretch back decades.
A key factor in this episode of the tariff war is the volume of household items that have been specifically targeted as opposed to raw materials.
Carpets, washing machines, furniture, fridges and even knives, forks and spoons are set to have tariffs applied by Canada.

While there is a risk prices on some of those goods being imported from the US could rise, the more likely scenario is that consumers will turn to domestic alternatives, according to Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics.
He says Carney's latest move has intentionally targeted goods where Canadians can "shift to domestic suppliers instead".
"Like hair care products, you really can just buy that domestically instead," he adds.
Saunders explains Carney's response aims to "minimise the impact on Canadian households as much as possible by picking very fungible goods".

The Budget Lab at Yale, which monitors the impact of US government policy on the economy, says it anticipates seeing marginal increases in furnishing and other household equipment for Americans largely due to tariffs on lumber and other materials.
There may not be a material impact on alcohol prices, but it's clear the trade war has had an impact on Canadians' choice of drink.
Many provinces in the country banned US alcohol sales last year in response to previous tariffs, with the American wine and spirits industry saying exports to the country dropped more than 70%.
Carney asked the provinces to restore US alcohol to the shelves during trade talks, but now that they have collapsed, it's likely the ban will return.
Saunders says there's been a big push to "buy Canadian" from politicians and it has been successful when it comes to the strong stuff.
"That's really had an impact on the American alcohol industry," he adds.

Saskatchewan and Alberta are ​the only provinces that still sell ​American alcohol, but the former has announced its own 50% charge on US imported booze, set to kick in on 8 September, when the wider Canadian tariffs do.
While tariffs can end up hitting consumers in the pocket, there are other impacts on households.

Import taxes can complicate trade for businesses that have cross-border supply. As well as the higher costs, the uncertainty created by the trade war could put off investment plans and stunt job creation.
Saunders suggests the biggest impact on households may not just be through prices, but job losses instead.

"If you're, let's say, a bespoke furniture producer in BC [British Columbia], you're now facing a 50% tariff on your exports to the US - that could really shut the business down. I think that would be more the direct impact on households as opposed to these retaliatory measures."

Canada's forest industry employs almost 200,000 people and has called on the government to boost domestic demand through federal housing programs to make greater use of Canadian wood, though it admits "no support package can replace reliable access to our largest export market".

When it comes to US, consumers are unlikely to see much of a difference in terms of the cost of living as result of this latest battle with Canada, but frictions to trade can have longer-term economic impacts.

Such tensions also feed into concerns over the free-trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA. Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form.
Despite the deal remaining operational, tariffs risk putting off talks in the near future, creating more uncertainty for cross-border trade.

John Iselin, associate director at the Budget Lab at Yale, estimates the cost will only be about $3 per American household on average, but when taking into account Trump's wider trade war with the rest of the world, and particularly China, the added costs rise to about $1,000 for the average family.

"It's hard to view this particular instance with Canada in isolation because we've had similar interactions with a range of other countries, all of which makes doing business harder. It's just another in a series of tariff shocks."

articles.title: The bond market prepares for a hike to interest rates, while US stocks drift lower
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — The bond market swung Friday as investors built bets that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates soon to get the nation's high inflation under control. U.S. stocks, meanwhile,…

blocks.text: NEW YORK (AP) — The bond market swung Friday as investors built bets that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates soon to get the nation's high inflation under control. U.S. stocks, meanwhile, dipped but not by much after economists said a speech by Chairman Kevin Warsh helped strengthen faith that the Fed will do what's needed to bring inflation down, even if it causes pain for the economy in the short term.
The S&P 500 fell 0.2% after flipping between modest gains and losses through the morning. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 9 points, or less than 0.1%, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.5%.

The reaction was stronger in the bond market following Warsh's first speech as chairman of the Fed at an annual economic symposium held in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The mountain setting has been the backdrop for major Fed policy announcements in the past, and the pressure was on Warsh.

Worries had grown that his tough talk about getting inflation down to the Fed's 2% target may be just that, unless the Fed backs it up with action. The Fed could hike short-term interest rates to get inflation under control, but it could also feel deterred from doing so because that would slow the economy and hurt prices for investments. And President Donald Trump, who appointed Warsh, has been vocal about wanting interest rates to be lower rather than higher.

Warsh was adamant again on Friday that he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed plans to do with rates for its two jobs of keeping inflation low and the job market strong. He has said he wants markets to react to what incoming data says about the economy and inflation rather than what the Fed says.

But Warsh also said Friday that "short-term interest rates are the predominant tool" for the Fed to do its job. And he said, "I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive," an implication that short-term interest rates may not be high enough to tamp down the economy and inflation.
The yield on the two-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for what the Fed will do with its federal funds rate, jumped to 4.35% from 4.22% just before the speech.

That's a big move for the bond market, and it was because traders upped their forecasts that the Fed will hike its federal funds rate as soon as next month. They're now betting on a nearly 58% probability of that, up from the 35% seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group.

Longer-term yields also rose following some initial zigzags, but not by as much as shorter-term yields. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.72% from 4.67% late Thursday, and the 30-year Treasury yield got to 5.21% from 5.19%.

All the moves, including the modest ones for stocks even though higher interest rates tend to hurt them, indicate investors "pricing a more credible Fed," according to economists at Bank of America led by Aditya Bhave.

"The positive market reaction highlights that investors place a premium on policy clarity, even when that clarity carries" a message implying higher interest rates, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management.

Yields had gotten so high for longer-term bonds this summer, in part because of worries about inflation staying high in the future, that the U.S. Treasury Department made an unusual move last week and said it would buy back more bonds, though analysts said it will likely have only a limited effect.

On Wall Street, Gap jumped 12.9% after the retailer reported stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also said Michael Francis, an industry veteran who began his career on the retail sales floor, will take over as head of its Old Navy stores.

Marvell Technology fell 10.3% even though the chip company reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts' expectations. CEO Matt Murphy said its business related to artificial-intelligence technology is strong, and it raised its forecasts for upcoming revenue growth.
But analysts said much of that optimism may have already been baked into Marvell's stock price, which came into the day with a surge of 184% for the year so far.

After rocketing higher for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks across the industry are confronting skepticism that they shot too high and that booming demand for AI chips may fade if the AI revolution does not produce as much profit as promised.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 19.23 points to 7,711.76. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 9.45 to 53,559.99, and the Nasdaq composite sank 138.93 to 26,402.42.
In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea's Kospi fell 1.8%, and France's CAC 40 rose 1% for two of the world's bigger moves.
