articles.title: B.C. NDP MLA Joan Phillip dead at 74
articles.summary: Joan Phillip, the NDP MLA for Vancouver-Strathcona and wife of Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs (UBCIC) Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, has died.

image.caption: Joan Phillip, a B.C. NDP MLA who died Friday at the age of 74, is being remembered as a tireless advocate for Indigenous peoples. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Joan Phillip, the NDP MLA for Vancouver-Strathcona and wife of Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs (UBCIC) Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, has died.
Phillip remembered as a tireless advocate for Indigenous rights
The UBCIC released a statement saying Phillip, also known as Amshen, died peacefully surrounded by her family on Friday afternoon.
She was 74. While an exact cause of death was not stated, the UBCIC asked people donate to the B.C. Cancer Society in lieu of sending flowers.
"British Columbia lost a powerful and respected leader when Joan Amshen Phillip died earlier today," said B.C. Premier David Eby in a written statement.
Eby said the NDP caucus and staff are grieving alongside Phillip’s family.
Earlier this year, Eby said that Phillip was "very ill" and that her colleagues were all praying for her.
He called Phillip a "hugely respected member of many communities" and a "loved and valued" colleague of those in the legislature from across party lines.
Phillip, an Indigenous leader, was credited by Eby as one of the reasons why the NDP halted its plans to suspend sections of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA).
She was first elected in Vancouver in a 2023 byelection, and won again in B.C.'s general election the following year.
'Impact was nationwide'
Judith Sayers, president of the Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council, said Phillip's willingness to vote against the B.C. NDP caucus on the matter of repealing DRIPA showed her principles.
"Her impact was nationwide," said Sayers. "She always pursued the best possible solutions for First Nations and Indigenous people in this country."
Sayers said she knew Phillip for about 40 years.
Whether it was as a member of the Penticton Indian Band council or as an MLA, Sayers said Phillip poured her heart into her work.
Sayers also remembered Phillip as a dedicated, proud mother who wanted to show her children everything about their culture and language.
A flood of tributes poured in across social media, remembering Phillip and lauding her legacy as a politician, advocate and a kind soul.
"She spent a lifetime at the front of the fight for justice," said federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis. "Now, it is up to all of us to carry her powerful legacy forward."
A storied past
Phillip was the granddaughter of Chief Dan George, a Tsleil-Waututh actor, poet and public speaker.
In her role as MLA, she served as parliamentary secretary for community development and non-profits.
Before her time as an MLA, Phillip worked as a youth counsellor at Britannia Secondary School and as education and program director at the Aboriginal Friendship Centre.
She served as a councillor and lands manager for the Penticton Indian Band, of which she was a member.
Prior to provincial politics, she ran federally for the NDP in 2019 and 2021, but was not elected.
She has five surviving children, 15 grandchildren, and one great-grandchild, according to her legislature profile.
With files from The Canadian Press and Hana Mae Nassar

articles.title: [Vantage Point] PROCAP: How a scam came to look legitimate
articles.summary: A look at how an apparently well-organized, cross-border operation combined gaming, cryptocurrency, referral networks, purported insurance, technology, international events, prominent personalities,…

blocks.text: A look at how an apparently well-organized, cross-border operation combined gaming, cryptocurrency, referral networks, purported insurance, technology, international events, prominent personalities, and genuine early payouts to manufacture credibility on an extraordinary scale

items: ProCap International (PROCAP) successfully deceived sophisticated individuals, including businessmen and politicians, by creating a facade of legitimacy and credibility, despite being identified as a Ponzi scheme by regulators.

The operation attracted participants through promises of high returns, purported insurance, and social proof from prominent figures, which obscured the underlying fraudulent nature of the investment scheme.

As withdrawals began to halt and legal actions were initiated against its operators, the complexity of the fraud revealed that even educated and wealthy individuals are not immune to sophisticated scams that exploit trust and credibility.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ProCap did not become believable by targeting only the gullible. It manufactured credibility so effectively that businessmen, academics, lawyers and even former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II appeared persuaded that nothing was amiss.
The most dangerous scams are not those that look like scams. They are those that look legitimate, behave legitimately and, for a surprisingly long time, pay people as promised.

PROCAP International (PROCAP) may be one of the more extraordinary examples because among those drawn into its orbit were precisely the people we normally assume should know better: businessmen, politicians, lawyers, academics and other sophisticated Filipinos accustomed to making intelligent decisions involving money.

And who wouldn’t be reassured when even former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II appeared convinced nothing was amiss? Aguirre attended an October 2023 PROCAP gathering at a Makati hotel raided by police, who arrested 20 people.

blocks.caption: INVESTMENT SCAM? Marketing firm ProCap International holds a ‘Galaxy Night’ at the Dusit Thani Hotel in Makati on October 15, 2023, prior to an “entrapment operation” leading to the arrest of 20 people related to the company. Courtesy of Presidential Anti-Organized Crime Commission

blocks.text: The Philippine National Police (PNP) Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) identified him as one of the company’s lawyers, while GMA News reported that Aguirre “insisted that there was nothing wrong with the company’s transactions.” (READ: Procap denies scam allegations as SEC reiterates firm’s illegal activities)

Israelito “Bobbet” P. Torreon, a prominent trial lawyer and academician, approached us with documents and an insider’s account of how PROCAP operated. He represents one of its biggest alleged victims, whose identity I am deliberately withholding because this story is not about her. What interests me is how an operation promising returns that should have triggered alarm bells became sufficiently believable to attract people nobody would ordinarily describe as gullible.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said in October 2023 that PROCAP offered investment contracts disguised as gaming packages ranging from about P73,000 to P4.3 million, promising returns of 6% to 42% monthly. Participants supposedly followed a prescribed gaming formula, while a “capital protection insurance” mechanism purportedly protected their money after successive losing predictions.

Forty-two percent monthly should ordinarily have ended the conversation. But PROCAP had an extraordinarily persuasive answer: people were getting paid. According to Torreon, participants funded gaming accounts using payments converted into USDT or Tether, a stablecoin pegged to the US dollar. Dashboards displayed daily winnings, supposedly split 50-50 between PROCAP and the player, and winnings initially could be withdrawn the following day.

That shifts the psychology completely. Imagine a trusted friend showing you his account, playing and successfully withdrawing his winnings. You try it yourself and get paid. At that point PROCAP no longer needs to convince you its system works; your own experience seems to prove it. Add purported insurance, cryptocurrency technology and a dashboard that Torreon says generated an insurance policy whenever an account was opened, and risk itself appeared to have been engineered away.

Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission independently warned in April 2024 about substantially the same proposition—packages costing 1,235 to 74,000 USDT, purported capital insurance, referral incentives and monthly returns of 6% to 42%.
Then came social proof. Torreon’s documents describe a lavish Dubai event featuring raffles for Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Mercedes-Benz and BMW vehicles, gold bars and luxury watches.

Businessmen, lawyers, politicians, media personalities and other prominent people participated. Each layer answered another doubt: the capital was supposedly insured, withdrawals proved the money was real, prominent participants supplied credibility and dashboards provided technological reassurance. PROCAP’s apparent genius was the industrialization of trust.

The SEC eventually reached a very different conclusion. It revoked PROCAP International’s corporate registration and found characteristics of a Ponzi scheme, where money from newer participants finances payments to those who entered earlier. (READ: From robots to beef pares: The classic Ponzi scheme is still scamming Filipinos)

blocks.caption: How I recovered the money I invested in MFT

blocks.text: If that characterization correctly describes PROCAP’s economic machinery, the successful withdrawals that convinced investors of its legitimacy were not proof of sustainability. They were precisely what enabled the operation to expand.

Then the machinery apparently began breaking down. Torreon says withdrawals stopped being released normally in December 2024. Participants were told that Singaporean PROCAP figure James Teo had been jailed in China and that his absence prevented access to funds because he supposedly controlled one of three security keys needed for blockchain transactions.
Torreon says his client’s group checked Teo’s whereabouts through the Singapore embassy and, by January 2024, filed a criminal case against alleged foreign PROCAP operators.

Another major victim filed separately in Santa Rosa, Laguna the following month. Torreon says both cases eventually reached court, producing non-bailable arrest warrants that were subsequently used in seeking Interpol Red Notices against the foreign respondents. Interpol Red Notice is a global request by International Police Criminal Organization to law enforcement agencies worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender or similar legal action.

That chronology is important because it complicates what happened next. In May 2025, another lawyer representing six alleged victims publicly announced a P42-billion large-scale estafa complaint and included members of the family Torreon represents among those accused.

Torreon disputes both their alleged role and the headline amount, pointing out that documents he provided show the six complainants’ own claimed placements were below P20 million. The P42-billion figure therefore should be treated for what it presently is: an allegation in a complaint, not a judicial determination of actual losses or criminal liability as claimed by the lawyer/vlogger.

More significantly, Torreon argues that his client had already gone after the alleged foreign operators more than a year earlier since January 2025 and helped pursue the warrants and Red Notices against them.

That does not by itself settle who ultimately bears responsibility; those are questions for prosecutors and the courts. But it is a material part of the chronology and demonstrates why we should distinguish allegations against particular Filipino participants from facts already established by regulators.

What regulators have established is serious enough. The SEC acted against PROCAP’s investment solicitation, while Hong Kong authorities separately warned investors about substantially the same products.

What deserves further investigation is how an apparently well-organized, cross-border operation combined gaming, cryptocurrency, referral networks, purported insurance, technology, international events, prominent personalities and genuine early payouts to manufacture credibility on an extraordinary scale.
PROCAP’s lesson therefore is not that foolish people chased impossible riches. That explanation is convenient but intellectually lazy.

A sophisticated investor is not immune from fraud merely because he is educated, wealthy, politically connected or surrounded by lawyers. A sophisticated fraud understands precisely what sophisticated people demand before surrendering their money: evidence, credibility, professional validation, successful transactions, and people they trust.
PROCAP apparently supplied them all. Perhaps that is the darkest triumph of a well-organized financial fraud: it never asks intelligent people to swallow an absurdity whole.

It buries the lie beneath payouts, dashboards, prominent names and every reassuring sign of legitimacy—until doubt feels foolish, belief feels rational and, one day, the screen still shows a fortune, but the money is gone. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Canada poaches dozens of top US researchers for its universities
articles.summary: Researchers in fields like climate and medicine are being lured north by new research funding.

blocks.text: Canada is hiring dozens of researchers away from US universities, including top research institutions such as Harvard as its relationship with its neighbour continues to sour.

More than three-fourths of the 64 professors who are moving to Canada from around the world will come from the US. Under a new government programme, they'll receive funding from a pool of C$504m ($362m; £268m) for research in fields such as climate change and medicine.
US President Donald Trump's administration has accused universities of being dominated by left-wing ideology and diversity policies, and of failing to tackle alleged campus antisemitism.
The BBC contacted the White House and US Department of Education.

The administration has also frozen federal research grants for many different institutions and groups that they have argued are wasteful, external. That uncertainty is helping lure researchers elsewhere.
Meanwhile, Canada is asserting itself more on the global stage while it pushes back against the US in their escalating trade war, which reached a major turning point over tariffs recently.
One climate researcher told the BBC he was relocating to Canada in part because his work in the US had become more difficult in recent years.

Seth Guikema, a climate resiliency researcher at the University of Michigan and one of the 48 US researchers relocating to Canada, said he decided to approach Canadian institutions last year in search of opportunities.

"The funding environment in the US for anything related to climate and resilience has become challenging," Guikema said. "I was looking for a good intellectual home where I could have practical impact."
Over the next eight years, Guikema said he would use C$8m to research tools for better preparing for natural hazards, like storms and wildfires, at the University of Western Ontario.
The University of Michigan, his former employer, declined to comment.
Canada's Industry Minister Melanie Joly said on Thursday the government was "very glad that these fantastic professors are coming".

Asked if the programme was poaching US talent and whether it could be viewed by the Trump administration as an escalation of the US-Canada trade war, she said on Thursday: "The US administration is taking its own decisions and we're taking ours."
Some of the researchers chosen for the programme, like Guikema, were born and raised in the US. Others are Canadians who worked abroad and are now returning home.

Peter Caravan, who worked for two decades as a biopharmaceutical researcher and professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, appeared emotional at a Thursday news conference announcing the research appointments.
Caravan is researching how illnesses like cancers and chronic diseases can be better detected - work that will now be done out of the University of British Columbia in Vancouver.
Steven Lamy, a professor of International Relations at the University of Southern California, argued that major grant agencies "have been cut and politicised" by the current US administration.
"All of a sudden employment offers from external universities are attractive," he said.
Stephanie Burt, an English professor at Harvard University, believed the funding cuts were "a generational disaster for science and scientists".
She told the BBC that Canada had offered a "far more welcoming environment" for academics.
US universities are still among the top ranked in the world, according to QS Universities Rankings, with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Stanford and Harvard in the top five.
Lynn Pasquerella, the president of the American Association of Colleges and Universities, said institutions feel "helpless" in the face of federal and state cuts.
The deeper concern, she added, "is not the short-term brain drain", but "the possibility that the US could become less attractive as a place to pursue knowledge".

articles.title: Controversial plans for a Daniel Andrews sculpture officially scrapped by Victorian government
articles.summary:
The $134,000 cost of the statue of the former Victorian premier has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Carroll government in Victoria has cancelled controversial plans for a statue of former Labor premier Daniel Andrews.
Work began in May on the statue commemorating the former premier’s more than 3,000 days in office, as part of a 1999 policy recognising long-serving Victorian premiers.

But the premier, Ben Carroll, announced an end to the Kennett government policy on Saturday, appointing an independent panel to review how Victoria commemorates officials with statues and state services.
He directed work on the Andrews statue to cease.
“We are grateful to former premiers for their service. But gratitude does not require a taxpayer-funded statue,” Carroll said.
“I respect your money. That means being careful and deliberate about how government spends it.”

The policy automatically recognising long-serving Victorian premiers with a statue on Treasury Place was introduced ahead of the 1999 state election by then-premier Jeff Kennett. Kennett himself fell short of the milestone.

The “independent and bipartisan” panel will make recommendations about the future state funerals and memorial services. The statue contract will not be cancelled, instead the panel will select an alternative subject and location for the commissioned work.
The $134,000 cost of the planned statue of Andrews has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition.

blocks.caption: A statue of former Labor premier John Cain stands outside Treasury Place in Melbourne. Photograph: James Ross/AAP

blocks.text: “If we come to government we will not allow that statue to proceed,” the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said on 30 July.
“Victorians are fed up with Labor’s waste – that’s why it’s time for a Government that treats your money with respect,” she wrote in a social media post.

Andrews was premier of Victoria from 4 December 2014 to 27 September 2023. While the former premier was yet to comment on the decision to axe his effigy, in 2023 he claimed there was “no magic” to the 3,000 day milestone.
“People who spend a lot of time talking about legacy usually spend not enough time actually building one,” he said at the time.

In May, the state government confirmed Meridian Sculpture, the company that created the statues of the other four Victorian premiers who reached the milestone, was selected after a standard procurement process.

At the time, a Victorian government spokesperson said: “Daniel Andrews led Victoria through some of its toughest moments and never stopped fighting for working people. Under a policy introduced by the Kennett government, Victorian premiers who serve more than 3,000 days in office are recognised with a statue along Treasury Place in honour of their service to the state.”

Four former Victorian premiers have been commemorated in bronze at Treasury Gardens, they include Sir Albert Dunstan, Sir Henry Bolte, Sir Rupert Hamer and John Cain junior. Sir James McCulloch, who served more than 3000 days over non-consecutive terms has not been recognised with a statue.

articles.title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela
articles.summary:
US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves

Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy…

blocks.text: Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.

The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.
The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more ​than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”.
Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves.
“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media.
Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves.
Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest.

Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment ​into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude.
Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, ​which could ​be eased through ​cheaper oil supplies and expanded output.
The US ​also has ‌been looking ​for solutions ​to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.

Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”.
The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.

“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.”
The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields, according to the Journal.
Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Trump says U.S. makes deal to control 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that his administration has entered a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that, if realized, could give the U.S. access to vast amounts of the South American…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump is seen at the Johnson Space Center's Mission Control Center in Houston on Friday. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that his administration has entered a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that, if realized, could give the U.S. access to vast amounts of the South American country's untapped oil reserves, at cost.
U.S. president touts agreement as 'biggest oil deal in world history'

Trump in a social media post announced the agreement he said was negotiated by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez.
"The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!" Trump wrote.

Rodríguez's government in a statement said the deal involves the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels. It said the agreement could draw $100 billion US in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over $209 billion US in taxes for Caracas.
Rodríguez in a posting on Telegram predicted the deal "will have a significant impact on our nation's revival."

The agreement allows for the United States to partner with an unnamed private operator in Venezuela to create a new private company to take hold of the reserves, according to a U.S. official familiar with the contours of the deal.

items: Trump administration tells prosecutors to avoid criminal probes of acting Venezuelan president
U.S. pressure on Venezuela hasn't eased, even as world's attention turns to Iran

blocks.text: The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, added that Rodríguez granted the company 100-year rights to develop the oil fields.

The deal gives the United States 55 per cent effective output of the new private company — including an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost. The company would be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the official.

The announcement of the deal comes nearly nine months after the U.S. military at Trump's direction carried out an operation to capture Venezuela's then-president Nicolás Maduro and spirit him to the United States to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.
U.S. gas prices put pressure on Trump
Trump faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran reaches a six-month milestone with no conclusion in sight.
The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.
The U.S.-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20 per cent of the world petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.
The average price of gas in the U.S. stood at about $4.09 US a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. The average price was $3.21 US at the same time last year.

items: Venezuela's collapse, Trump's military buildup and Maduro's capture: How did we get here?
Who is Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela's recently captured president?

blocks.text: A significant drop in U.S. gas prices tied to the agreement should not be expected immediately. Experts have repeatedly warned that a substantial boost in Venezuelan oil production will not happen quickly as repairing and expanding infrastructure takes years and requires billions of dollars.
Persuading big American oil companies to return to the region could face headwinds given the political uncertainty and decades of badly damaged infrastructure.
Trump wants oil companies in Venezuela

Days after the ouster of Maduro, Trump gathered oil executives at the White House and called on them to rush back into Venezuela. Executives expressed interest in the opportunity but there was also a measure of caution given their past experience in the country.
Trump pushes wary U.S. oil execs to move into Venezuela
Darren Woods, CEO of ExxonMobil, the largest U.S. oil company, said at that moment he saw the country as "un-investable."
But Trump has insisted that his administration has brought a measure of stability to Venezuela.

Trump has argued that Venezuela stole U.S. oil when former Venezuelan president Hugo Chavez moved decades ago to nationalize hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those owned by American oil companies.

Rodríguez, in one of her early moves after taking power, signed a law that opens the nation's oil sector to privatization and reversed a bedrock tenet of the self-proclaimed socialist movement that has ruled the country for more than two decades.
Rubio said on X that the agreement would usher in billions in private investment into Venezuela and lead to lower gas prices in the United States.
"This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people," Rubio posted.
The oil bought from the new company would go toward filling the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve and toward military use, according to the U.S. official.
Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground.
That's about 17 per cent of the world's supply, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela's soil are largely mapped and known, experts say.
But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1 per cent of the world's oil.

articles.title: US, Venezuela announce 'historic' oil deal
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil. The South American country has the largest proven oil reserves in the world.

image.caption: Venezuela has been reported to have among the world's largest oil reserves [File Photo: January 2026]Image: Anatoly Zhdanov/Kommersant Photo/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said on Friday the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves.
He said the deal was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
"The United States of America has just entered into an agreement with the country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He added that it would be "at no cost to the American taxpayer."
Rodruiguez welcomed the "historic" deal that would "have a significant impact on the rebirth of our nation."
She said it would bring in $100 billion (€86.3 billion) in private investment and generate more than $209 billion in tax revenue for the treasury.
What do we know about the deal?
Few details were clarified in Trump's initial announcement, but the deal promises to eventually more than double US oil stocks at a time when the strategic petroleum reserve is at a 40-year low.
Trump said the deal would cover 65 billion barrels worth of oil — a little over a fifth of the country's proven reserves.
Reuters news agency reported that one model under consideration would see Venezuelan oil fields leased to US producers.
American news website Axios, meanwhile, reported that the deal was a kind of "public-private partnership" between both governments and US oil companies.
The huge problem with Venezuela's oil
Rubio said the deal would secure "stable reserves and low-cost oil" for the US while also driving "the reconstruction of Venezuela's economy."
"This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people," he said.
The world's largest oil reserves

The deal comes nearly nine months after US forces deposed and kidnapped Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro. He is now detained in New York City, where he faces federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.
Since then, and under intense pressure, Rodriguez has moved to open up Venezuela's oil sector to American investment.

Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves totaling 303 billion barrels. But production has long lagged behind other major oil producing countries due to chronic mismanagement, decaying infrastructure and sanctions.

articles.title: Warnings over squishy toy hazards expand globally
articles.summary: Squishy toys have triggered recalls, seizures and burn warnings abroad. Health Canada has received 36 reports involving squishy dumpling toys, including injuries, but says it has not confirmed a…

image.caption: Squishy bun toy containing water beads. (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission)

blocks.text: Health

Squishy toys have triggered recalls, seizures and burn warnings abroad. Health Canada has received 36 reports involving squishy dumpling toys, including injuries, but says it has not confirmed a specific health or safety risk.
Regulators have flagged benzene in some products, burn risks from counterfeits and toys bursting in heat

Some trendy squishy toys have prompted burn warnings and enforcement action in several countries, while Canadian regulators say they've received dozens of reports but have not confirmed a specific health or safety risk.

The soft, palm-sized toys come in a variety of shapes, including cubes and spheres, as well as food shapes such as dumplings and sticks of butter. Their squishy texture is a defining feature of toys marketed for sensory play and sold through online marketplaces, discount stores and other retailers.
Regulators raise concerns abroad
This week, Cornwall Trading Standards in southwest England, warned that some squishy toys they tested failed U.K. safety standards.

Separately, Hull City Council in northeast England said it seized and destroyed toys from local retailers after testing found high levels of benzene, a carcinogen. Hull officials said high levels of exposure can cause irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, skin irritation and, if ingested, a burning sensation.
The local actions in England followed a recall by the U.K.'s Office for Product Safety and Standards of Squeezy Dumplings in June.
Some squishy toys are not safe, health officials warn

Earlier this month, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission reiterated a warning about serious burn hazards associated with fake and counterfeit squishy toys that do not comply with U.S. safety requirements.
Shipments of what the agency called "violative squishy toys" have also been seized at U.S. ports.
In Australia, Schyling, the manufacturer of NeeDoh toys, has reportedly asked the Australian Border Force to intercept counterfeit versions of its products.
Health Canada has received 36 reports
From April 23 to Aug. 24, Health Canada said it received 36 reports involving squishy dumpling toys.

"There were 30 reports of odours, four reports about the sale of these products but with no mention of odour or injury, and two reports of the product exploding, with 6 of these reports mentioning an injury (e.g., headache, skin rash, difficulty breathing)," Health Canada said in a statement to CBC News. "These reports include both children and adults."
Health Canada said it has not identified any failures to comply with health or safety regulations and has not confirmed that the toys pose a specific health or safety risk.
Separately, Amazon Canada said in a statement that it proactively removed some squishy dumpling toys following reported safety concerns.
What is actually inside the toys?

Toy manufacturers are not obligated to disclose the ingredients and may not always know exactly what is in their products, said Miriam Diamond, a professor and environmental chemist at the University of Toronto who studies microplastics and chemicals in consumer products.

items: Do kids still want toys? Toy stores are struggling, but don't just blame screens
CBC's What on Earth | Is plastic-free plastic even possible?

blocks.text: "There could be chemicals there that are fairly benign, but there could also be chemicals that are of concern. I don't know, and that's actually concerning in and of itself," Diamond said, calling on manufacturers and importers to be vigilant.
Do squishies actually work? The history of sensory toys
The product safety group Consumer Reports said concerns are not necessarily limited to counterfeit or off-brand products.

"We kind of feel that it's not just about the counterfeit," said Ashita Kapoor, director of product safety and personal care at Consumer Reports. "We're actually seeing incidents of products that are happening that are purchased directly from retail."
Tips for parents
For now, the U.S. Product Safety Commission advises families to:

items: Keep affected toys away from heat, including hot cars and prolonged sunlight, and never intentionally heat them.
Inspect toys regularly for leaks.
Use caution when cleaning up after a toy bursts to avoid direct skin contact.

blocks.text: Diamond also suggests families declutter and stick with a few simple toys.
Families should also follow recommended age limits.
NeeDoh and Squishy Dumpling did not respond to requests for comment.
With files from CBC's Tahlia Sarv

articles.title: Number of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnel
articles.summary: There are now 41 Australians missing, and four rapid response team members are expected to arrive in Kathmandu
articles.byline: Stephanie Convery and Cait Kelly in Kathmandu

blocks.text: The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, as one family celebrates after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.
It means three additional Australians were confirmed missing overnight – up from 38 who remained unaccounted for on Friday evening.

The Australian government’s Department of Foreign Affairs has been urgently working with local authorities to contact Australian woman Cara Severino, 25, who became the first Australian reported missing who has been confirmed safe.

Severino contacted her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, on Friday morning, informing them she was hiking away from the disaster zone to Kathmandu with a group of Nepali hikers – a trek of more than 110km.

The Red Cross has said about 600 people are dead and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, with a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.
Dfat has received more than 450 calls in relation to the disaster.

blocks.caption: Some of Australia’s missing in Nepal as of Friday, 28 August. Clockwise from left: Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan. Composite: Supplied by the families

blocks.text: Nepal’s disaster management agency says there are 1,924 people unaccounted for – 517 of those people are foreign tourists.
About 7:30pm on Friday evening, the authority said 121 foreigners had been rescued – none of them were Australians.
View from Kathmandu hospital
Outside the hospital in Kathmandu yesterday, there were scenes of anxiety as families put up posters of loved ones, and authorities hung pictures of the dead that need to be identified.
One woman said her cousin was on his way back from Australia because his brother had gone missing.
Like many others, she was putting pictures of him up, in case he was brought back to the hospital.

Australian charities are starting to pump in aid, with the Emergency Action Alliance – a peak body representing major Australian charities – raising funds to build emergency shelters, get food and safe drinking water, hygiene supplies and medical care to communities.

But conditions on the ground are difficult and unpredictable owing to the scale of the damage and the heavy monsoon. Rescue operations in Nepal and China resumed as of Saturday morning after being suspended due to the risk of further flooding.
“The gravity of the situation is worse now because whole towns have swept away,” Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre vice president Keshav Kadel said.
“Now there is nothing, it’s just a mudslide.”

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows the aftermath of massive flooding along the Bhotekoshi River, which affected low-lying areas and settlements near the riverbanks in Nuwakot, Nepal.  Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
The flooding caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridge, hydropower station and other infrastructure in the area.  Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Four Dfat crisis response team officers are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later on Saturday to support consular efforts on the ground.
Four rapid response team members are also expected to arrive in Kathmandu – humanitarian response specialists with expertise in communications, logistics and planning.
These extra deployments add to about 20 personnel Australian already has on the ground with the Australian embassy in Kathmandu.

On Friday night, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, spoke with the Nepali foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, to affirm that Australia would provide further humanitarian assistance, including to aid rescue and recovery efforts, where required.

Australia has pledged $5m in aid and support for the disaster, with $2m going to the World Food Programme to provide emergency food and water provisions, and the remaining to the Emergency Action Alliance.

Australia’s assistant minister for foreign affairs and trade, Matt Thistlethwaite, said on Saturday morning that the aid was being provided on request of the Nepalese authorities. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Thistlethwaite said Australian officials in Beijing were also working with the Chinese Government, but that China had not so far requested support.
“We’re doing our best to support both the Nepalese and Tibetan diasporas here in Australia,” Thistlethwaite said.

“Yesterday I held two online forums, one with the Nepalese community one with the Tibetan community to outline the latest situation, to advise of the support that Australia is providing, the $5m in humanitarian aid, and the best way for us to keep in contact with them. We’re providing them with the latest information through our officials.

“I also attended a vigil last night with the Nepalese community in Strathfield and obviously there was quite a bit of despair and anxiety in that community, but we’re doing our best to support the Tibetan and Nepalese communities here in Australia.”

items: The Australian government’s 24-hour consular emergency centre can be contacted on 1300 555 135 within Australia or +61 2 6261 3305 from overseas.

articles.title: Ottawa couple's 'Lake Ontario' hats selling like hotcakes after Trump's executive order
articles.summary: Before the ink had even dried on U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order to rename Lake Ontario, a Canadian company was already selling hats with the Great Lake's true name emblazoned on it.

image.caption: Canadian company Jackpine began selling Lake Ontario hats just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename the Great Lake on U.S. maps. (jackpine.co)

blocks.text: As It Happens
Before the ink had even dried on U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order to rename Lake Ontario, a Canadian company was already selling hats with the Great Lake's true name emblazoned on it.
Canadian company Jackpine also behind the viral 'Canada's Not For Sale' hats
LISTEN | Interview with Ottawa apparel company owner Liam Mooney:
As It Happens6:01Ottawa company's 'Lake Ontario' hats selling like hotcakes in wake of Trump executive order
The baseball caps from Ottawa company Jackpine went up for sale online just hours after Trump signed the order to call the body of water that borders Canada and New York "Lake America."
Jackpine founder Liam Mooney says he came up with the idea for the design the night before.
"It was just clear that he was going to do this to us, and so we jumped on it," Mooney told As It Happens guest host Paul Hunter. "The timing was certainly fortuitous."

Jackpine, which Mooney owns with his wife Emma Cochrane, is also responsible for the "Canada Is Not For Sale" hats that became a sensation last year after Ontario Premier Doug Ford started sporting one during public appearances.
"I feel like, you know, in a certain sense, like an obligation, like I'm a chief propagandist for Canada," Mooney said.

"I'm just sort of doing whatever I can to activate our made-in-Canada supply chains so that if there is demand from this, that we can onshore that manufacturing and that we use the project itself to activate the industrial base of our country."
Trump's executive order, which changes the Great Lake's name on U.S. maps, comes after trade negotiations broke down between Canada and the U.S. last weekend.
The Trump administration has slapped 50 per cent tariffs on a wide array of Canadian goods, and Canada has responded in kind.
Canadians have flatly rejected the executive order.

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on social media that the name Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io," which means “'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big," and noted it predates "both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America."
Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard also issued a statement accusing Trump of trying to "eradicate" the nation's history.
Trump orders Lake Ontario be renamed 'Lake America'
U.S. political commentator Charlie Sykes told CBC Radio's Day 6 the move shows how unserious Trump is as a leader.

"He's trying to portray himself as this, you know, great world-bestriding leader, comparing himself to the Caesars and the Napoleons and the Attila the Huns of history. But what is he doing? He's sitting around on social media, putting out, you know, slop about changing the names of lakes," Sykes said.
"A clown with a flamethrower still has a flamethrower, but he's still a clown too."
Cashing in on patriotism?
Mooney says the minute Jackpine posted the hat online, the orders started flooding in.
"It's been a really awesome day, a really tremendous response," he said. "Canadians, I think, are looking for opportunities right now to channel their patriotism."
But the customer base, he says, extends beyond Canada's borders.
"We're getting order in Paris, Tokyo, London, Berlin," he said. "People around the world are standing in solidarity with Canada."

items: 'Lake America'? Trump's 'utterly ridiculous' renaming met with laughter in Kingston
Despite Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario, Great Lakes endure as symbol of U.S.-Canada collaboration

blocks.text: His isn't the only Canadian company that's found a way to cash in on the trade war that's expected to wreak havoc on many businesses and industries.
In 2025, "Elbows Up" apparel was flying off the shelves of Canadian companies, including Timeless Memories in Yarmouth, N.S., and Toronto's Shop Love Collective.
The hockey phrase, coined by legendary player Gordie Howe, became a national rallying cry last spring when Trump was making repeated jokes and threats about annexing Canada as a 51st state.
This Windsor, Ont., woman is making hundreds of 'Elbows Up' pins
Asked whether selling the Lake Ontario hats could be seen as a cynical ploy to make a buck off a bad situation, Mooney maintained he's motivated by patriotism, not profits.

"When people are looking for a way to express how they feel, to take a lot of complex ideas and put it somewhere really simple, there are ways to do that. And it just so happens that we've been fortunate enough to be a part of some moments where we've actually accomplished that," he said.
"And thankfully, it's been to Canada's benefit. We've invested millions into the Canadian textile industry, into Canadian workers."
Interview with Liam Mooney produced by Chris Harbord

articles.title: Postpartum psychosis is terrifying but treatable, this survivor says. The challenge is finding support
articles.summary: A decade ago, Meghan Cliffel believed she was being watched by members of a cult who were out to kill her and her young daughters. In fact, she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, the condition at…

image.caption: Meghan Cliffel is pregnant here with her second daughter. In December 2015, she experienced postpartum psychosis, and she says she wants people to know that it's treatable. (Submitted by Meghan Cliffel)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and suicide.
When Meghan Cliffel stepped onto the subway in New York City after work and caught the eyes of her fellow passengers, she felt as though something had gone gravely wrong.

While those around her scrolled on their phones or listened to music, the mother-of-two believed they were surveilling her. She switched trains, trying to throw off the supposed pursuers and then continued on to a gathering of old friends.

But the unease persisted; eventually, she ran across the city to get home, thinking someone might be about to harm her family when a friend innocuously asked who was watching her daughters, then two and eight months old.

"My brain is knitting things together into this kind of complex reality where I believe there's some kind of cultish scheme running the city," she said. "I am in the centre of it in some way and they're out to get me and my kids."

In fact, she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that affects about one to two mothers per 1,000 births and is currently at the heart of Lindsay Clancy's defence in her first-degree murder trial in Massachusetts, where she is accused of killing her three children.
LISTEN | What postpartum psychosis feel like:
The Current24:41Lindsay Clancy trial shines light postpartum mental health

The disorder is considered a psychiatric emergency and requires immediate treatment, said Nicholas Leyland, president of the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) who is based in Ontario. Symptoms include delusions, visual or auditory hallucinations, distorted thinking, paranoia, mania or depression, insomnia and confusion.
But when Cliffel experienced her first delusions on Dec. 4, 2015, she said neither she nor her husband had heard of the disorder.
'Excruciating to watch'

Now, a decade later, she is healthy, a mother of three and a writer and maternal mental health advocate. And she finds it "excruciating to watch" the Clancy proceedings, she said, because she can envision her own experience ending similarly had her husband left her alone with the children — and because postpartum psychosis is temporary and treatable.
One of the biggest challenges, however, as she and Clancy found, can be getting a diagnosis.

Jurors are now deliberating whether the 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse should be held criminally responsible for killing her children, Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan in 2023 while her then-husband was out on an errand.

She is accused of strangling the children with exercise bands in the basement of her Boston-area home before leaping out a second-storey window after cutting her neck in an attempt to take her own life. She is now paralyzed and uses a wheelchair.
Her defence team has argued that Clancy cannot be held criminally responsible, saying her medical condition created a distorted sense of reality.

Her lawyers described Clancy as doing all she could to get help for her deteriorating mental health — both from family and through numerous health-care providers, who, collectively, prescribed her 13 different medications. She called a suicide hotline, went to the emergency room and checked herself into a psychiatric facility. She had been denied an outpatient spot at a postpartum mental health program.
These attempts, women's health advocates and Clancy's supporters say, underscore the systemic failures of the health-care system for women and, by extension, their children.
Missing from the DSM-5
In custody, Clancy got her diagnosis: bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis.
"It feels a little bit like a different version of my life," Cliffel said. "And the second reason it feels excruciating is because I know we can do so much better."

Now a postpartum mental health advocate based in Cleveland, Ohio, Cliffel said it is critical to update the DSM-5 — the handbook of psychiatric and mood disorders used across North America — to include postpartum psychosis as a standalone condition, not a subcategory of psychosis.
Doing so would create more awareness among doctors, psychologists and other maternal health specialists, she said, and likely increase the amount of investment and research into the condition.
And it might help others get an early diagnosis.

Cliffel spent 12 days at Bellevue Psychiatric hospital in New York City; her husband called emergency services the morning of Dec. 5, 2015, when she began punching him to try to get to their children and also threatening to jump from the roof.
"I wake up in a twin bed in the dark and I think I've been captured," she recalled. "I try and escape several times, because I think maybe my baby girls are still alive."

items: What is postpartum psychosis, the illness at the centre of Lindsay Clancy's murder trial?
Postpartum depression or anxiety reported by nearly a quarter of moms: StatsCan

blocks.text: Her condition improved with medication. After she was discharged, she spent six weeks in outpatient care but still didn't get a diagnosis.
Without answers about such a "ground-shifting experience," Cliffel said she had even more difficulty trusting whether her thoughts were real.
So she asked to see a psychiatrist who was also a mother.
"That got me into the chair of somebody who understood reproductive psychiatry," she said. "So it took, you know, about two months after I experienced it for somebody to label it."
Misdiagnoses

After nearly four decades of teaching health-care providers about maternal mental health, Karen Kleiman said she is still surprised by how many obstetricians consider sending patients to the emergency room for psychiatric evaluation instead of doing an assessment.
She blames some missed cases or misdiagnoses of postpartum psychosis on the businesslike evolution of medicine.

"The reality is in the medical community, they've got what? Three, four, seven minutes … to do a rapid assessment," said Kleiman, founder of The Postpartum Stress Center in Pennsylvania and author of Good Moms Have Scary Thoughts. "It's not part of their job description; it's beyond the scope of their practice. But at the same time, how long does it take to ask one or two good questions?"
Questions can help assess whether the patient is manic, whether the thoughts are manifesting in a more psychotic way — not worries about how to safely hold a baby.

"We cannot expect a woman who's very, very, very sick to tell us how bad she feels," said Kleiman, a registered social worker. "If there are psychotic symptoms going on, it's our burden to find that, to ask the right questions and to get her the help that she needs."
Risk assessment

It's why Elise Gwyn also does a risk assessment on new clients, whether it's before birth or afterward. The Ottawa-area psychotherapist specializes in perinatal mental health, which covers from pregnancy to a year postpartum, and encourages partners to join sessions so they can offer insight.

Risk factors for postpartum psychosis include a diagnosis or family history of bipolar disorder, while sensitivity to hormonal shifts can be a signal someone might experience a mood disorder after delivering, Gwyn said.

But it can be hard to parse the symptoms of postpartum psychosis, such as fearful delusions, from the intrusive thoughts of a healthy new mother or someone experiencing postpartum depression, anxiety or perinatal obsessive-compulsive disorder, Gwyn said, because the brain's "alarm system" is on high alert for risk to the baby.

That's why collateral information from partners can be critical, Gwyn said, since a psychotherapist, family doctor or obstetrician might only see a patient for a short period of time. Partners have the advantage of a shared home and history and can raise red flags a clinician might miss.
She, Kleiman and Cliffel all emphasized that while more education around diagnosis is important, the message that postpartum psychosis is temporary and treatable is just as critical.

With systemic change, Cliffel said — especially a standard of care that includes psychiatric screening and support — women with postpartum psychosis can not only recover but can be a healthy parent and even go on to have more children.
In November 2019, Cliffel gave birth for the third time: a baby boy.

She worked with a reproductive psychiatrist and therapist to create a plan for pregnancy and beyond. After delivery, she took lithium prophylactically for a year, and she wrote, practised mindfulness and stayed out of the labour force.
"We not only staved off recurrence but we experienced so much more joy the third time around," Cliffel said.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:

items: Postpartum Support International Canada: Call 1-800-944-4773 or visit the website for support online.
Canada's Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
