articles.title: Health advocates push P80 vape tax to curb youth vaping
articles.summary: Public health advocates are urging Congress to impose a tax of at least P80 on vapor products, saying higher taxes are needed to discourage vaping among young Filipinos and prevent long-term health…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 5:58am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

Public health advocates are urging Congress to impose a tax of at least P80 on vapor products, saying higher taxes are needed to discourage vaping among young Filipinos and prevent long-term health costs.

The Healthy Philippines Alliance (HPA), with HealthJustice as its convener, said the proposed unified tax rate of P72.93 by 2027 for cigarettes, heated tobacco products (HTPs), and vapor products remains insufficient to curb access to vaping products.
The proposed rate was recommended by the Department of Finance (DOF) and the Department of Health (DOH).
HPA Lead Convener and former Health Secretary Dr. Jaime Galvez Tan said vaping products should not be considered harmless, warning of their potential impact on young people’s health.
“Vapes are far from harm-free,” Galvez Tan said, adding that the early development of chronic heart and lung conditions could eventually result in significant costs for the healthcare system.
HealthJustice also opposed proposals from some lawmakers to lower the vape tax to as little as P15 per milliliter.

HealthJustice Legal Adviser Atty. Benedict Nisperos called such proposals “reckless and unacceptable,” arguing that lower taxes could make nicotine-containing vape products more accessible to young people.
“We cannot allow lower tax rates that enable more addictive substances, like nicotine salt vapes, to proliferate in the market,” Nisperos said.
The group also raised concerns over what it described as regulatory gaps in the Philippines compared with other Southeast Asian countries.

Nisperos said eight of the 11 ASEAN countries have completely banned vapor products, while the Philippines continues to allow their sale under Republic Act 11900, or the Vaporized Nicotine and Non-Nicotine Products Regulation Act. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: US arrests far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos
articles.summary: Yiannopoulos, a far-right commentator, was an early supporter of Donald Trump and his immigration crackdown, but they have since fallen out. DHS said he was an "illegal alien" who overstayed his…

image.caption: DHS said Yiannopoulos legally entered the US in 2019 and then 'chose to overstay his welcome' [FILE: Nov 16, 2021]Image: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: US authorities have detained right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos and plan to deport him, the Department of Homeland Security said on Friday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested the British provocateur at New Orleans International Airport on Thursday for overstaying in the US, the department said, describing him as an "illegal alien from the United Kingdom."

"Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing," the agency said. "He will remain in ICE custody pending removal."
ICE directed family and legal representatives to contact the agency’s office in Alexandria, Louisiana, which serves as a deportation hub for international flights.
Far-right activist Laura Loomer, who routinely takes credit for action against those who have fallen out with the US president, posted about the incident shortly after.

"I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene," Loomer wrote on X, referring to the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene who stepped down after a feud with Trump.
Loomer went on to say that she "reported him to ICE and the FBI."
Yiannopoulos previously supported ICE
Once a Donald Trump supporter and advocate of the president's immigration crackdown, Yiannopoulos has since fallen out with the Trump movement.
Yiannopoulos first gained notoriety in the early 2010s as a writer for the right-wing website Breitbart News, where he played a key role in the "Gamergate" anti-feminist harassment campaign.
He resigned from Breitbart in 2017 after a video of him appearing to condone pedophilia resurfaced online. He later apologized for the remarks.
Yiannopoulos has continued to espouse far-right views, including calling for a stop to immigration and mass deportations.

As recently as June last year, he said California "needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections ​and government buildings, with on the ⁠spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally."

Celebrity news website TMZ suggested that Yiannopoulos may have been in New Orleans ahead of a scheduled performance by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West. Yiannopoulos has worked for Ye in various capacities, first as part of his aborted 2024 presidential campaign, followed by a brief stint at fashion label Yeezy, and most recently as a personal spokesperson.

articles.title: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers, mayor says
articles.summary: Kai Wegner says the German capital and city-state would not cave in to a ransom demand for data stolen in a cyber-attack.

blocks.text: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers who were able to compromise city systems and steal data earlier this month, its mayor has said.

Kai Wegner said officials would not cave in to the ransom demand, which came on Thursday evening. He did not say how much was being sought, though Der Spiegel reports the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin, worth around €2m (£1.7m).
Some of the German capital's online systems were forced to close down as a result of the attack, while investigators were working to understand what data had been taken.
The Rhysida group, which is thought to operate from Russia and eastern Europe, and was behind a previous attack on the British Museum, has reportedly taken responsibility.
It has said on its website it intends to begin auctioning the 5.79 terabytes of data it was able to steal from Berlin in seven days' time, according to news agency Reuters.
"Berlin will not be blackmailed," Wegner said on Friday.

He said state police, prosecutors and federal security services were working to investigate the suspected perpetrators "with the utmost urgency", adding that inquiries into the "content and scope of the compromised data are being pursued with great intensity".
Officials for the city-state said an initial data leak occurred between 7 and 12 August.
Then, on 14 August, two department networks were shut down, making applications for housing benefits and payments impossible for several days.
Forensic investigations had since revealed further data leaks within Berlin's transport and environment department, officials said.
"It cannot be ruled out that personal or other non-public data may also be affected," the mayor's office said in a statement on Friday.

Authorities in the capital have not named the suspected cyber-attackers, though Der Spiegel is carrying a screenshot of the Rhysida group's dark web site claiming to possess files including contracts, non-disclosure agreements, personnel files, passwords and thousands of personal contact details.

It is also displaying a countdown, after which it says it will begin auctioning off the data with a starting price of 30 bitcoin - the same amount of the cryptocurrency being sought from Berlin, the German newspaper reports.
The Rhysida group has claimed hundreds of attacks since it emerged in 2023, studies say, and the group has targeted government insititutions and businesses of varying sizes in numerous countries.
It successfully infiltrated the British Museum's computer systems in 2023, disrupting services and stealing around 500,000 files.
When the UK institution refused to pay the ransom, the group published the files - containing the personal data of visitors, subscribers and staff - on the dark web.
The Berlin cyber-attack comes roughly a month before the city holds elections, though state senator Iris Spranger insisted that election infrastructure had not been compromised.

articles.title: Spain asks EU's Frontex for help in processing Ceuta migrants
articles.summary: Of the over 70,000 migrants who illegally crossed into Ceuta from Morocco in late July, some 5,000 still remain in the Spanish exclave. Ceuta residents have been angrily protesting their continued…

image.caption: Some Ceuta residents have attacked tents set up by the migrants along the beachImage: Antonio Sempere/AFP

blocks.text: Spain has asked for help from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in processing migrants who crossed into Ceuta last month and still remain in the North African Spanish territory.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska sent a request to Beate Gminder, the European Commission's director general for migration and home affairs, to help with screening migrants in Ceuta.
Madrid has also requested 10 more Frontex officers to help with the screening.
Frontex is the European Union agency responsible for managing the bloc's external borders and fighting cross-border crime.
Why is Spain asking for help with the Ceuta migrants?
Over 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco to Ceuta illegally in late July. The incident triggered a massive EU migration emergency and brought Spain's leftist government much criticism.
Though the majority of people were quickly sent back to Morocco, at least 5,000 migrants still remain in the Spanish territory of roughly 80,000 residents.
Madrid cannot deport the remaining migrants quickly as a collective return without individual assessment is prohibited under international law and Spanish court rulings.
Unaccompanied minors at risk of sexual assault in Ceuta
Rising anger against migrants in Ceuta
Ceuta's residents loudly reject the migrants' continued presence and have made their voice heard via protests which have sometimes turned violent.
Spain has ruled out moving the migrants into the mainland as that would invite further criticism from the opposition as well as some EU members.
Migrants have set up camp on Trampolin Beach, where some tents have been attacked and set on fire amid the residents' rising anger.

On Thursday, protests turned violent with 12 migrants arrested after stoning an army vehicle, injuring one soldier and other migrants. Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that 11 migrants were expelled from the territory, citing sources from the city's main court.

blocks.caption: Anti-migrant protests took a violent turn this weekImage: Antonio Sempere/AFP

articles.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
articles.summary: A 97-year-old woman, Guna Maya Bohara, survived the flash floods and was rescued using an excavator.

blocks.text: A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.
Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.
The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.
Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.
Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.
Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

articles.title: How and why CBC News will adjust its 9/11 language guidance
articles.summary: CBC’s reporting on terrorism, wherever it occurs, has always been guided by the principle of attribution, and like other major news organizations, it has been our practice for decades.

image.caption: Confusion has been swirling about how CBC News journalists use the words 'terrorist' and 'terrorism,' particularly in connection with the al-Qaeda attacks on New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania on Sept. 11, 2001. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Editor's Blog
CBC’s reporting on terrorism, wherever it occurs, has always been guided by the principle of attribution, and like other major news organizations, it has been our practice for decades.
Attribution no longer required for describing Sept. 11 attacks as terrorism
We use this editor's blog to explain our journalism and what's happening at CBC News. You can find more blog posts here.

CBC News finds itself once again in a swirl of confusion about how our journalists use the words "terrorist" and "terrorism," this time about the al-Qaeda attacks on New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania on Sept. 11, 2001.

The confusion stems from the leak of an excerpt from our internal language guide that was published and amplified by a number of outlets without full context or explanation. It has caused significant concern, anger and hurt for many people who believe CBC News seeks to minimize or obscure the horror of that day and who was behind it.

That is the last thing we want to do. And our reporting on 9/11, through thousands of stories over the past 25 years, is an unflinching account of the devastating attacks by al-Qaeda, the hunt and prosecution of those responsible, the thousands of lives that were lost on that day and the incalculable loss and grief experienced by so many others as a result.
And we intend to mark the forthcoming 25th anniversary of 9/11 with extensive, special coverage that will continue to respectfully and thoughtfully reflect on the monumental nature of this tragedy.

CBC's reporting on terrorism, wherever it occurs, has always been guided by the principle of attribution, and like other major news organizations, it has been our practice for decades. The reason for the extreme care around the use of the words "terrorist" and "terrorism" was detailed in this earlier editor's blog.

But to be clear, CBC News has never said what happened on Sept. 11, 2001, was not terrorism, as some commentators have stated in recent days. We have reported fully and accurately on the reasons and motivations for those attacks as determined by police, governments and an independent commission. We've just made sure to do it with attribution.
Clarity and understanding are at the heart of our journalism. The leaked excerpt without context or explanation has raised more questions for the public that we must now answer.
After reviewing our current language guidance, we have decided to adjust it to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism.
We are doing so to remove what has unfortunately (and unintentionally) become an impediment to clarity and public understanding.

At the same time, as new acts of politically or ideologically motivated violence occur in our world, we will continue to follow the journalistically sound practice of attributing causes and motivations to officials and experts.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Basem Boshra
Senior director of journalistic standards and public trust

Basem Boshra is the senior director of journalistic standards and public trust at CBC News. He was previously the director of journalism and programming for CBC Quebec (English Services) from 2022 to 2025. Before joining CBC, Basem spent more than 20 years at the Montreal Gazette, where he held key leadership roles including deputy editor, managing editor, digital editor, city editor, and columnist. His career also includes positions at CTV News Montreal, the National Post and Dose Magazine.

articles.title: Andreescu, fellow Canadian Draxl lose in final round of U.S. Open qualifying
articles.summary: No Canadians will enter the singles draws at the U.S. Open through the qualifying tournament after Bianca Andreescu and Liam Draxl lost in final round action Friday in New York.

image.caption: From left: Bianca Andreescu, the 2019 women's U.S. Open champion, fell 2-6, 6-3, 6-4 to Slovenia's Tamara Zidansek in the final qualifying round Friday, while fellow Canadian Liam Draxl dropped a 4-6, 7-5, 7-6 (7) decision to Australia's Tristan Schoolkate. (Dave Shopland/Associated Press, Minas Pan

blocks.text: Tennis·ROUNDUP
No Canadians will enter the singles draws at the U.S. Open through the qualifying tournament after Bianca Andreescu and Liam Draxl lost in final round action Friday in New York.
Teammates Auger-Aliassime and Shapovalov in men's main draw that begins Sunday

Andreescu fell 2-6, 6-3, 6-4 to Slovenia's Tamara Zidansek. The 2019 U.S. Open women's champion from Mississauga, Ont., fired seven aces across the two-hour 44-minute match but struggled on net points, winning just 10 of the 21 available.
The match started Thursday but had to be suspended due to rain. Andreescu was up 2-0 at the time.
Draxl of Newmarket, Ont., also had his qualifying match against Australia's Tristan Schoolkate pushed to Friday before losing 4-6, 7-5, 7-6 (7).

items: Andreescu, Branstine advance to U.S. Open final qualifying round
Andreescu bounced from NBO, compatriot Kayla Cross secures 1st WTA win

blocks.text: Both players scored four breaks, but Schoolkate was the last to win against serve to go up 4-3 in the third set and erase an early Draxl advantage.

Montreal's Felix Auger-Aliassime and Denis Shapovalov of Richmond Hill, Ont., will be on the men's side when main draw action begins Sunday, while 2021 runner-up Leylah Fernandez of Laval, Que., will be on the women's side.
Sabalenka, Pegula want prize money boost, new player council

Aryna Sabalenka ​and Jessica Pegula praised the U.S. Open's record prize money allocation and the creation of a Grand Slam player advisory council, saying calls for competitors to get a larger share of the revenue were beginning to gain traction.

The U.S. Open announced a ‌record $108 million US prize purse for this year's tournament, while the four Grand Slams unveiled plans for an advisory council following growing pressure from leading players for increased prize money and a bigger role in decisions affecting the sport.
World No. 1 Sabalenka, a ​vocal supporter of efforts to improve player compensation, said ​the developments could help ease tensions between players and tournament organizers.
"We're super happy … that we're finally getting to the point where we wanted to be at ​the very beginning," the Belarusian told reporters on Friday.

items: Djokovic-Sabalenka, Williams-Alcaraz suffer first-round losses in U.S. Open mixed doubles

blocks.text: "Hopefully we're not gonna boycott ⁠media or tournament or anything ⁠in the future. We all going to be ‌happy, and that's all we wanted from the very beginning."

Sabalenka and men's world No. 1 Jannik Sinner were among the top players who limited their pre-tournament media availabilities at the French Open and Wimbledon this year to 15 minutes as part of ⁠a protest to demand a higher percentage of tournament revenue for prize money.
Unity helped in player council talks
The 15-minute limit was intended to symbolize the roughly 15 per cent of tournament revenue that the tournaments allocated to player prize money.

items: More tennis coverage

blocks.text: American Pegula, ‌who has taken on a leadership role in discussions involving players and tennis' governing bodies, said unity between the men's and women's tours had helped produce tangible progress.

"I think it's been amazing what the players have been able to accomplish," Pegula said. "They have never ​had anything like this as far as with the slams being able to generate a council, also the player welfare contribution, ⁠and then another increase in prize money."
The world No. 3 said the initiatives reflected sustained pressure from ⁠players as they seek a greater voice in a sport long criticized for its fragmented ⁠structure.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Austria museum heist: Thieves snatch diamond necklace
articles.summary: The stolen necklace, studded with 673 precious stones, belonged to Egypt's Queen Nazli. It was being displayed as part of the museum's exhibition for designs by France's Van Cleef and Arpels.

image.caption: The two robbers bought tickets to enter the MAK museum. But once inside, they 'smashed a glass display case' with a hammer and fled with the priceless jewelry, police has saidImage: Jeremy Audouard/AFP

blocks.text: Two men walked into Vienna's Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) as visitors only to storm out with a priceless 200-carat platinum and diamond necklace worth several million dollars, police said on Friday.
The broad-daylight heist on Thursday, the latest in a series of high-profile thefts to have hit European museums in the past year, triggered a search that grew beyond Austria's borders.
What do we know about the heist?
The two robbers bought tickets to enter the museum.

But once inside, they made their way to the temporary exhibition for French designers Van Cleef and Arpels and "smashed a glass display case" with a hammer before "fleeing with the jewelry in an unknown direction," according to a police statement.
Police added that they did not wear masks and could be clearly seen on surveillance cameras.
A police spokeswoman told the German DPA news agency that one of the robbers was carrying what is believed to be a real firearm.
She said visitors and security staff were in the room when the display case was smashed, adding that it was understandable that the security staff did not stand in the way of the armed perpetrator.
The MAK museum confirmed the theft but did not comment further. On its website, the museum continues to promote its exhibition, which is due to run until September 27.

blocks.caption: The stolen necklace, made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats, was designed for Egypt's last royal familyImage: Landespolizeidirektion Wien/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the stolen necklace?

The stolen necklace belonged to Egypt's now-deposed Queen Nazli and was designed for her in 1939 for her daughter's marriage to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose family has also since been removed from power.
It is made of platinum and 673 precious stones said to weigh over 200 carats.
Van Cleef and Arpels describes the necklace on its website as a "triumph of white jewelry."
The case is only the latest in a string of heists to have hit European museums in recent month.

The most high profile was last October's Louvre museum break-in in Paris, which saw thieves snatching in jewellery worth $102 million (roughly €88 million) in under eight minutes. Museum thefts have also been reported in Italy and Spain.

articles.title: Death toll rises in Nepal-China border disaster; lake poses new threat
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety Friday, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety Friday, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that killed more than 500 people and left more than 1,500 missing.

Rescue teams were put on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that has formed high up on the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday. Experts warn that the lake, formed after the glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow.

Nepal’s army was deployed to help rescue more than 100 people believed trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower plant located in the country’s worst-hit district. Like elsewhere in the disaster zone, their work was complicated by thick layers of mud that covered the site.

The floods have killed 538 in Nepal, the country’s disaster management authority said Friday. Nepali police later put the number of deaths higher at 547. There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to five Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders’ efforts to direct the relief response.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far, but 977 people remain unaccounted for in the country. China’s state media previously said 558 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak.
Authorities warn of further flooding from a new lake

Nepali police issued a fresh alert Friday after receiving information that a dam on the Tibet side has burst. Security personnel and rescue and relief workers were told to stay on high alert and immediately move to a safe location if necessary.

It is unclear if the dam bursting is related to flooding concerns over a barrier lake that formed after the initial flash floods. Chinese broadcaster CCTV said the newly-formed lake, located more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal, sits at an elevation of 2,950 meters (9,680 feet.)

Nepali and Chinese authorities earlier warned of further flooding from the barrier lake, which was already overflowing. Rescue workers heading to the disaster zone were ordered to stop temporarily Friday morning due to concern the lake would release more torrents of water and debris, and people in potentially affected areas were urged move to safer ground.
Some 680 rescuers eventually reached the hardest-hit area at Gyirong by foot and via rafts after much effort. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area, CCTV footage showed.
Nepali police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told The Associated Press that the rescue operation was continuing but with high alert. “It hasn’t stopped,” he said.
Thousands of people have been evacuated, others await rescue

In Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Nepali Army rescuers were struggling to help more than 100 people believed trapped by thick mud in a tunnel that’s part of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project. The army said it has rescued 350 people from the tunnel so far.
Video from the scene show rescuers helping a man, covered in dark brown mud, out of the tunnel by pulling and pushing.
Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told the AP the focus was on survivors.
“It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud,” Basnet said. “Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people.”
Nepal’s disaster management authority said 3,253 people had been airlifted by helicopter from the disaster area. Survivors, including injured people, were taken to Kathmandu and other locations.
Some felt the ground shake, then saw a ‘black storm’

Scientists who’ve studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it reached a magnitude 5.2 seismic measurement. The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.
Customs officer Karbir Gaire was among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with China, where some 1,500 people had lived.
Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. Wednesday and was working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

“Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us,” he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. “We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.”

Gaire doesn’t remember exactly how many people were in the office when the disaster struck, but 15 colleagues have gone missing. “It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don’t call it a flood, it was a tsunami.”
Families around the world hope for news of loved ones
Nepal’s tourism board has said that among the missing are more than 500 foreigners.

About 90 Americans were unaccounted for. U.S. President Donald Trump said the flooding was terrible to see, and he told reporters in the Oval Office he offered to provide Nepal’s leaders “anything they want.”

Rajan Tamang, a restaurant owner in New York City, said he learned from family in Kathmandu that his mother and sister were among those who died, while many other relatives and friends remained missing.

“My family was just waking up, and they didn’t even get any information, and suddenly this flood came. Some of them are missing, some of them lost their life and only a few is alive,” he told the AP after a vigil in New York.
Some of the missing may have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy, who works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry, said that he last spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on that pilgrimage Wednesday morning. It was a highly anticipated trip, something his mother had always wanted to do, he said.

“My mother said they were on their way towards the border area and said they’ll reach their hotel and call us,” he said. While he’s in touch with government officials, and the travel agency, there’s been no news.
“This was the last we spoke to them. They have been unreachable since.”

articles.title: Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final
articles.summary: Experts examined the use of forced contraception on the Inuit community during the 1960s and 70s.

blocks.text: Greenland's justice minister has said the government cannot conclude whether genocide was committed against the Inuit community after experts examined the use of forced contraception in the 1960s and 70s.
"We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide," Marianne Paviasen told reporters. "This is something we can continue to debate."
Two reports on the practice were released on Friday, a year after Denmark apologised for the treatment of Inuit women and girls in its autonomous territory.
Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a "reconciliation commission" would be set up while Danish PM Mette Frederiksen promised the governments would work together.
Denmark has passed a compensation law to pay 300,000 Danish crowns (£34,404; $46,800) to each woman affected by the policy.

Records from the national archives show that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls, some as young as 13, had an intra-uterine device (IUD) implanted under a birth-control programme administered by Danish doctors.
In recent years, many women came forward to say they had been fitted with an IUD without their knowledge or consent.
Use of the birth control was so widespread that Greenland's population growth severely slowed.
Frederiksen issued an apology last August to Greenlandic women and their families affected by "systematic discrimination".
In 2024, a former prime minister of Greenland, Mute B Egede, described the practice as "genocide".

Under the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, external, one definition of genocide is "imposing measures intended to prevent births" within a "national, ethnical, racial or religious group".
The territory tasked a panel of four experts with establishing whether human rights had been violated and whether such violations met the definition of genocide.
However, the panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report.

The two experts who remained, Alaskan lawyer Dalee Sambo Dorough and University of Copenhagen law professor Miriam Cullen, found in their report that the rights of Inuit women in Greenland had been violated.
But they said that they could not conclude that genocide had taken place "on the basis of contraceptive practices alone".

They added that genocidal intent by Denmark remained a "possible inference" that a court might establish, based on evidence that fell outside the scope of their report, such as the removal of Inuit children to be raised by Danish families.

The rival report, produced by Jonas Christoffersen, former head of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, and Jensine Nedergaard, a psychologist who had worked in Greenland, accepted that women had been wronged but could not establish the extent of their mistreatment.
They found no evidence "any authority or health professional at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population".
Reacting on Friday, Greenland's justice minister said the two reports were so different that one "says there was no genocide at all" while the other "says there could have been".

One woman affected by the forced contraception policy, Henriette Berthelsen, told news agency AFP before the reports were presented that their conclusions had been skewed from the start because no Greenlandic Inuits had been appointed as experts.
"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said.
"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."
Another woman, Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters that she remembered waking up from what she had been told was a minor operation to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.
"It turns out we were treated like animals," she said. "Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act."
A doctor, she added, later told her complications from the coil had left her unable to become pregnant. She went on to adopt two children from Colombia.
"We are very deferential to authority because we are colonial children," she said.

Reacting to the reports on Friday, Frederiksen said: "We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together."
Greenland was a Danish colony until 1953 and did not gain home rule until 1979. Copenhagen continued to oversee its healthcare system until 1992.
The Inuit, or mixed Danish and Inuit, make up nearly 90% of the island's population of 56,000.

The birth-control campaign was designed to control the territory's population, which had ballooned since the 1950s, aided by modernisation and better healthcare. This growth, in addition to an increasing rate of teenage pregnancies, had alarmed the Danish authorities.

In 1970, the campaign was considered a "success" as fertility rates had fallen sharply, though the rate continued to fall for some time after that. In the eight years from the campaign's inception in 1966 until 1974 when it levelled off, Greenland's fertility rate plunged from seven children per woman to 2.3.

articles.title: Animal Justice urges investigation into Marineland beluga death in Chicago, wants relocation efforts halted
articles.summary: Animal Justice is calling for Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) to investigate the death in a Chicago aquarium of Peekachu, a 23-year-old beluga from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., that was part…

image.caption: One of four belugas shipped from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., arrives at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago on Thursday. One of the whales has since died. (Shedd Aquarium and Brenna Hernandez)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Animal Justice is calling for Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) to investigate the death in a Chicago aquarium of Peekachu, a 23-year-old beluga from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., that was part of ongoing relocation efforts involving other whales and dolphins.
Rescue plan gives the whales 'best chance at survival,' says office of Canada's fisheries minister
Animal Justice is calling for Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) to investigate the death in a Chicago aquarium of Peekachu, a 23-year-old beluga from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont.
The national animal law advocacy organization also wants DFO to halt the ongoing relocation efforts of marine mammals from the shuttered theme park until an investigation is completed.
Peekachu arrived at Shedd Aquarium on Aug. 13 and died on Aug. 25.

Kaitlyn Mitchell, Animal Justice's legal advocacy director, has asked in a letter to Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson that DFO determine how Peekachu was approved for transport "despite apparent underlying health problems."

Health assessments of the whales by an accredited Canadian veterinarian were required before the move. A source also told CBC News in January that Marineland had to confirm the assessments in writing.
Shedd Aquarium has said Peekachu was dehydrated and wasn't eating well.
"On Tuesday evening, as teams worked to provide her with medicine and fluids, Peekachu passed away suddenly," it said in an earlier statement, adding a necropsy is being conducted.

"From the outset of this rescue, we understood each animal would be navigating a significant transition and that their complete health picture, including conditions that may have developed over time, could only become clearer through ongoing assessment and care."
DFO says 'reasonable steps' taken for whales' safety
CBC reached out to Marineland for comment but hadn't heard back by publication time.
In a statement, Thompson's office said "Peekachu’s death is difficult news."

It said the Canadian government has "taken reasonable steps" to ensure the whales' safety. Those steps included issuing the necessary CITES permits following a review of the transportation plan, and issuing Fisheries Act authorizations after individual health assessments for each whale were done.
"The minister has the utmost confidence in the rescue plan, which gives these animals the best chance at survival, and in the experienced professionals caring for them."

Mitchell's letter asks that the transportation of six remaining belugas — the last captive whales in Canada — be halted until an investigation into Peekachu's death is completed and it's proved that the other whales are healthy enough to make the trip to their new homes.
"Cetacean transport is an inherently stressful and potentially dangerous process, particularly for animals whose health may already be compromised," it says.

A total of 30 belugas and four dolphins were set to be relocated as Marineland moves all of its animals off the property. The park, which is for sale, has said it's running out of money and can no longer afford to care for the animals.
'Emergency rescue' of Marineland belugas begins

Marineland had originally sold its belugas and dolphins to an aquarium in China, but Ottawa blocked the move, saying it violated the spirit of a 2019 law. That law bans whale and dolphin captivity, and doesn't allow breeding and performances.
After Thompson nixed the move to China, Marineland threatened to euthanize its whales unless Ottawa provided an emergency infusion of cash.

The park then turned to a consortium of American and Spanish aquariums for help. Its belugas have also been shipped to SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio, and the Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta.
Concerns of more whale deaths
Naomi Rose is a senior scientist for marine mammal biology at the Animal Welfare Institute in Washington, D.C., and a member of the board for the proposed Whale Sanctuary Project in Nova Scotia.
Rose agrees with Animal Justice's call for an investigation.
She accused Marineland of "washing their hands" of the whales.
"[Belugas] are intelligent, social, long-living animals. They deserve someone to be accountable. And the accountable party is not stepping up to the plate."
Rose also expressed concerns that "more whales will die."
"Peekachu is just the first."

Rose said Peekachu may have been suffering from storage disease — a genetic condition that causes buildup of fats, sugars and other cellular material "that can damage organs," and is exacerbated by stress.
"They're already stressed out just living at Marineland, and then they're transported."

Referring to the relocation process, Rose added that the whale are "taken out of the water, they're put in stretchers, they're put in boxes, they're put on planes, they're put on trucks, there's a lot of noise, they're stranded."
Two of the three whales that died at Mystic Aquarium from 2021-2023 after being moved from Marineland were diagnosed with storage disease after their deaths, according to Mystic.
Looking for 'the right answer'
Rose said the Marineland whales are being transported to different facilities and being separated, causing them more stress.
She said these issues aren't the fault of the facilities receiving the whales, and feels Marineland should have waited to send the whales to a sanctuary.
However, Marineland's owners said in a report in 2025 that the proposed Nova Scotia sanctuary is too polluted and isn’t on track to being developed soon enough.

items: Why it’s so hard to find a new home for Marineland’s 30 belugas
Marineland says its belugas shouldn't go to Nova Scotia's Whale Sanctuary Project

blocks.text: Rose, who described a lose-lose situation for the whales, said she disagrees with the Animal Justice letter asking that the whales be kept at Marineland for the time being, because she feels the belugas would still be at risk.
"I don't know what the right answer is. None of us do."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Aura Carreño Rosas is a reporter at CBC Hamilton. She's originally from Venezuela. She has extensive experience in covering stories about immigrants and migrant workers as well as interesting people with diverse journeys. You can contact her at aura.carreno.rosas@cbc.ca
With files from Carly Thomas, Saira Peesker, The Canadian Press

articles.title: Rob Reiner's son Jake on his parents' killings: 'I will never understand why this happened'
articles.summary: Jake Reiner this week gave his first sit-down interview since the killing of his parents, filmmaker Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, in California in December. He told KABC-TV about the shock he…

image.caption: Jake Reiner appears in this screenshot from an interview on KABC-TV — his first interview since his parents, Hollywood filmmaker Rob Reiner and photographer Michele Singer Reiner, were killed on Dec. 14. (ABC7/YouTube)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Jake Reiner this week gave his first sit-down interview since the killing of his parents, filmmaker Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, in California in December. He told KABC-TV about the shock he felt after being told his parents were dead and the complicated feelings he has for his younger brother, Nick, who's currently facing murder charges in the killings.
Jake Reiner gives his first interview since the deaths of his parents 8 months ago
For Jake Reiner, ever since Dec. 14, 2025, time has moved both excruciatingly slowly and impossibly fast.

"It's been eight months. It feels like eight years at the same time, and it also feels like eight minutes," he told KABC-TV's Mark Cota-Robles in his first sit-down interview since his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, were found fatally stabbed in their Los Angeles home that Sunday afternoon. Hours later, the couple's 32-year-old son, Nick Reiner, was arrested and later charged with murder in their deaths.

items: Rob Reiner, dead at 78, remembered as Hollywood legend in his own right after following father's footsteps

blocks.text: "Every moment that I wake up, I'm reminded of my reality and you're living through that every single day," Jake said.
In the interview, which was released on Thursday, he recalled getting a call that day from his younger sister, Romy, who had made the discovery.
"Romy told me that our dad was dead and then she said, I can't find mom," he told Cota-Robles in the hour-long interview. "I immediately went into shock."

items: What we know about Nick Reiner, in custody following his parents' deaths

blocks.text: Nick was formally indicted on July 20 on two counts of first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of Rob Reiner, a prolific Hollywood filmmaker, actor and political activist, and his wife, Michele, a photographer and producer. He pleaded not guilty.

In the indictment, unsealed on Aug. 12, the LA County grand jury alleged that Nick, who had a long documented history of mental health challenges and struggles with addiction, was lying in wait before attacking his parents.

In 2016, Rob and Nick Reiner released a film they worked on together called Being Charlie, inspired by Nick's struggles with addiction. The film tells the story of a rebellious, drug-addicted teenage son of an actor-turned-politician father, who falls in love with a fellow addict.
At the time, Rob told the media that the film was "by far the most personal thing that I've ever done," and that filming the movie brought him closer to his son.

items: Indictment alleges Nick Reiner lay in wait before killing his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner

blocks.text: In Thursday's interview, when asked about previously describing the aftermath of the killings as losing half of his family — including Nick — Jake doubled down, while seemingly struggling to find the right words.
"I mean he's in jail so, you know it's — it's like I physically lost my parents and then Nick was arrested and it's like, no it's just me and Romy," he said.
He also addressed the complicated feelings he now has toward his younger brother, saying he will "never understand why this happened."

"For me, it manifests into anger, it manifests into rage, into how unfair this was, how I didn't get a say in what happened," he said. "I didn't get to stop it from happening. I had no choice in the matter, and I just have to accept the reality of it. And to me, that's one of the most infuriating parts of all of this."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.
with files from Abby Hughes

articles.title: US plans to cut off military aid to key Middle East ally, BBC told
articles.summary: Iraqi Kurdistan fears the Trump administration's plan will make the region more vulnerable to further attacks from Iran.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Iranian drones have hit the Iraqi city of Irbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region
ByDaniel Bush
Washington correspondent

The Trump administration is planning to cut off military aid to a key Middle East ally that helped the US defeat the Islamic State group (IS) and is now facing punishing attacks from Iran, according to four sources familiar with the matter.

The US Department of Defense has told leaders of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region in recent meetings that the administration is not planning to renew an expiring agreement that provides security assistance to the Peshmerga, the Kurdish security force.

The BBC spoke to two officials who participated in the talks and two other sources with direct knowledge of the issue. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the talks, details of which have not been previously reported.

Kurdish officials fear the funding cut would create a power vacuum and embolden Iran, which has fired hundreds of missiles and drones into Iraqi Kurdistan since US President Donald Trump started the war with Tehran.
Ending the Peshmerga's security assistance would undermine a longtime partner in Iraq, analysts said, and send the message that the US cannot be trusted to back its allies in the region.

"The US would be cutting off the Kurds, who shed so much blood to help the Americans achieve their goals in Iraq and the wider Middle East," Yerevan Saeed, the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, said.
"This is going to be a big win for Iran, China, and Russia if the Kurds are left so exposed."

blocks.caption: A map showing the Kurdish region of Iraq shaded in yellow, and a disputed area in red and white crosshatch. Iraq is surrounded by Syria to the west, Turkey to the north, and Iran to the east

blocks.text: In his second term, Trump has pledged to reduce America's foreign entanglements in regions like the Middle East. He also launched the war with Iran, which reached the six-month mark on Friday with no end in sight.

The memorandum of understanding between the Pentagon and the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) is set to expire on 30 September, the same day the US and other nations are withdrawing their last remaining troops from Iraq.

The troop withdrawal will formally end the international military campaign against IS, in which the Peshmerga fought alongside coalition troops to end the jihadist group's control of parts of Iraq and Syria. The sole remaining US military base in the country, located in the Iraqi Kurdish capital of Irbil, is set to close next month once coalition troops leave.

The Peshmerga, which has approximately 180,000 troops in Iraqi Kurdistan, received $61m (£45m) in the fiscal year 2026 for weapons, military training and stipends through the Pentagon's counter-IS programme.

The Pentagon proposed cutting all the group's security aid in its fiscal year 2027 budget request - arguing that since IS was defeated the money should now be reallocated - but the spending plan is on hold amid a broader budget battle in Congress.
The request raised alarm bells in Iraqi Kurdistan, but officials had held out hope that the US would renew the funding through an extension of the current deal.

The fears have only grown as Iran has stepped up attacks against the KRG. Iran and Iranian-backed militias had conducted 158 missile or drone attacks inside Iraqi Kurdistan by late May, according to reasearch on the latest available data compiled by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington DC think tank.

But despite the surge in attacks, in recent talks with Iraqi and Kurdish leaders, defence department officials said the US was not planning to extend the memorandum of understanding, multiple sources with knowledge of the discussions said. The Pentagon signed the initial memorandum of understanding giving military assistance to the Peshmerga in 2016 and renewed it in 2022.

A final decision on security engagement between the US and Kurdistan is still being reviewed, according to one source familiar with the Pentagon's thinking. The US is considering ways to maintain some security support in both Iraq and Iraqi Kurdistan after the troop withdrawal, the sources said.

The KRG declined to comment. The White House referred the BBC to the Pentagon where a spokesperson pointed to a statement by the department summarising Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in July.

"The United States, Iraq and Coalition partners have achieved tremendous success in defeating ISIS and now the Iraqi Security Forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, will lead the fight against terrorists in Iraq," the statement said.

A State Department spokesperson told the BBC it was focused on implementing the troop withdrawal, and "ensuring that Prime Minister Zaidi is positioned to disarm Iran-aligned terrorist militias and safeguard Iraqi sovereignty."
The expiration of the security aid for the Peshmerga would come less than one year after the US opened its largest consulate in the world, in Irbil.

At the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the $800m complex last December, Michael Rigas, a senior US State Department official, said the consulate was "a testament to the value of the relationship between the United States and the Iraqi Kurdistan Region".

The recent discussions around Kurdish security were part of larger conversations between the US, the Iraqi government and KRG over the upcoming troop withdrawal. That date was set under a 2024 agreement between Washington and Baghdad to withdraw the US troops that remain in Iraq from the campaign against IS. American combat troops left Iraq in 2011 but returned after the power vacuum led to the rise of IS in 2014.
The US could avoid repeating the same mistake by continuing to back the Peshmerga, said James Jeffrey, who spearheaded the global coalition against IS in Trump's first term.
"It's money well spent, as we found out when the Islamic State rolled into northern Iraq," said Jeffrey, a former US ambassador to Iraq and Turkey under the Obama administration.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Al-Zaidi met Trump at the White House in July

blocks.text: Al-Zaidi met Trump at the White House in July

The Trump administration has not said how many US troops brought in to fight IS more than a decade ago remain in Iraq. Experts believe it's under 1,000, down from 170,000 at the height of the Iraq War.

The recent meetings on Iraqi security included the White House, Defense and State Departments, with Tom Barrack acting as a principal US voice on Iraq, four sources said. A close Trump ally, Barrack is the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Iraq and Syria.

The administration has said publicly it's open to a bilateral security agreement with Iraq. The countries discussed a possible defence pact in the recent meetings, but it's still unclear how the agreement might be structured or what Iraqi Kurdistan's role might be.
Al-Zaidi touted the troop withdrawal during his visit to Washington last month. Al-Zaidi, who was elected in May, met Trump at the White House, as well as Hegseth and members of Congress.
"October 1 will mark a new day in the trajectory of the Iraqi state, as Iraq will be free of any foreign military presence," al-Zaidi's office said in a statement at the time.

The withdrawal will reduce the exposure of US troops in the Middle East who have been targeted by Iran during the war, analysts said. Tehran has attacked US bases across the region, including the base in Irbil.
But it will leave the Peshmerga security force and the rest of the region it helps protect even more vulnerable than before, said Jason Campbell, a former US defence official.

"The Peshmerga have been the frontline in the US and international war with ISIS," said Campbell, an expert at the Middle East Institute. "If the US moves forward with this, it'll make the Kurds perhaps the most vulnerable potential targets of Iran."

articles.title: Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne
articles.summary: Mourners gather outside the palace as royals, politicians and citizens remember a beloved king, whose son has adopted the family motto "all for norway".

blocks.text: Image source, Cornelius Poppe / NTB / AFP via Getty Images) / Norway OUT
Norwegians are grieving the death of the beloved King Harald V, as a period of national mourning begins and his son Haakon VIII assumes the throne.
After Harald's death was announced early on Friday, crowds amassed at the royal palace in Oslo, laying flowers and flags, some mourners visibly in tears.
The 53-year-old new king held an extraordinary council of state meeting with government ministers, saying he was taking on the royal family's motto "All for Norway".

Harald - who was on the throne for 35 years - died in hospital at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) aged 89, after being treated there for a rare blood condition. His coffin was later taken to the palace in a public procession.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Memorials outside the palace included a candle with the word "thanks" written on it

blocks.text: Image source, Odd ANDERSEN / AFP via Getty Images
Memorials outside the palace included a candle with the word "thanks" written on it
An estimated 10,000 people lined the streets in the capital to see the late king go past, Norway's public broadcaster reported.
The late monarch has been described as an inclusive, transparent and empathetic "people's king" who modernised the Norwegian monarchy.

European royals, including King Charles III - whose mother Queen Elizabeth II was Harald's second cousin - as well as political leaders and ordinary citizens, paid tribute to his service and the stability he brought to the country.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".

In a televised memorial address - one of multiple eulogies by ministers - he said the late king's "legacy lives on" and offered condolences to the royal family and Queen Sonja, who would have celebrated her 58th wedding anniversary with Harald on Saturday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Støre was joined by ministers and a crowd of citizens grieving outside the palace

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Dylan Martinez
Støre was joined by ministers and a crowd of citizens grieving outside the palace

Norway's superstar footballer Erling Haaland thanked Harald for "everything you meant to Norway" in a post on Instagram, adding that it had been an honour to meet him earlier in the summer at the palace following the Fifa World Cup.
In the country's capital, Norwegians shared their grief and affection for the late king.
"I personally will say he was everything for us, especially being an immigrant," Biteya Terfassa, an Oslo resident who was born in Ethiopia, told news agency Reuters outside the palace.
"He made us feel at home and he made us feel loved. So he was like a grandfather that I never had."
Norwegians have been laying tributes and remembering the late King Harald V following his death.
At noon, the Norwegian Armed Forces honoured Harald with a funeral salute of 21 shots from Akershus Fortress in central Oslo.
Later on Friday, a procession left the chapel at Rikshospitalet, where Harald died, taking his coffin in a hearse to the royal palace.
The date of Harald's funeral is yet to be officially announced. Until then, he will be lying in state in the palace chapel so the public can pay their last respects.

During the national mourning period, flags will be flown at half-mast across the Nordic country, while Harald's portrait will be displayed, candles lit and moments of silence held at professional events.
All non work-related social events will be cancelled or postponed. Oslo Mayor Anne Lindboe, who was due to get married on Friday, even postponed her wedding.
King Harald's coffin moving from Oslo hospital to Royal Palace
King Haakon, who is Harald's younger child, is now the monarch and his wife Mette-Marit queen.
He is due to take an oath before the Norwegian parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer has.

His daughter, the 22-year-old Ingrid Alexandra, who joined her father to meet ministers at the palace on Friday, is next in line to the throne as crown princess after the rules of succession changed in 1990 to allow firstborn women to inherit the crown.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, second from right, stood by her father's side

blocks.text: Image source, NTB/Lise Aserud via REUTERS
Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, second from right, stood by her father's side
Haakon assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.

Now-Queen Mette-Marit came under scrutiny earlier this year when it was revealed that she had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she has publicly apologised.

Later in the year, she received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.
Meanwhile, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.
Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when now-King Haakon married his mother.

blocks.caption: Family tree of King Haakon's family

blocks.text: Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year found that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

articles.title: Germany news: Baltic summit plans hybrid-threat task force
articles.summary: Ministers from countries bordering the Baltic Sea have agreed on a rapid response force to counter hybrid threats. Meanwhile, the far-right AfD has failed to topple a state premier. DW has more…
articles.byline: Mark Hallam, Rana Taha, Richard Connor

image.caption: Germany hosted the Baltic Sea Security Summit in the light of attempted drone attacks in the countryImage: Christian Charisius/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026last updated August 28, 2026
Dobrindt: Security task force and enhanced drone defense agreed at Baltic summit

blocks.caption: Dobrindt said the assembled politicians agreed to set up a Baltic security taskforce and to expand their drone defense capabilitiesImage: Christian Charisius/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that Baltic and European leaders at a special hybrid security meeting agreed to plans to set up a new security task force and to enhance collective drone defense capabilities.

The assembled politicians discussed "urgent security policy questions for a shared future in the Baltic Sea region," Dobrindt said amid the meeting at the Mürwik naval training center in Flensburg on Germany's northeast coast

"Foreign powers are trying to attack our security with hybrid measures, to destabilize our democracies, to weaken our economy," he said. "Drone attacks, cyber attacks, spying, disinformation, arson attacks on critical infrastructure, covert operations and the use of 'disposable agents' are all rapidly increasing in number."

Dobrindt warned that the recent past had shown a pronounced increase in the "quality and intensity" of such attacks and surmised that "we must prepare ourselves for the hybrid threat situation continuing to intensify."
He said the shared goal was to bolster defense against such hybrid threats.

"We want to investigate, deter and defend altogether more quickly," Dobrindt said, saying they wanted to work together to transform the Balitc from a "collective risk area" into a "collective defensive area."

The assembled politicians from Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Sweden, Norway and Ireland — the current holder of the rotating EU presidency — had a working lunch at the Mürwik base amid the talks.
They were also taken out on the Baltic Sea in a German Federal Police motorboat.

blocks.caption: The 'BP 82 Bamberg' police boat took some of the visiting dignitaries for a ride around the harborImage: Christian Charisius/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say
articles.summary: But they say Moscow will likely continue its "hybrid activity" against Nato members, short of direct military action.

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe.
Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance.

But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new".
They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West.

The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia.

Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader – saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory".

Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing.

However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts.

They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation.
Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries.

Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role.
It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this.
Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil".
Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine.
The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns.
Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home.

They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power.
Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties.
The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit.
That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation.

articles.title: ‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe return
articles.summary: Relatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disaster
articles.byline: Henry Belot, Nino Bucci and Kat Wong

blocks.text: The families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parents in Nepal remain hopeful they will be found safe.

Dozens of Australians are missing after devastating flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday that the total number of people missing had risen sharply to more than 1,900 swelled by 933 workers on hydropower projects on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning. The number of people killed is at least 584.
One Australian woman contacted her family on Friday morning to tell them that she had survived the flood, the first of those reported missing to be confirmed safe.
Among the missing Australians is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian air force who was travelling in Nepal with Kailash Journeys.
“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen, who did not want her surname published.
“He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”
Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their two sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were taking part in a pilgrimage when the flood hit on Wednesday.
Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said that she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.
The family of four planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour.
“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said.
“Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.”

Vaishnavi, who asked that her surname not be published, confirmed the family were close with other members of the group who had also travelled from Sydney for the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet.
The family had been training together for the long walk, she said.
“They had been planning for some time, and preparing, because it’s quite a trek.
“They were all working very hard together to make sure they could successfully complete it.
“We just didn’t expect anything like this.”
Vaishnavi said it was difficult to get clear information about what was being done to find those missing. She has spoken with Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials.
“We do want to know what efforts are being made … we’re not aware of what is actually happening there.”
Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was at an immigration office at the Gyirong Post crossing when the flood waters hit. She was travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage to the region.
Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal and is desperately seeking information about her whereabouts.

“She was in the same area when the flood happened,” said a flyer produced by Adhikari’s family, and published with their permission. “If anyone has seen her or has any information about her, please contact the family immediately.”

blocks.caption: Sumi Adhikari was travelling as part of an Isha Foundation pilgrimage. Illustration: supplied

blocks.text: Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.
He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu and then Delhi, his close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.
Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has gone on to Kathmandu to look for any information.
“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” Tiwari said.
Suhasini Kandimalla, a mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, has also been reported missing.
Her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla, said that she was doing the hike with another Springfield local.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Suhasini Kandimalla from Queensland who has been reported missing in Nepal. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.
“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini told the Guardian.
“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”

A Brisbane man, Narayan Panthi, is also missing in the region. According to Nepal police, he was travelling with Kathmandu Holiday but he has also been conducting charity work in the capital with an education fund, the NeNas Foundation.

blocks.caption: Narayan Panthi from Brisbane is missing in Nepal. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, said his family was devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.
“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”
Bhusal said Panthi was “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.
New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife, Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were also among the 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash.
So too were Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer, and their adult sons Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20.
The brothers played cricket for West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.

“WPHCCC is aware of the reports that two of our players, Rishab and Rudhra Iyer, along with their family members and other Australians, are unaccounted for in the ongoing floods in Nepal,” the club said in a statement.
“We continue to live in hope, and our thoughts are currently with them, their loved ones and all affected by this tragedy in Nepal.”
The University of Newcastle’s vice-chancellor, Alex Zelinsky, said Rishab and Rudhra were both medical students the at the university.

“We are thinking of them, their families, their fellow students and teaching staff, as well as the many people who have been impacted by this devastating event and we hope that both students can be located soon,” Zelinsky said in a statement.
Separate groups of Australians – 11 travelling with Trekkers Society and six with Kailash Journeys – are also unaccounted for. Both tour companies have been contacted for comment.
Several other Australians were travelling with other tour groups. It is understood the majority of missing Australians are from New South Wales, but there are also some from Victoria and Queensland.
The founder and chief executive of Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Sagar Pandey, said he had lost all contact with his tour group of 47 people, which included the 15 Australians.
Pandey told the Guardian on Thursday he had flown by helicopter over the Rasuwa area, where the tour was staying, since the flood and had little hope they survived.
“To be honest … you would think there was no human civilisation there at all.
“The flash flood swept away everything, everything. You couldn’t see any human creations.
“Still, I have a hope.”
The Isha Foundation confirmed that 11 Australians were among a group of 80 missing pilgrims who had been in an immigration building when the flood hit.
The foreign minister, Penny Wong, spoke to her Nepali counterpart, Shisir Khanal, on Friday evening to convey Australia’s deepest condolences following the devastating floods.
She outlined Australia’s humanitarian assistance package in which Australia was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response” to the flooding.
Wong said the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours’” to help Australian staff already on the ground.
“The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.”

articles.title: Family seeks help locating Filipino doctor missing after Nepal floods
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The family of Filipino doctor Juan Carlos Manalo has appealed for help locating him after losing contact with him following flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border. Manalo’s…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The family of Filipino doctor Juan Carlos Manalo has appealed for help locating him after losing contact with him following flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Manalo’s sister, Chiara Manalo, said on Friday that the family had not heard from him since Tuesday, a day before the disaster struck the area.
In a Facebook post, Chiara said the family’s last contact with Manalo was at 1:21 p.m. Philippine time on Tuesday or 11:06 a.m. Nepal time.
She said Manalo was traveling with the Isha Sadghuru group on a Kailashyatra tour. The group’s last known location was at the Immigration Office in Gyirong, according to the family.
“Please help us look for my brother,” Chiara said.

The family appealed to anyone with information about Manalo or members of the group to contact them. It also asked for help connecting with agencies that could coordinate with Nepali authorities and assist in search operations.
“Receiving and seeing the news about the catastrophe has been very difficult for us. We humbly ask to include him in your prayers, that he may return to us safely soon,” the family said.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Friday that the Philippine Embassy in New Delhi and the Philippine Honorary Consulate General in Kathmandu were coordinating with local authorities and were ready to assist Filipinos affected by the disaster.
DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel said the agency was awaiting confirmation from Nepali authorities on a Filipino national who was reported missing.
Ratonel also said the DFA had forwarded to the concerned office information provided by Chiara about her brother.

The reported missing Filipino appeared in a preliminary record released by the Nepal Tourism Board, which listed one Filipino among travelers unaccounted for in the affected areas. The Philippine government has yet to independently confirm the report.
The disaster struck Wednesday after a glacial collapse triggered a massive debris flow, sending water, mud, rock and ice through communities along the Nepal-Tibet border.
The DFA has not confirmed that Manalo is the Filipino listed in the preliminary Nepal Tourism Board record.
Chiara said receiving news of the disaster had been difficult for the family and asked the public to pray for her brother’s safe return. /jpv

articles.title: Impeachment prosecutor Mae Divinagracia and her comfort cross go viral
articles.summary: Atty. Mae Divinagracia, one of the private prosecutors in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, conducted her direct examination of hostile witness Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 1:42am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

Atty. Mae Divinagracia, one of the private prosecutors in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, conducted her direct examination of hostile witness Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio while holding what appeared to be a wooden cross.

The "comfort cross" has since gone viral following the many short-form videos posted about it, after its noticeable presence while the prosecutor sought answers regarding the disbursement of confidential funds from the Vice President's deputy chief of staff.
