blocks.text: In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.
Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

blocks.caption: Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.
Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”
It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Protests in Malaysia in 2012 against the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. Meta was alleged in a lawsuit to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya. Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”
The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.
That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

articles.title: Protesters set fire to migrant camp in Ceuta
articles.summary: The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish exclave in North Africa.

image.caption: Police had to intervene when protesters began setting fire to the parts of the campImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRES/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters in Ceuta set fire to a migrant camp and clashed with police on Thursday. The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish enclave in North Africa.
Footage on Spanish television showed a group of demonstrators on a beach, throwing objects into the fire. Police pushed the protesters back while the migrants retreated to a pier.
Earlier on Thursday, a military vehicle was attacked with stones and other objects by about 70 people, a police spokesman in Ceuta told the AFP news agency.
Local protesters tried to stop Red Cross vehicles from reaching the beach to distribute food to migrants. People waving Spanish flags shouted "They should leave" and "Out with the Red Cross."

blocks.caption: Locals in Ceuta accuse the government of mishandling the situationImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: How many migrants are still in Ceuta?
In July, more than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly in the hope of reaching the European mainland.
While the vast majority of them have since returned to Morocco, several thousand remain in Ceuta, living on the streets or on the beach.
Spain's government in Madrid puts the number at below 7,000 while Ceuta officials say it's at least 10,000. Ceuta's population is about 84,000 people.
Growing pressure on Madrid

The Spanish government is under growing pressure over the situation in Ceuta. The conservative opposition is accusing left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to act and abandoning Ceuta's residents.

Madrid has recently moved to speed up efforts to identify the migrants and decide who will be sent back to Morocco. The government also approved extra funding to help unaccompanied minors entitled to special protection.
The crisis comes ahead of general elections next year and has deepened political divisions in Spain. The conservative opposition is calling for a tougher stance on migration.
The mass influx in July had also led to tension within the EU over how to respond to the situation in Ceuta.

articles.title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Mark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the move

blocks.text: Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario, making it Lake America, amid his escalating trade war with Canada.

The order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases. But Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.
The move follows a similar action the president took on the first day of his second term in office, when he signed an order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.

“We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” he told reporters, sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “Maybe we’ll change them both.”
Propped behind the US president was a large map of the Great Lakes region, with “Lake America” printed in red lettering above Lake Ontario.

Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, rejected the US’s attempt to rename the body of water, explaining in a post on social media that its name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he wrote on X. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia, responded: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
Several US governors in the Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change.
“New York won’t be calling it that,” the state’s governor, Democrat Kathy Hochul replied. New York borders the lake.

Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, recalled that schoolchildren learn the acronym H-O-M-E-S for the names of the five great lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior. And the Wisconsin governor, Democrat Tony Evers, mocked the move by sharing a video of himself changing the name of Lake Michigan to Lake Wisconsin, signed on a restaurant napkin.

The latest tweak of Canada’s nose by the US president comes as tensions increase between the US and its northern neighbor. Over the weekend, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed and the US imposed a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports, with Trump threatening another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney hit back with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

“They want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said, a nod to his previous suggestions that Canada should become the “51st state” in the union, a prospect that has enraged Canadians. “But they want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that any more.”

Trump complained about a $60bn US trade deficit with Canada, which economists note is attributable almost entirely to US imports of oil; without that exchange, the US runs a sizable trade surplus. Trump claimed that American farmers were being charged a 400% tariff; about 97% of US agricultural exports to Canada enter duty-free under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, though over-quota eggs, milk and dairy have Canadian tariffs of up to 300%.

“As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade. Sad,” Trump said after signing the executive order updating the Department of Interior’s naming conventions. “Even the military: we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything. They don’t pay us to defend Canada. But we defend Canada.”
Both Canada and the United States are Nato members and have treaty obligations of mutual defense under the North Atlantic Treaty, the Ogdensburg Agreement and numerous other treaties.
Trump claimed the name change was something he had been considering for “a long time”.
“We’ve notified all the various people we have to notify,” he said after signing the order … This is official effective immediately.”
An administration official noted that the lake bordering Canada and the state of New York has most of its volume in the United States and that the deepest part of the lake is in US territory.

articles.title: Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold in lightning raid on Villena Museum
articles.summary: One of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections has been swiped, almost in its entirety, from Villena Museum. A highly professional group of thieves were in and out in four minutes flat…

image.caption: The Bronze age collection's historical value is incalculable, but even the gold is worth a pretty penny if melted down and therefore lost forever [FILE: Nov 10, 2016]Image: Lanmas/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months.
The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes.
A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items.
What happened in the heist?

"The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation.
The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province.

"They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth."
The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.

Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind.
"All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.

blocks.caption: The collection was discovered more than 60 years ago and is thought to be a little more than 3,000 years oldImage: Museo de Villena

blocks.text: What is the Treasure of Villena?
The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed.
They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE.
The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets.

The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum.

The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million.

According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor.

blocks.caption: The collection includes some of the oldest known iron metalwork, seemingly thanks to the raw materials landing as part of a meteoriteImage: Museo de Villena

blocks.text: Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre
Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year.

Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October, escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period.
Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily.

Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma. Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes.
Louvre heist inspires freight lift ad campaign

articles.title: The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84
articles.summary: For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian War. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and of other war crimes. Now he has died in detention at The Hague.

image.caption: Ratko Mladic in the courtroom in The Hague on June 8, 2021Image: Jerry Lampen/REUTERS

blocks.text: More than 30 years after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992-1995), Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.

Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later.

At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children.

Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the four-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country, half of its total population at the time.
Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead
'The butcher of the Balkans'
In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague.
International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans."
He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian War.

Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy.
"Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying.
Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre
Career in the Yugoslav army

At the beginning of the Croatian War in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentally changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence.

Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic.

blocks.caption: Ratko Mladic (left) and Radovan Karadzic, the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs during the Bosnian War, on August 5, 1993.Image: picture-alliance/ dpa

blocks.text: Flight, arrest and final verdict

At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just two years old when his father, one of Tito's Partisans, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview.

As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class. He quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state.
Serbian nationalist

Before the end of the Bosnian War in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure.

The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison at trial, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian War.
Ratko Mladic life sentence upheld
A war criminal who saw himself as a hero

Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. United Nations officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long-overdue but important acknowledgment of their suffering.
Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained that he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic."

Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls.

While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding. He survived several strokes while in prison.
Ratko Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Tragedy in Nepal: How do flash floods happen?
articles.summary: When flash floods sweep through the Himalayas, there is often little time to react. Scientists are working to understand the risks and improve early warning systems.

image.caption: Flash floods are a recurring threat in the Himalayas. Climate change contributes to the problemImage: Sunil Pradhan/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The disaster in the border region between China and Nepal was as sudden as it was unexpected: Within just 10 minutes, enormous volumes of water and debris swept 20 kilometers downstream on Wednesday, with devastating consequences for thousands of people in the region.

Flash floods are a frequent occurrence in the Himalayas. "They are more the rule than the exception," says Niels Hovius, head of the Geomorphology Section at the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam. He has worked in the Himalayas and other mountainous regions for many years and is an expert on early warning systems.
What triggered the flash flood?

Scientific data indicate that the disaster began with a glacier collapse in the northern part of the Langtang massif: a large amount of ice broke away and turned into a massive ice avalanche. The Langtang massif is located in central Nepal near the border with China.
Devastating flash floods hit northern Nepal

"This glacier collapse sent huge amounts of ice rapidly downhill," says Hovius. The heat generated by friction melted the ice into water, which then swept up debris and mud. The resulting mudflow moved downhill at speeds "reached by passenger cars on German highways."

Seismological instruments recorded an earthquake measuring 4.4 on the Richter scale at the time of the glacier collapse. However, Hovius says, it was not a "classic" or tectonic earthquake. Instead, the instruments measured the force of the falling glacier.
Why can flash floods in the Himalayas be so devastating?
Flash floods in high mountain regions can be triggered in different ways — by glacier collapses or by so-called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs, or Glacier Lake Outburst Floods).

In such cases, the topography around a glacial lake suddenly changes, for example when a slope collapses into the lake. The large volume of water that suddenly spills over the lake's banks can then turn into torrents rushing downstream. In this particular case, however, it is clear that this was not a GLOF, says Hovius.

Landslides can also cause deadly mudflows without any glaciers or glacial lakes being involved. In the Himalayas, all three types of events are possible, and historical data show that all three occur regularly, Hovius says.
Compared with the Alps, the valleys of the Himalayas are relatively narrow. The water and mud cannot spread out but are instead forced into a confined space, increasing their depth and speed.
Alps warming fast: Europe’s water lifeline is running dry
In addition to the speed of the water and debris, the extent of the devastation caused by a flash flood depends on how far local populations are from the source.
How can people be protected from flash floods?

Nepal faces two major challenges. Many people have settled along rivers in the valleys of the Himalayas — in precisely the areas that are vulnerable to flash floods. Secondly, there are very few early warning systems in the country, which is one of the poorest in Asia.

Even with a timely warning, the particularly devastating flash flood would have given people only a few minutes to reach safety. Hovius describes a flood that occurred in the same region last year. It was smaller, and therefore less severe. At the time, it took the water an hour to reach a settlement — enough time for people to escape if they had received a timely warning.

"There are initiatives in Nepal to establish local acoustic early warning systems," says Hovius. However, these systems are available only on a very limited scale. At most, they cover one percent of areas at risk. The GFZ researcher adds that mobile phones should be used to send people warnings via push notifications. Hovius is researching how the data needed for such a system could be generated.

Checks should also be made on how settlements are planned, Hovius says. At present, the bulk of a community's infrastructure is concentrated along rivers. "People have moved down from the mountains and settled in the valleys over the past few decades. Perhaps it would make sense to move back to higher ground."
Are flash floods in mountainous areas more frequent amid climate change?

"Attributing individual events to climate change is always difficult," Hovius says. But it is clear that glaciers in high mountain regions become less stable as temperatures rise. Larger volumes of water are also accumulating in glacial lakes, making GLOFs more likely.

As for the current flash flood, it is too early to say whether climbing temperatures caused the glacier to collapse. Flash floods have long been a regular occurrence in the Himalayas. "But I think it is likely that we will see more and more of these events," Hovius says, warning that future disasters could be even more serious.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Nepal flash flood death toll climbs to 579, with 32 Canadians, permanent residents among missing

image.caption: Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home Friday following flash floods in Devighat, Nepal. A sudden flood swept through the Bhote Koshi River basin in northern Rasuwa on Wednesday. (Ezra Acayan/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Thirty-two Canadian citizens and permanent residents are among the nearly 2,000 people missing after the catastrophic flash flood along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand confirmed Friday.
Anand confirmed during a media conference that 579 bodies had been recovered in the area so far and 1,924 people were still unaccounted for. Of those, 517 are foreign nationals, she said.
No Canadians are among those confirmed dead, Anand added.
"Nepal is facing a devastating humanitarian emergency with catastrophic damage," she said.
Canada also announced it was providing $5 million to support emergency relief funds to Nepal.
Meanwhile, rescuers worked through mud and debris Friday in areas devastated by the flood, continuing the search for those still missing.

Nepalese and Chinese authorities also warned of further flooding from a lake that formed upstream after Wednesday's disaster and was already overflowing. They urged people in potentially affected areas to move to safer ground.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says 3,742 people have been rescued.

The missing include tourists from several countries. Nepalese army spokesperson Brig.-Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told The Associated Press that a team had been deployed Friday to the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project near the Nepal-China border following reports that people were trapped inside a tunnel.
"It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud," Basnet said. "Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people."

The rescue effort has been challenging, and it's difficult to access some of the communities that have been most affected, Santosh Pandey, Oxfam's humanitarian lead in Nepal, told CBC's As it Happens from Kathmandu.
"Entire villages, entire communities, have been swept away. There is no one actually in the community to help each other," Pandey said.
"A lot of public infrastructure has been damaged, a lot of hospitals and health facilities have been completely swept away.
"It's a very chaotic situation right now."
Rescue workers climb through mud to free people trapped in tunnels
'We have to find him'

As rescuers work to reach remaining survivors, desperate families have crowded around hospitals trying to see if their loved ones can be identified among the hundreds of bodies that have been recovered.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, relatives peer at grim images lining a wall outside the forensic identification unit.
The photos show the badly battered bodies of victims, including young children who had been pulled from the mud.
“I came here because I hope I find [my brother]. I will search until my last breath is gone,” said Nirmala Sapkota Koholi, 49, who lives in the city of Lalitpur, south of Kathmandu.
“I have to go everywhere, we have to find him.”

Koholi told CBC News that her younger brother, Pradip Kumar Sapkota, was working as a driver with a group of pilgrims, including some from the United States and India. He had been on his phone with his daughter at 8:45 a.m. Wednesday. His daughter heard a loud boom and then the call suddenly cut off. They haven’t been able to reach him since.
Koholi has been to three hospitals and believes one of the victim photos could be her brother.
“He was a very good person. That is why God took him away.”
Lake formed from glacial debris poses new flood threat at Nepal-Tibet border
Red Cross raises alarm about secondary flood

Red Cross officials, at a news conference in Switzerland, expressed concern about a secondary flood and said that the organization's rescue operations were temporarily halted after trucks with relief supplies were were blocked ⁠by further flooding.

"We believe that at ​least 93,000 people have been ​affected and are in great need," said David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation ​of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies ⁠in Nepal.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry said on Friday that it appreciated the offers of help from several countries ‌with nationals missing amid the disaster but that it was able to manage the rescue efforts at present.

items: 10 Toronto residents on a trek in Nepal unaccounted for after deadly flash floods: non-profit group

blocks.text: Flood survivors, including injured people, were taken to Kathmandu and other locations.
The affected areas are popular with hikers and for pilgrimages to religious sites.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry and said that he last spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash on Wednesday morning at 9 a.m.
"This was the first time they had gone on this pilgrimage and it was something my mother always wanted to do," he said.
Survivor sees 'black storm'
Customs officer Karbir Gaire is among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with Tibet.
Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. on Wednesday and was busy working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

"Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us," he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. "We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us."
The disaster started with a glacier collapse that sent ice and rock flowing downstream, and which registered as a magnitude-5.2 seismic event at the U.S. Geological Survey.
The science behind Nepal's catastrophic flash floods
Gaire doesn't remember exactly how many people were in the office when the disaster struck, but his 15 colleagues have gone missing.
"It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don't call it a flood, it was a tsunami," he said.
Gaire described Timure as a vibrant place filled with government offices, hotels, cafes, banks, primary schools, tea shops and residential buildings, where more than 1,500 people were living.

articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
articles.summary:
Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime

The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release…

blocks.text: The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.
Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.
Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.
The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.
Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

articles.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
articles.summary:
Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking

South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents…

blocks.text: South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

blocks.caption: The seized parrot eggs. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment

blocks.text: The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.
South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

articles.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?
articles.summary:
The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected

A fresh outbreak of mpox

blocks.text: A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?

Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.
What is mpox?

Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.

blocks.caption: A colourised electron microscope image shows Mpox virus particles, represented in green, found within infected cultured cells, represented in blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for their differences in shape. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox.

It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US.
Why is it spreading to new countries?
There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.

The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk.

blocks.caption: A Red Cross worker disinfects a tent in the Don Bosco camps for internally displaced people in Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Moise Kasereka/EPA

blocks.text: In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.

“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.

“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.
What happened to those two big outbreaks?

The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.

blocks.caption: A passenger passes mpox alerts at Chennai airport in India. Photograph: R Satish Babu/AFP

blocks.text: The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.

If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.
How worrying is the new outbreak?
Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.

“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.”

blocks.caption: Furaha Elisabeth applies medication to the skin of her child, Sagesse Hakizimana, at a health centre near Goma, in the DRC. Photograph: Arlette Bashizi/Reuters

blocks.text: However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”

Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”
Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.
Are there vaccines and treatments?

The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.

Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”

A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.

blocks.caption: A young mpox patient receives treatment at the Kavumu hospital in Karanrhada, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Michael Lunanga/EPA

blocks.text: An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.

While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.

“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”

articles.title: Midnight blaze hits Mabolo warehouse; damage reaches P1.4M
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A fire broke out shortly after midnight on Wednesday, gutting a hardware warehouse along St. Jude Street in Barangay Mabolo, Cebu City. Fire authorities estimated the damage…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A fire broke out shortly after midnight on Wednesday, gutting a hardware warehouse along St. Jude Street in Barangay Mabolo, Cebu City.
Fire authorities estimated the damage caused by the fire at P1.4 million.
Ronieglen Lopez, a 20-year-old mechanic at the warehouse, said he noticed smoke coming from inside the building at around 11 p.m. on Tuesday, August 25.
Lopez lives in a company-provided workers’ housing facility adjacent to the warehouse.

“Pag-abli nako sa bintana, didto nako nakita nga nagbaga na. Mao to nibaba ko kay nagkuha og tubig kay abi namo nga matabang ra namo pero wala na jud. Mao to namukaw nalang ko sa akong mga kauban,” he said.

(When I opened the window, I saw that the fire was already blazing. So I went downstairs to get some water because we thought we could still put it out, but we really couldn’t anymore. So I just woke up my companions.)
The fire was reported to authorities shortly after midnight.
The first alarm was raised at 1:06 a.m. as flames rapidly spread through materials stored inside the facility. The fire was placed under control at 1:14 a.m. and declared out at 1:24 a.m.
As of this posting, fire investigators are continuing to determine the cause of the fire.
The 13 warehouse employees displaced by the fire were also transferred to another area, where they will stay temporarily.

articles.title: Ligutan tells defense: Post not for you, but for law students, public
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Counsel for the prosecution Amando Virgil Ligutan has countered the defense panel’s criticism of his Facebook post about misleading questions not being allowed even during…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Counsel for the prosecution Amando Virgil Ligutan has countered the defense panel’s criticism of his Facebook post about misleading questions not being allowed even during cross-examination, noting that the statement was not issued for them, but for law students and the general public.

In his counter-manifestation on Wednesday, at the start of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Ligutan said nothing in his post was personal, noting that he intended to clarify to the public that misleading questions are not allowed.

Last August 12, Ligutan made a post stating that a “principle all lawyers and law students know by heart” is that “misleading questions are not allowed even on cross-examination” — which led counsel for the defense Sheila Sison to claim was an attack on counsel for respondent Kristine Ferrer — particularly the exchange between Ferrer and private prosecutor Atty. Lorna Kapunan.

“To the defense, the post is not about you. It is not personal. It is about the law that we all adhere to. It is about what we teach the public who are watching our trial. Correcting a mistake is never wrong. Doing it while a hearing is ongoing, online, does not make it wrong,” Ligutan said.
“Ang pagtatama ng mali ay hindi kailanman ipinagbabawal. Kahit sa loob ng impeachment court na ito (Correcting any mistake is never prohibited. Even inside of this impeachment court),” he added.
LINK TO POST: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/19JKzuzt2a/

Ligutan also reminded the defense and the Senate Impeachment Court that, beyond being a lawyer, he is a teacher—a law professor—and he cannot help but correct wrong perceptions being floated on social media.
According to the lawyer, his instincts as a teacher kicked in amid questions on whether misleading questions were really applied.

“But more than just a lawyer, first and foremost I am a teacher. Isa po akong guro and I am proud to be one […] At alam ng ating mga magigiting na guro sa buong kapuluan na ang pagtuturo ay likas sa atin. Ang pagtuturo, ang pagtatama ng mali, ay walang pinipiling lugar, at walang pinipiling panahon. That’s why I made that post,” Ligutan said.

(But more than just a lawyer, first and foremost I am a teacher. I am a teacher, and I am proud to be one […] And our honorable teachers across the archipelago know that teaching is second nature to us. Teaching and correcting mistakes don’t pick an area or a time. That’s why I made that post.)

“I was concerned that the statement made in open court — that misleading questions are allowed — will go unchecked. My teacher’s instinct kicked in. I wanted the students I left in Cebu and in Diliman, and all law students out there, to know that a teacher had heard that wrong statement in open court, and he is correcting that mistake on Facebook, as I have been doing the past years,” he added.

In a tense moment during the cross-examination of state auditor Xylene Mae del Campo, Kapunan strongly objected to Ferrer’s habit of cutting the witness off before she is even able to provide an answer to the questions, and insisting that questions be answered by yes or no only.
Ferrer asked that she be allowed to conduct the cross-examination in her own manner, but Kapunan noted that some questions are not simply answerable by yes or no.
Later, Kapunan said that “misleading questions are not allowed,” to which Ferrer responded by saying that “it is allowed.”

But Sison said that Ferrer’s “it is allowed” quip was not a reply to Kapunan’s “misleading questions are not allowed” even on cross-examination statement — making Ligutan’s social media post as something done in “bad faith.”

But several members of the prosecution team stood by Ligutan, like Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon, who told Sison not to gaslight the country, as the transcripts would show that Ferrer really was responding to Kapunan and to her insistence that misleading questions are not allowed.

After Sison’s manifestation, Presiding Officer and Senator-judge Francis Escudero warned both the defense and the prosecution after both were observed making social media posts in relation to the proceedings.

“The presiding officer is already in the process of drafting a ruling and a warning and an order pertaining to this. Because clearly, I can even name all of you who’ve been commenting on social media in violation of Rule 18 of the impeachment rules,” he announced.

In response, lead public prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said in an interview with INQUIRER that the prosecution has been following the rules — that they have been very mindful not to go over the prohibition, and that their interpretation is that as long as they do not touch on the merits of the case, they can speak about these matters.
Luistro also stressed that Rule 18 of the Senate’s Rules of Impeachment applies not only to the prosecution and the defense lawyers, but also to Duterte and even senator-judges. /mr

articles.title: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?
articles.summary: Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran’s nuclear program and its standoff with the United States…

blocks.text: Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran’s nuclear program and its standoff with the United States continue.
Iranian MP Ghasem Ravanbakhsh said a proposal to withdraw from the landmark treaty had been submitted and was being considered.
Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said a withdrawal would be the “best response” to increased US economic pressure.

The idea is not new. Iranian officials and lawmakers have repeatedly raised it during periods of tension with Western governments. However, it remains unclear whether Tehran is actually preparing to leave the treaty or whether the threat itself is the objective.
What would leaving the nuclear treaty mean?
In 1970, Iran ratified the agreement, which is the main international treaty on nuclear non-proliferation.

blocks.caption: Iran has been repeatedly accused of having hidden its nuclear programImage: Planet Labs PBC/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: The NPT has 191 member states and is based on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursuing nuclear disarmament.
Any member can withdraw if it believes that extraordinary events related to the treaty have put its supreme national interests at risk.
It must give three months’ notice to the other members and the UN Security Council and explain its reasons. Leaving the treaty is therefore legally possible.
Behrooz Bayat, a nuclear expert and former consultant to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), told DW that the process would take time.
“A withdrawal would almost certainly be seen internationally as a signal that Iran intends either to keep open the option of developing nuclear weapons or to move toward doing so,” Bayat said.
He said such a perception could sharply increase political and economic pressure and potentially raise the risk of further military action.
For that reason, Bayat believes Tehran’s repeated threats are more useful as diplomatic leverage than as a policy it actually intends to pursue.
Why withdrawal may not benefit Tehran

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst and researcher at LUISS University in Rome, told DW that the renewed debate should be seen in the context of stalled negotiations over uranium enrichment and Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
Iran has about 440 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%, according to the IAEA.
Inspectors from the UN’s nuclear watchdog were unable to verify the location of much of the material after the June 2025 US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities.

blocks.caption: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?

blocks.text: Iran has already sharply reduced international oversight. In July 2025, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian signed legislation to suspend access for IAEA inspectors into the country until the “security” of its nuclear facilities is guaranteed.
That created what Modarres describes as a potentially more useful position for Tehran than formally withdrawing from the treaty.
“Withdrawal would remove that ambiguity without offering any clear advantage, turning a dispute over compliance into an explicit declaration of intent,” the analyst said.

“By remaining formally within the NPT while limiting inspections, Iran can maintain uncertainty about its capabilities and intentions without openly leaving the global non-proliferation system,” he added. “Withdrawing would remove much of that uncertainty.”
A countdown could increase military risk

Withdrawal could also have security implications for Tehran. Under Article X of the treaty, states must give three months’ notice before withdrawing. That period would give Israel, the United States and other governments time to reassess Iran’s intentions.

Some analysts argue that governments already concerned about Iran’s stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium could interpret a withdrawal as a sign that Tehran was moving closer to a nuclear weapons capability.
Bayat said that makes actual withdrawal considerably less attractive than threatening to do so. He added that leaving the treaty could also “complicate Iran’s civilian nuclear cooperation.”

Membership in the treaty “provides the broader legal and political framework through which non-nuclear states gain access to peaceful nuclear technology,” he said. “Russia remains involved in Iran’s civilian nuclear sector, particularly at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.”
“Formally withdrawing from the treaty could make future cooperation much more difficult politically and legally, even though existing agreements would need to be assessed separately,” added Bayat.
Opposition inside Iran

There is no clear consensus in Iran. Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based analyst who has written extensively about Iran’s nuclear program, told DW that withdrawing from the treaty has been discussed repeatedly but has never become government policy.

“The issue of leaving the NPT is not new and has been raised many times before,” he said. “But right now, there are significant legal and political obstacles, and there is still no full consensus within Iran.”
Ghahremanpour said the international community would closely examine any attempt to invoke Article X. He points to the ongoing legal debate over North Korea’s withdrawal as an example.

North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003. Although Pyongyang is generally treated internationally as no longer being a party to the treaty, some UN documents note that its formal status remains uncertain.
The treaty itself, however, does not require UN Security Council approval for withdrawal. It requires only that states notify the council.
For Ghahremanpour, the political message is more important than the legal process.
He believes talk of leaving the NPT is mainly aimed at pressuring Washington, and particularly European governments, to make concessions. /dl
