articles.title: Dolly Parton’s greatest songs, philanthropic works
articles.summary: Dolly Parton was more than a musician, actor, author, philanthropist, or theme-park entrepreneur. Parton, who died Tuesday at age 80, occupied a space in our global cultural imagination — a figure of…

blocks.text: Dolly Parton was more than a musician, actor, author, philanthropist, or theme-park entrepreneur. Parton, who died Tuesday at age 80, occupied a space in our global cultural imagination — a figure of American mythology, someone best described as larger-than-life and then a little bit more. But from the very beginning, at the heart of everything she accomplished, she was a songwriter.

Selecting 11 songs across her many decades of recorded music is a fool’s errand, but there are some classics that stand above others. Here are a few across her discography — from country songs that challenge traditional gender dynamics to the greatest ballad ever committed to record.
1968: “Just Because I’m a Woman”

Parton was long celebrated for the feminist themes throughout her music. That progressive sociopolitical stance is evident from the beginning of her career, which overlapped with the emergence of the women’s liberation movement. On the country classic “Just Because I’m a Woman,” Parton’s protagonist reminds her partner he need not judge her for having previous sexual partners — after all, he’s had some, too. “My mistakes are no worse than yours,” she sings, “Just because I’m a woman.” She said the song was inspired by a conversation with her late husband, Carl Dean, who asked her if she’d been with any men before they met.
1971: “Coat of Many Colors”

The quintessential example of Parton the raconteur is “Coat of Many Colors.” It’s an autobiographical tale about her mother, who made a coat for Parton out of rags. She was mocked by other kids but understood its value. “Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be,” she sings, “In my coat of many colors my momma made for me.”
1973: “Jolene”

It is not only one of Parton’s best-known hits, but also one of the best-known country music songs of all time. “Jolene” was inspired by Dean; Parton told NPR in 2008 that she wrote the song about a flirty bank teller who seemed to take an interest in him.

“She got this terrible crush on my husband,” she said. “And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us — when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So, it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one.”
1974: “I Will Always Love You”

The second single from Parton’s 13th studio album, “I Will Always Love You” is most known for its rendition by Whitney Houston. But the Parton original was written for Porter Wagoner ahead of her departure from “The Porter Wagoner Show.” (She left in 1974, having collaborated with him since 1967.) There have been several versions, but none as resonant as Houston’s, recorded in 1992 for the soundtrack to “The Bodyguard.” The song topped the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for a then-record-breaking 14 weeks.
1977: “Here You Come Again”

Parton wrote an overwhelming number of her hits, which makes “Here You Come Again” an interesting outlier. It was penned by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, first recorded by B.J. Thomas and originally conceived with the idea that Brenda Lee would record it. The song made its way to Parton and became a tentpole pop crossover hit for the country artist. But make no mistake — Parton made sure the steel guitar was heard loud and proud.

Enter Parton, the Hollywood star. It begins with the sound of a typewriter. (That clacking sound? Parton originally conceived of it by striking her long acrylic nails together.) The ebullient “9 to 5” was written for the 1980 film of the same name, which starred Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Parton in her acting debut. The song also appears on her album “9 to 5 and Odd Jobs.” Lyrically, it celebrates women in the workplace and serves as a battle cry for pay equity; it earned Parton her first Oscar nomination.
1983: “Islands in the Stream,” with Kenny Rogers

By the 1980s, Parton had fashioned herself as a mainstream celebrity. On “Islands in the Stream” with Kenny Rogers, her clarion soprano makes for perfect harmonies. That shouldn’t come as any surprise, but perhaps this will: The song was written by the Bee Gees. Barry Gibb maintained it was meant for Diana Ross, while Robin Gibb said it was meant for Marvin Gaye. Whatever the case, it got to Parton and Rogers, and the rest is history. It’s also a reminder of how R&B and country music are inextricably linked.

blocks.caption: Dolly Parton, left, and Kenny Rogers rehearse a song for their appearance on the TV show “Live… And in Person” in Los Angeles on Sept. 27, 1983. (AP Photo/Doug Pizac, File)

blocks.text: 1989: “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That”

Before this triumphant return to capital-C country music, there was a deeper detour into ’80s drum machine-heavy pop. (If there’s a single Parton album to consider skipping, it is 1987’s “Rainbow.”) But what came after, 1989’s “White Limozeen,” should be celebrated for “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That,” with its steel guitar, banjo, mandolins, Pedabro and a fierce fiddle courtesy of Ricky Skaggs — all while Parton playfully objectifies a man with a cheeky wink.
1999: “The Grass Is Blue”

“I’ve had to think up a way to survive,” Parton opens the title track to her 1999 album “The Grass Is Blue.” She said she wrote the bluegrass ballad in 30 minutes, during a lunch break while filming “Blue Valley Songbird,” a made-for-television musical drama about a woman who tries to leave an abusive partner. It features her scratch vocals — a demo meant to serve as a blueprint for the final recording — providing an additional rawness to a song of impossible pain. “And the sky is green / and the grass is blue,” she sings. “And I don’t love you.”
2001: “Little Sparrow”

If there is anything resembling a dip in Parton’s overwhelming popularity, it arrived in the ’90s, when country listeners instead embraced the glossy pop-country of Shania Twain and LeAnn Rimes. A pivot arrived at the end of that decade and into the one that followed, when Parton endeavored to make roots albums — pulling from bluegrass, country, gospel and Appalachian folk — that reinvigorated her music career. The heartbreaking a cappella harmonies of the title track on her 2001 album “Little Sparrow,” released one year after the death of her father and dedicated to him, are further evidence of her greatness. Parton’s is a voice that knows no bounds. But to remind people of that fact? Sometimes it takes going back home.
2014: “Blue Smoke”

No one writes place like Parton. On “Blue Smoke,” with its youthful choo-choo spirit, Parton brings the listener into her childhood home in the Blue Ridge Mountains, gorgeous, desolate and nostalgic. “Blue Smoke climbin’ up the mountain, Blue Smoke windin’ ’round the bend / Blue Smoke is the name of the heartbreak train that I am ridin’ in,” she sings. “I left a note, I wrote, ‘I’m leaving and I won’t be coming back’ / Blue Smoke rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling down the track.”
Philanthropic works

Beyond her music and entertainment career, Parton has built a lasting philanthropic legacy, particularly in education and literacy. In 1988, she established the Dollywood Foundation, initially focusing on scholarships for students in her hometown of Sevier County, Tennessee.

Her best-known initiative, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, was launched in 1995 as a way to encourage children to develop a love for reading. Inspired in part by her father, who could not read or write, the program began by sending free, age-appropriate books to young children in her hometown before expanding across the United States and other countries.

The program has since grown into a global literacy effort, with more than 270 million books mailed to children as of 2026. Its reach has made Parton synonymous with childhood literacy, earning her the affectionate nickname “The Book Lady.”

Parton’s charitable work has also extended to communities affected by disasters. Following the 2016 wildfires in Sevier County, Tennessee, which destroyed thousands of structures and killed 14 people, Parton and the Dollywood Foundation established the My People Fund. The initiative provided $1,000 a month for six months to families whose homes were damaged or rendered uninhabitable. It ultimately raised more than $9 million for wildfire survivors, while a subsequent partnership with the Mountain Tough Recovery Team provided an additional $3 million for longer-term recovery.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for research into the coronavirus. Her contribution supported research that became part of the work that led to Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccine, making her one of the notable entertainment figures whose philanthropy helped advance vaccine research.

She also made major donations to pediatric infectious disease research. In early 2026, the East Tennessee Children’s Hospital announced it was naming its campus the Dolly Parton Children’s Hospital in honor of her ongoing support.

Her commitment to disaster relief continued in 2024 after Hurricane Helene devastated parts of the southeastern United States, including East Tennessee and western North Carolina. Parton pledged $1 million of her own money to the Mountain Ways Foundation, with her East Tennessee businesses, including Dollywood, matching the contribution and bringing the total from her side to $2 million.

Her philanthropy has earned major recognition, including the Library of Congress’ David M. Rubenstein Prize for her work through the Imagination Library. In 2022, she also received the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy, which recognized her contributions to education, poverty alleviation and medical research, among other causes.
Following her passing, her family requested that in lieu of flowers, fans send donations to continue supporting Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library./ra

articles.title: Sara Duterte: Prosecution is resorting to 'theatrics, insults'
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday blasted the prosecution in her impeachment trial for allegedly using “theatrics” and “insults.” She said that doing these…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday blasted the prosecution in her impeachment trial for allegedly using “theatrics” and “insults.”
She said that doing these actions is a sign of “feigning confidence” in presenting what she says is a weak case.
Duterte made the pronouncement as her trial before the Senate impeachment court entered its 19th day.
“They should not be fishing for evidence during the trial or desperately try to turn something they wish to be true into a wild story of alleged wrongdoing,” said Duterte in a statement.
“A strong case does not need the adornment of theatrics,” she noted.
“A Senator calling a witness ‘stupid,’ a lawyer calling me the ‘mastermind of a scam’ or another witness referring to me as a ‘brat,’ does not prove a case, nor does it produce evidence,” she added.
According to Duterte, resorting to such insults does nothing but reveal the need to “feign confidence in the face of a weak presentation.”
Meanwhile, the vice president then alluded to the flood problem in the country, including the flood control scandal—accusing the administration of preparing to divide the 2027 budget.
“Lubog na ang bansa sa baha at kahirapan, pero tila walang mananagot, dahil ang impeachment, ang paghati-hatian ang 2027 budget,” Duterte said.
(The country is already inundated with floods and poverty, but it seems no one is taking responsibility, because the impeachment, will divide the 2027 budget.)
“At ang paghahanda kung papaano baliin ang Constitution para manatili sa puwesto ang prayoridad ng administrasyon at lahat ng kaalyado nito,” she added.
(And preparing how to break the Constitution to stay in office is the priority of the administration and all its allies.)
Duterte is currently facing the Senate impeachment court through her lawyers on allegations of misusing confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery and grave threats. /apl

articles.title: Keeping flu protection within reach: Watsons makes vaccination more accessible to Filipinos
articles.summary: With frequent rain and the rainy season, many Filipinos are finding themselves moving between rainy streets, air-conditioned spaces, and crowded areas as they go about their daily routines. While flu…

blocks.text: With frequent rain and the rainy season, many Filipinos are finding themselves moving between rainy streets, air-conditioned spaces, and crowded areas as they go about their daily routines. While flu remains a year-round health concern, the rainy season serves as a timely reminder to pay closer attention to respiratory health and the preventive steps that can help protect ourselves and our loved ones.

Flu can begin with symptoms that may seem simple or familiar, such as fever, cough, colds, sore throat, headache, or body aches. Most people recover without serious complications, but some may be more vulnerable to severe illness, including older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with certain underlying health conditions. Staying informed and taking preventive measures, including flu vaccination, can therefore be an important part of maintaining good health.

For many Filipinos, however, knowing what to do is only part of the challenge. Busy work schedules, school activities, family responsibilities, and everyday errands can make it easy to put preventive healthcare on hold, especially when getting vaccinated means making a separate trip to a healthcare facility.

Watsons is helping make vaccination more accessible by bringing these services closer to where Filipinos already live, work, and shop. Vaccination services are available at more than 300 Watsons stores nationwide, many of which are located in SM Malls. Of these, 22 vaccination hubs offer daily services, giving individuals and families greater flexibility and more opportunities to make preventive care part of their regular routines, at a time that works for them.

More than 85,000 patients have already received vaccinations through Watsons, reflecting the growing demand for accessible preventive healthcare. Among the vaccines offered, flu vaccines remain the most in demand, followed by HPV, pneumonia, shingles, and pertussis vaccines.

“We understand that with busy schedules, preventive care can sometimes be put off, so we continue to make vaccination services more accessible through our stores. With flu vaccines among the most in-demand vaccines, and as the rainy season continues, we hope to give more Filipinos the flexibility to get vaccinated as part of their everyday routines and take an important step toward protecting themselves and their loved ones,” said Danilo S. Chiong, Managing Director of Watsons.

Beyond vaccination, simple everyday practices such as washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes, and staying home when feeling unwell can also help reduce the spread of respiratory illnesses. Those experiencing severe, persistent, or worsening symptoms should seek appropriate medical advice.

Whether you’re heading to work, bringing the kids to school, or simply doing your weekly errands, staying protected against the flu can be one simple step toward keeping yourself and your loved ones healthy.
For the latest updates on vaccination schedules and participating stores, customers can also follow Watsons Philippines on social media or visit the Watsons website.

articles.title: PH urged to push Asean action vs harmful social media content
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Internet security watchdog Scam Watch Pilipinas urged the Philippine government to push the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to take joint action against harmful…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Internet security watchdog Scam Watch Pilipinas urged the Philippine government to push the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to take joint action against harmful content on social media.

“For too long, countries like the Philippines have been dealing with the world’s biggest technology companies individually,” Scam Watch Pilipinas lead convenor Jocel de Guzman said in a statement on Wednesday.

“When we ask platforms to act on harmful content, scam advertisements, fake accounts or other digital threats, cooperation often depends on the willingness of the platform because our jurisdiction and enforcement reach are limited,” he added.
He cited that the Philippines currently chairs the Asean.

On Tuesday, Sen. Erwin Tulfo slammed social media companies for allowing the spread of content from the fatal school shootings in Tacloban City last June 22 and in Zamboanga City last August 18 despite the sites’ existing community standards.
The Tacloban shooting was perpetrated by two teenagers and left three students dead, while the Zamboanga shooting was perpetrated by a lone teenager and left him and another schoolmate dead.
The latter incident had been livestreamed by the gunman on his Facebook account and on another livestreaming platform, the footage of which has since circulated online.

Meanwhile, in Thailand last August 7, after reportedly being exposed to violent content and learning to use a gun on social media, another teenage gunman had opened fire inside a school and killed himself and six other people.
“Big Tech operates across borders… harmful content spreads across borders. Regulation cannot remain trapped within national borders,” de Guzman stressed.
“If Big Tech wants access to nearly 700 million Asean consumers, accountability to those same consumers cannot be optional,” he added.
The Scam Watch Pilipinas lead convenor also responded to calls by government officials to implement a ban on social media for minor users in the wake of the shootings.
“Blocking should not be our default answer,” he said.
“The better solution is to strengthen the ability of governments to regulate these companies, compel cooperation and hold them accountable when they repeatedly fail to act,” he added.

At the Asean Chiefs of Police (Aseanapol) conference last July, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said it was considering a recommendation for the country to adopt a measure similar to Australia’s social media ban for users aged 16 and younger.
Following the Zamboanga shooting, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center said it was also considering recommending a ban on Facebook in the country.
On Tuesday, Malacañang said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. was open to recommendations to ban social media platforms that could influence young people to engage in harmful behavior. /dl

articles.title: Who is Kristine Ferrer, one of Sara Duterte's counsels?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Kristine Ferrer serves as one of defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte as she faces the Senate impeachment court on allegations of misusing confidential funds,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Kristine Ferrer serves as one of defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte as she faces the Senate impeachment court on allegations of misusing confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery and grave threats.
Ferrer, like several other members of the defense such as lead counsel Sheila Sison, is a partner lawyer of the Fortun, Narvasa and Salazar (FNS) Law Firm.

Since the trial began, Ferrer has so far led the defense’s cross-examination on two of the prosecution’s witnesses, particularly state auditor Xylene Mae del Campo and Office of the Vice President assistant chief-of-staff Lemuel Ortonio, as the court tackles Article I or Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds..
She is so far most known in the context of the trial for taking on private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan, known as a giant in the field of law, in one of its proceedings.
According to the FNS website, Ferrer earned her degree in Bachelor in Accountancy at the Ateneo de Davao University and was admitted to the Bar in 2011.

In 2009, her team during her law school years emerged as champion in the First National Debate on International Humanitarian Law, where she was awarded Best Debater of the Tournament. She was also a finalist in the first season of the ANC’s CVC (Villaraza Cruz Marcelo and Angangco firm) Law Debates in 2008.
She is also certified negotiator, as she has obtained her Certification in Negotiation Mastery from Harvard Business School Online.
Ferrer now has around 15 years of legal practice as a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) Lawyer, first beginning her career as a tax lawyer at Sycip Gorres Velayo & Co., before joining the firm.
Her practice areas revolve mostly around arbitration corporate and commercial practice and corporate rehabilitation, litigation and dispute resolution, as well as taxation.
The FNS also said that the lawyer possesses “extensive experience” in handling matters before the Bureau of Internal Revenue BIR) and the Court of Tax Appeals.

Listed as one of her notable achievements was leading the team that facilitated what was widely regarded as the largest tax compromise settlement in the country, the P25 billion tax compromise settlement between Mighty Corporation and the BIR.

The FNS also regards Ferrer as an “outstanding litigator who has successfully represented clients in civil, criminal, commercial, and intra-corporate disputes, including those regarded as high-profile cases.”
Apart from being a lawyer, Ferrer serves as a lecturer in Taxation Law and Special Proceedings at the Ateneo de Davao University College of Law. /mr/dp

articles.title: Dizon: Flood mitigation structures master plans not yet complete
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon on Wednesday said various master plans for flood mitigation structures across the country are not yet complete, citing climate…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon on Wednesday said various master plans for flood mitigation structures across the country are not yet complete, citing climate change concerns and a lack of plans in some areas.
Dizon shared this update during the House Committee on Appropriations’ briefing on his agency’s proposed 2027 budget.
“Hindi pa po kompleto ang ating master plans nationwide,” Dizon said, noting that many river basin master plans across the country are either outdated already or not yet finished.
(Our master plans nationwide are not yet complete.)
He said that the agency can’t just utilize old master plans or studies from several years ago, as he pointed out the effects of climate change.

“Alam naman po natin given what we have seen with climate change, the updating of master plan is critical because they have a direct impact on the engineering design of the infrastructures that need to be built,” Dizon added.

(We know that given what we have seen with climate change, the updating of the master plan is critical because they have a direct impact on the engineering design of the infrastructures that need to be built.)

He also shared that there is no master plan for the National Capital Region yet, except in some areas such as Quezon City, Pasig City, Marikina City, and Manila City. He noted that many master plans being formed are being patterned with Quezon City’s drainage master plan.

He then emphasized the importance of coordination among the agencies and regional, provincial, and local authorities to ensure that projects worth millions or billions of pesos are properly accounted for.

“Kaya pumapasok yung requirement yung regional development councils, provincial development council, local development council or at the very least, certificate of no objection from the LGUs [local government units] para coordinate ang mga proyekto ng DPWH sa ating regional, provincial, local authorities,” he said.

(This is why the requirement of regional development councils, provincial development council, local development council, or at the very least, a certificate of no objection from the LGUs [local government units] comes into the picture to coordinate the projects of DPWH with our regional, provincial, local authorities.)
No national plan for flood mitigation

In the same hearing, Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno asked Dizon if the agency still has no national master plan for flood mitigation. Dizon answered in the affirmative, citing the agency’s strategy.
Dizon noted that while it has no national flood control master plan, it has master plans per river basin and urban center.

“Apparently when I asked the same question, ito raw yung recommendation ng ating foreign partners to do it per major river basin and also on per urban center basis especially for drainage master plan,” Dizon answered.

(Apparently, when I asked the same question, this was the recommendation of our foreign partners to do it per major river basin and also on a per urban center basis, especially for a drainage master plan.)

Diokno also asked Dizon if the executive department is abandoning the idea of coming up with a national flood control master plan. While Dizon said that he thinks the plan is not being neglected, he noted that there are general principles applicable nationwide that are “standard to all the other river basin master plans.”

He said that such general principles include focusing on retarding basins rather than simply putting up dikes, focusing on needs-based approaches, and focusing on upstream intervention rather than downstream interventions.

The secretary also shared that of all the 18 major river basin master plans across the country, 14 are being updated. He said that the agency asked its consultants to complete the updates by the first half of 2027.

The agency noted that of the 18 master plans of major river basins, seven are located in Luzon, three in the Visayas, and eight in Mindanao. It underscored that the Japan International Cooperation Agency said master plans must be updated within five years, while the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development advised updating them within three years due to the effects of climate change.
Dizon then expressed support for the proposed Master Plan on Infrastructure and National Development Act. /mr /jpv

articles.title: Duterte Impeachment Trial: Who is Prosecution Counsel Amando Virgil Ligutan?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Amando Virgil Ligutan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Since the trial began,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Amando Virgil Ligutan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Since the trial began, Ligutan has conducted the prosecution’s direct examination of National Bureau of Investigation Regional Director Jeremy Lotoc and Gina Acosta, a former special disbursing officer of the Office of the Vice President who testified as a hostile witness.
The Cebuano lawyer is not afraid to use his native language during trial, even at times translating for Acosta when the latter said she found some Tagalog words quite deep.
Ligutan is the managing partner of SALiGAL Law (Sapayan Lim Alvarez & Ligutan Law Offices) in Cebu.

He is also actively teaching Labor Law, Remedial Law, and Public International Law as a lecturer and law instructor in University of the Philippines, University of San Jose-Recoletos School of Law, and University of Cebu School of Law.
Ligutan was valedictorian when he graduated High School from Sacred Heart Seminary in Palo Leyte in 1999.
Four years later, he completed his undergraduate degree in AB Philosophy from University of San Carlos in Cebu, and was awarded Summa Cum Laude.
He then pursued Law in University of the Philippines Diliman and graduated in 2009.
Among his expertise are civil and criminal litigation, political and administrative law, and public interest cases.
He also has expertise in labor relations law, risk and crisis management, and local government and election law.

This Wednesday, Aug. 26, Ligutan is set to explain his Facebook post, which read, “A principle all lawyers and law students know by heart: Misleading questions are not allowed even on cross-examination.”

The post became a point of concern when defense lead counsel Sheila Sison raised to the impeachment court that the post was seemingly referring to a statement made by defense counsel Kristine Ferrer during her cross-examination of state auditor Xylene del Campo.

articles.title: Mirra Andreeva and her 'crush' Rublev win in US Open mixed doubles
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Mirra Andreeva revealed a secret Tuesday after she and Andrey Rublev ended the reign of the two-time US Open mixed doubles champions. She used to have a crush on her partner. “I’ve never…

blocks.text: Mirra Andreeva, of Russia, and Andrey Rublev, of Russia, react after winning a mixed doubles match at the U.S. Open tennis championships, Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
NEW YORK — Mirra Andreeva revealed a secret Tuesday after she and Andrey Rublev ended the reign of the two-time US Open mixed doubles champions.
She used to have a crush on her partner.
“I’ve never said anything, I’ve never told him anything as well, but I used to have a little crush on him as well,” Andreeva said during an interview on the court.
That’s just adorable 🤗 pic.twitter.com/R3bunVJUzj — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026

The French Open champion added that it was “like a dream come true to play with my favorite” before being unable to finish that sentence when Rublev interrupted to give her a hug as the crowd cheered.

The crush is over — the 19-year-old Andreeva said it was when she was 15 or 16 — but their tournament goes on. The Russians will play Wednesday night in the semifinals against Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik.
They began the event by outlasting Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori 1-4, 4-1 (11-9), then emerged from another match tiebreaker to edge Diana Shnaider and Casper Ruud for their semifinal spot.
Rublev, 28, is perhaps most recognizable for his red hair and his occasional outbursts on the court. Andreeva definitely noticed his appearance, but thought he was kind despite the tirades.
“I mean, first of all, his hair, OK?” she responded when asked why she was drawn to him.
What. A. Finish 💥 Andreeva and Rublev stare down match point before dethroning Errani/Vavassori! pic.twitter.com/gYta8R0N8L — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026

“So many interviews I saw and so many things that I heard from other people, I just knew he’s a great person. I didn’t know him at that time yet. I don’t know, I just feel like he’s super kind, very nice with everyone. Again, the hair. I don’t know, everyone said that every time he would step on court, he would look tired. I don’t know, he was looking great every time for me.”
Rublev’s response to Andreeva’s revelation?

“You know this typical moments when the kids, they don’t have taste yet, they need to try some stupid things before they start to have it?” Rublev said. “I was in the part of stupid thing, in the transition moment.”
Rublev has reached 10 Grand Slam quarterfinals, including four at the US Open, in singles. Now he’s in the semifinals at a major.
“We see how Mirra affects me,” he said.

articles.title: From Strategy to Execution: Powering Central Luzon’s AI future through regional digital transformation
articles.summary: The Department of Science and Technology Regional Office No. III (DOST-III / DOST-CL) and WPH Digital, a Singapore-based AI and digital innovation company, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding…

blocks.text: The Department of Science and Technology Regional Office No. III (DOST-III / DOST-CL) and WPH Digital, a Singapore-based AI and digital innovation company, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to accelerate regional digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption across Central Luzon.

The collaboration brings the Philippines’ National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS-PH) closer to regional implementation by combining DOST-III’s public-sector mandate with WPH Digital’s expertise in AI, digital transformation, and practical technology implementation.

The agreement was formally signed by Dr. Julius Ceasar V. Sicat, Regional Director of DOST Central Luzon, and Mr. Vincent Leoh, Managing Director of WPH Digital, on 19 August 2026. Held at the opening of the joint program, the ceremony was witnessed by over 50 key delegates and industry leaders representing diverse business, technology, and public sectors from across Central Luzon.

“We believe AI adoption is not a technology challenge — it is a capability challenge,” said Mr. Vincent Leoh, Managing Director of WPH Digital. “Through WPH Academy, we help people build AI capabilities, and through WPH Digital, we help organisations apply those capabilities using practical AI solutions. When capability building and practical implementation come together, organisations start seeing real value from AI.”
Democratizing Generative AI Across Central Luzon

By bringing enterprise-grade digital expertise directly to Region III, the collaboration demonstrates how government and private-sector organisations can work together to democratize access to advanced Generative AI and cloud computing technologies beyond Metro Manila. The initiative positions Central Luzon as a key regional innovation hub, driving competitiveness across local micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), industries, and public sector operations.
Human Capital and Workforce Readiness First

At the heart of the partnership is a strong emphasis on talent reskilling, practical capability-building, and workforce development. Rather than viewing technology solely as a displacement risk, the collaboration equips local professionals and civil servants to use Generative AI as a productivity multiplier—fostering a resilient, highly competitive regional talent pool equipped for modern, future-ready workflows.

As an immediate step toward putting the partnership into action, DOST-III and WPH Digital conducted the Generative AI for Modern Business Operations workshop. The practical capacity-building session provided business leaders, IT professionals, and regional stakeholders with hands-on exposure to practical AI solutions, cloud-native platforms, and execution strategies designed to deliver practical business value.

Beyond training and capability-building, the collaboration is intended to help organisations translate these capabilities into actual implementation, enabling them to identify practical AI opportunities and develop solutions that can be applied within their operating environments.
International Cross-Border Tech Collaboration

The MOU highlights cross-border technology transfer between Singapore’s private sector and the Philippine government. By bringing Singaporean tech consulting expertise to Central Luzon, WPH Digital showcases how international private-sector solutions can actively contribute to regional development goals in organisations and communities across Southeast Asia.

“AI is already here, and it is becoming part of how businesses plan, create, communicate, and improve their operations,” said Dr. Julius Caesar V. Sicat, Regional Director of DOST Central Luzon. “This training is not just about learning AI — it is about empowering our MSMEs to confidently embrace change and turn technology into opportunities.”
Trusted AI with Certified Governance

The partnership also underscores the importance of responsible and governed AI adoption as organisations move from experimentation to implementation. WPH Digital brings AI governance expertise backed by the internationally recognised ISO/IEC 42001 standard, which provides a structured framework for responsible, secure, ethical, and governed AI adoption.
WPH Digital is one of the first AI and Digital Service Providers in Singapore to achieve ISO/IEC 42001 certification for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems, and is the first in the world

to achieve ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI systems in the oil and gas industry. This experience supports the company’s approach to helping organisations move beyond AI concepts and strategy toward practical, production-ready solutions.

By combining AI expertise, enterprise technology experience, cloud capabilities, and ISO/IEC 42001-based AI governance, WPH Digital brings an implementation-focused approach to AI adoption. Under the DOST-III partnership, this approach complements workforce training and technical capability-building, helping organisations explore how AI can be applied responsibly and effectively within their operating environments.
A Replicable Blueprint for Regional Action

The alliance establishes a repeatable model for regional government-industry partnerships throughout the Philippines. Moving beyond high-level strategy, DOST-III and WPH Digital provide a structured model for continuous technical implementation, capacity building, and enterprise enablement across provincial economies.

The longer-term ambition is for this model to extend from national government agencies to provincial and local government units (LGUs), and eventually across other regions of the Philippines. By connecting national AI priorities with regional capability-building and practical implementation, the collaboration has the potential to provide a scalable model for AI capabilities.
ADVT.
This article is brought to you by WPH Digital.

articles.title: Spouses Svitolina, Monfils reach US Open mixed doubles semis
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils have both gone far but never all the way to the US Open title. Maybe the married couple can finally win a trophy together. The spouses made quite a pair on…

blocks.text: Elina Svitolina, of Ukraine, left, and Gael Monfils, of France, kiss after winning a mixed doubles match at the U.S. Open tennis championships, Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
NEW YORK — Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils have both gone far but never all the way to the US Open title. Maybe the married couple can finally win a trophy together.
The spouses made quite a pair on the court Tuesday, becoming the first team into the mixed doubles semifinals by edging Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten 5-4 (6), 4-5 (3) (10-8).
Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz won their first-round match but were then ousted after a 5-4 (4), 4-1 loss to Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli.
“Happy wife, happy life.” Gael Monfils and Elina Svitolina are lifting each other up ❤️ pic.twitter.com/7c2NrmHyVq — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026

Svitolina and Monfils will face Bencic and Cobolli in one semifinal Wednesday, with Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev to meet Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik in the other. The winning team will earn $1 million.
That would be quite a payday for Monfils to share with his wife in his final Grand Slam tournament before retiring.
“Happy wife, happy life,” Monfils said in their postmatch interview after a kiss and hug on the court.
Williams and Alcaraz beat Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool 5-3, 4-1 in Williams’ first match at the U.S. Open since 2022.
“It’s always such an amazing place to be here,” Williams said. “I never expected to be back on this court, so it was just a really cool moment. I never thought this would happen.”

But the 44-year-old Williams, a 23-time Grand Slam singles champion, and the two-time U.S. Open champion Alcaraz appeared to run out of steam after dropping the first-set tiebreaker after quickly returning to the court for their second match.
New champions will be crowned and an old crush is revealed

Williams and Alcaraz began their opening match just as the two-time defending champions were eliminated. Andreeva and Rublev saved a match point and outlasted Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori 1-4, 4-1 (11-9). The 19-year-old Andreeva revealed afterward that she used to have a crush on her partner and fellow Russian, who is 28.
They then recovered after blowing four match points in the second set to beat Diana Shnaider and Casper Ruud 4-1, 4-5 (9) (10-5).
The US Open tinkered with the format of the tournament this year to allow more doubles specialists back in, but it was the singles players who had the upper hand.
Monfils, who will turn 40 on Sept. 1, reached the US Open semifinals in 2016. Svitolina, who is eight years younger, got to the final four in Flushing Meadows in 2019.
Chemistry 💯 Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils are the first pair into the mixed doubles semifinals! pic.twitter.com/haD8IMSepi — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026
Now it’s another semifinal — and an unlikely one — after they outlasted a team featuring the No.-1 ranked players in men’s and women’s doubles.

Monfils, who is from France, was given a wild card into the singles tournament. He and Svitolina, who is from Ukraine, were given wild cards to compete in mixed. They were married in 2021 and daughter Skaï was born the next year.
Because they were unsure at first they would be in the field in New York, Svitolina said they entered with no expectations, having not even worked on their tactics until Monday.
“I mean, we practice quite a lot together back at home or on the tournaments. Only yesterday we worked on few things for doubles,” Svitolina said.
“When we warmed up this morning, yeah, I told my coach it would be amazing if we can win just a few games.”
Czech duo has the look

Muchova and Mensik reached the semifinals with a 4-1, 5-3 victory over American pair Emma Navarro and Tommy Paul. Mensik texted Muchova on the eve of the tournament so they could coordinate outfits, and both wore pink tops and maroon bottoms.
“It’s definitely one of the most important things, to look good on the court, as well,” Mensik said.
Siniakova and Patten ousted Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic 1-4, 4-2 (10-2) in the first round. Siniakova ended the match with an ace while serving to Djokovic.

The tournament was overhauled last year in an effort to get more top singles players to compete. It was moved to a two-day event well before the singles main draw begins, with a scoring format that guarantees quick matches that shouldn’t tax the players too much.

The matches in the first three rounds feature sets to four games, with a tiebreaker at 4-all and a 10-point tiebreaker instead of a third set. Only the final will resemble a regular match, with traditional sets to six games.
“I will say if we play until basically regular rules, until six games, will be much more difficult,” Mensik said.

Sabalenka, the two-time defending U.S. Open women’s champion, and 24-time Grand Slam champion Djokovic are exactly the types of players the U.S. Tennis Association was seeking. They had the No. 1 seed based on the lowest combined singles ranking of any team, but their loss was far from an upset.

Doubles specialists such as Siniakova and Patten were shut out of the U.S. Open last year, when teams qualified directly based on the two players’ singles rankings, or were given wild cards by the USTA. Errani and Vavassori, who had won the title in 2024, were the only doubles players in the field after they were given a wild card to return, and went on to defend their title.
An eight-team qualifying tournament was added this year, giving two teams, composed mostly of regular doubles players, the chance to earn their way into the main draw.
Svitolina and Monfils routed Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime 4-1, 4-1 in their opening match. Muchova and Mensik edged Kristina Mladenovic and Marcelo Arevalo 4-1, 2-4 (10-7) in their opener.

articles.title: P129M abandoned cigarettes destroyed in Bulacan – BOC
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Around 3,000 cases of abandoned cigarettes, amounting to over P129 million, were destroyed from three containers in Santa Maria, Bulacan, according to the Bureau of Customs…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Around 3,000 cases of abandoned cigarettes, amounting to over P129 million, were destroyed from three containers in Santa Maria, Bulacan, according to the Bureau of Customs (BOC).

In its statement on Wednesday, the BOC said its Port of Subic disposed of the assorted-brand cigarettes through shredding and pyrolysis (melting through extreme heat) from July 28 to August 3 at its accredited disposal facility.
The bureau noted that it livestreamed the destruction process through the Port of Subic’s official YouTube account for the public to witness and “to ensure transparency and accountability.”
According to the BOC, the three 40-foot containers are part of the 10 identified containers of abandoned cigarettes with a total estimated value of P413 million that the bureau intends to dispose of.
The bureau said it is also in the process of disposing the contents of the remaining seven containers.
The ongoing destructions are still being livestreamed and conducted according to established disposal procedures, said the BOC.

articles.title: El Salvador, Panama sound alarm on El Niño-fueled drought
articles.summary: SAN SALVADOR — Panama on Tuesday became the latest Central American country, after Honduras and El Salvador, to declare an emergency over El Niño, which has already forced a reduction in…

blocks.text: SAN SALVADOR — Panama on Tuesday became the latest Central American country, after Honduras and El Salvador, to declare an emergency over El Niño, which has already forced a reduction in shipping through the Panama Canal.

Panama’s Interior Minister Dinoska Montalvo said the declaration will allow authorities “to be prepared for what may come with El Niño,” which has fueled a severe drought that is ravaging harvests and sparking fears of famine.
Meanwhile, El Salvador declared a state of maximum alert on Tuesday to activate monitoring, surveillance and aid efforts for affected communities.
“We are declaring a red alert for meteorological and farming drought across the national territory,” the Civil Protection department wrote on X.

El Niño is a weather pattern that raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, generating global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions.
It is also nudging up global temperatures in a year predicted to be the hottest on record.
El Niño occurs on average every two to seven years, but this year’s is shaping up as the most intense in recent years.

Central America is in the throes of a severe drought that has already prompted Honduras to place 80 percent of its territory on alert and caused the Panama Canal to cut shipping traffic because of its dwindling water levels.
In El Salvador, the lack of rain, which is usually abundant at this time of year, has wiped out crops.
The agriculture ministry has announced food assistance for rural families that do not have irrigation systems.
Several municipalities in El Salvador are located in the Central American Dry Corridor, an arid strip that also includes parts of Honduras and Nicaragua and is vulnerable to extreme weather events.
All three countries broke their monthly temperature records in both June and July, exacerbating famine concerns.
So far in August, 14 temperature records have been smashed in El Salvador.
Further south, Peru last week declared a state of emergency in a third of its cities over El Niño and said intense heat and rain could also cause havoc for food production. /dl

articles.title: Drought-hit Danube gives way to fossil hunt in Bulgaria
articles.summary: RYAHOVO, Bulgaria — Volunteers scanned the dried-up bank of the Danube in northern Bulgaria, close to where receding waters laid bare mammoth bones last month, hoping to find more fossilized…

blocks.text: RYAHOVO, Bulgaria — Volunteers scanned the dried-up bank of the Danube in northern Bulgaria, close to where receding waters laid bare mammoth bones last month, hoping to find more fossilized fragments exposed by Europe’s parching drought.
“I’ve found a tooth!” exclaimed Aleksandar Denkov, a 30-year-old amateur photographer, holding up a yellowish fragment protruding from the sand.

Denkov last week joined some 20 other volunteers, many hoping to find more mammoth fossils during the search organised by the regional history museum of the nearby city of Ruse, around 250 km (155 miles) northeast of Sofia.

Though their hopes were not fulfilled, the group found remains of a mammal — “probably an aurochs or a European bison,” according to the museum — a horse jawbone in a subfossil state and a cluster of fossilised oysters dating back around 60 to 65 million years.

Europe’s drought, exacerbated by human-induced climate change according to experts, has seen major rivers slow to a trickle, causing serious problems for cargo shippers and nuclear plants normally cooled by river water.
But the low waters have also revealed remains and historical artefacts not seen for decades — or even millennia.

Finds in recent weeks along the Danube, Europe’s second-longest river, have included World War II shipwrecks in Austria and Serbia and the remains of two German soldiers and a motorbike in the middle of Budapest.
‘Close to history’

Ruse Regional History Museum curator Krasimir Kirov said the museum decided to organize the field day “to teach people how to recognise different finds, show them what they might uncover, and give them safety tips.”
“After the mammoth was discovered, I started getting dozens of calls from people telling me about what they’d found,” he told AFP.

Last month, a resident of the village of Ryahovo — some 30 kilometers from Ruse — spotted by chance what museum specialists then identified as a mammoth jaw bone, fragments of tusks, part of a shoulder blade and a femur.
Announced on social media, the initiative to gather near Ryahovo for a guided search quickly sparked keen interest, with requests already pouring in for the next outing, according to Kirov.
The search began with a few instructions: the volunteers must advance in a line and, if someone spots something, raise a hand so that the whole group stops.
Above all, they must not touch any metal objects, which could be ammunition or explosives.
But the walk had barely begun when the line broke apart: enthusiasm won out over discipline.
“It’s a very rare opportunity to feel this close to history,” Ekaterina Yordanova, a 34-year-old psychologist, told AFP.
“Seeing the Danube in this state is worrying, but it also gives us the chance to discover new things.”
Vladimir Tsvyatkov, a 44-year-old business owner, said he, his wife and their two children mainly came “for the adventure”.
Having grown up on the banks of the river, he said he had “never seen the Danube so dried up.”
WWII remnants
Further upstream in Bulgaria, the low Danube levels have also allowed archaeologists to document the foundations of a bridge, more than two km long, inaugurated under Emperor Constantine I in 328.
And elsewhere along the Danube, World War II weaponry and other remnants have been found.
In central Austria, two wrecks of German warships are protruding from the water.
Damaged in fighting with American tanks in 1945, they were later sunk by their own crews, according to local media.

In Serbia, near Prahovo, the receding river has likewise exposed wrecks of German warships, which were among dozens sunk by their own side in 1944 in an attempt to slow the Soviet Red Army’s advance along Europe’s second-longest river.
And in Budapest, a motorbike and the remains of two German soldiers were found, according to the German War Graves Commission.

The findings come as vast tracts of many of Europe’s largest rivers have fallen to levels never recorded before in the month of July, according to data from European climate observatory Copernicus. /dl

articles.title: What went wrong with U.S. trade talks, according to Canada's chief negotiator
articles.byline: Benjamin Lopez Steven, Catherine Cullen, Derek Vanderwyk

image.caption: Janice Charette, Canada's chief trade negotiator to the United States, speaks at a Canadian Chamber of Commerce summit in Ottawa on April 21. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada's chief U.S. trade negotiator is disputing several claims made by American officials about why trade talks fell apart last week, namely that the Canadian side brought forward last-minute demands on autos and that U.S. negotiators weren't interested in French language discoverability rules.

"Canada has been resolute throughout these negotiations that we were talking about the entirety of our automotive sector," Janice Charette said in an exclusive interview with CBC's The House airing Saturday morning.

Charette's comments clash with those made by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who told reporters Thursday that the Canadians only brought up tariff relief on medium- and heavy-duty trucks at the last minute — and further alleged the Canadians did so to kill the deal.

"The words 'medium- and heavy-duty trucks’ were raised in these negotiations on Friday at 4 o'clock," Lutnick said. Those trucks include some models of Ford's F-series pickups and the General Motors Silverado, which are made at Ontario plants.
Charette refrained from calling Lutnick wrong, but said the Canadians raised the issue on "Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday."
Charette says Canada consistently raised auto industry in U.S. trade negotiations
"Howard Lutnick was not at the negotiating table," Charette told host Catherine Cullen.
She added that the Canadians were speaking with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, and it was very clear they were seeking tariff relief for those types of autos, among other sectors.

Both countries have been trading barbs over the past week about who — and what — ultimately killed a prospective trade deal that could have granted Canada tariff relief in key sectors such as autos, steel and aluminum, and lumber.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has maintained it was late U.S. demands that prompted him to call negotiators back to Ottawa, while Lutnick and Greer argue the Canadians are at fault.
Carney outlines the last-minute changes U.S. tacked onto trade deal terms
Asked whether she views the U.S. claims on what went wrong as dishonesty or merely a question of perspective, Charette chalked it up to differing opinions.

According to Charette, the Canadians were seeking an arrangement with "the lowest rate of tariffs on the narrowest basket of goods with the best market access — so the best deal overall, and the best trade deal for each of our key strategic sectors. That's what we were working towards."

items: Trump's top trade negotiator disputes Canadian assertion that U.S. made last-minute demands

blocks.text: The Canadian government understood that a U.S. trade deal would involve some degree of tariffs on its goods and tariff-free access on American products, Charette added.
"In no case has any country been able to secure an agreement unless they agreed that U.S. goods were going to enter into their market tariff-free," Charette said.
French discoverability, Canadian free trade deals

Carney has told reporters that at the last minute, the U.S. took issue with Canadian rules that ensure French language content is easy to find on streaming platforms such as Netflix, and that the Americans tried to restrict Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.
This week, both Greer and Lutnick pushed back on Canada's claims on French language discoverability, arguing the U.S. would not jeopardize a deal over that issue.

"If you think I ever said the word 'French' — do I care about how the Québécois speak? I mean, what could matter less to America? We don't care," Lutnick said Thursday, adding that Carney "manufactured" the issue to influence the provincial election in Quebec.

Charette pushed back on that version of events and said the Canadians were prepared to look at financial obligations imposed on streamers, but would never offer movement on measures to protect the French language.
"And it is also true that right up until the final negotiating session, Friday night, the Americans were still asking for us to remove those provisions," Charette said.

As for restrictions on Canada's future trade deals, Greer told CBC News earlier this week that there was no requirement in the text, but rather that the U.S. sought to discuss how Canada could align its tariffs so it doesn't become a backdoor for steel and aluminum from other countries.

What we know about how the Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart

blocks.text: Charette said the topic came up "quite late" in discussions, and it was unclear to the Canadians whether the Americans wanted a consultation on future free trade agreements, some kind of sign-off or a veto.

"But it was clear that there was an interest on the part of the United States in constraining or limiting Canada's ability to enter into future free trade agreements for important products like primary steel that would come into the Canadian market," she said.

A source has previously told CBC News that the U.S. wanted Canada to apply sectoral tariffs, primarily on steel and aluminum, to its trading partners, and countries that have a free trade deal with Canada would face tariffs on imports above 2025 levels.
Where does Canada go from here?
Charette said as it stands, Canada's "pens are down, but the door is open."
"We're prepared to go and work with the United States on a deal that would be in the economic interest of Canadians, as long as it doesn't impact Canadian sovereignty," she said.
As for whether Canada can trust the U.S. as negotiating partners, Charette said that remains to be seen.
"Trust is earned, and trust is earned through the fine print of a trade agreement that was under negotiation right up until those final moments in the night on Friday."
Canada won't accept U.S. attitude that we're a 'subsidiary,' Carney says

Greer has said there are no open channels right now, but he has a good relationship with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc. Meanwhile, Lutnick has claimed Canadian negotiators will kickstart talks again once the Quebec election and Alberta referendum are complete.

The Canadian government is bracing for a long fight. On Tuesday, it announced it will match U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods by tariffing $27.6 billion of comparable U.S. goods.

blocks.text: The Liberal government is also rolling out $7.5 billion to help workers and businesses weather the U.S. tariffs. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said that the federal government will continue its support for "as long as it takes."
Asked how she feels about where everything stands now, Charette said she's proud of the work the Canadian team did.
"We didn't leave anything, we put it all out on the field. There was no stone unturned, we did everything we thought we could," she said.
